Issues are grouped by cause rather than by row, with a good/warning/error breakdown, and each group links back to the review queue or exports a summary of the affected rows. Maturity: Active. Draft reader preview — an admin-only preview of how approved rows will read on your public entry surface, rendered by the same machinery the real import uses. Restructured fields are marked in the preview, including "keep both" companion fields. The preview publishes nothing. Maturity: Active. Saved setups and format recognition — a successful import creates or updates a saved setup. When you upload a familiar shape again, Step 2 shows "We've seen this format before" with a confidence figure, and every choice stays editable. Saved setups store structure, never your source rows. Maturity: Active. Decisions carried forward on re-import — when you re-import over already-imported data, decisions that are structurally unchanged from your prior import are carried forward instead of re-asked. Anything new, changed, or ambiguous goes back to review; uncertainty always routes to review, never to a silent carry-over. Maturity: Active. Two-step approval with risk levels — every suggestion gets a risk level (low, medium, or high) with visible reasons. A suggestion held for review goes through two steps: a reviewer approves first, then an administrator applies. When your autonomy setting lets a confident structural reading move ahead for you, the decision is system-mediated and the undo window applies; for audit-sensitive imports, ask your platform operator to check the auto-apply markers and status reason rather than relying only on a visible reviewer name. Suggestions refined by AI always go through human review; AI never changes your environment directly. If the risk level changed while a suggestion sat in review — because the environment changed around it — apply is blocked until you read and acknowledge the new level. Maturity: Active. Needs revision — a reviewer can send a suggestion back with a required note instead of rejecting it outright. The suggestion blocks the final import until it is revised, and the note travels with it. Maturity: Active. Restructure suggestions — the wizard can propose shape improvements it detects in your source: a lookup column becomes a picker field, a supporting table becomes the option list behind a picker, or sibling language columns merge into one multilingual field. You choose Keep both (the original field plus a typed companion field) or Replace. Approved restructures are carried through the final import. These suggestions never apply automatically, whatever their confidence. Maturity: Active. Honest receipts, with progress still being hardened — the final run records per-table outcomes and the completion receipt leads with what happened: record and connection counts, "references not linked yet" with a per-link breakdown, and an Open your workspace action. Every table in the plan produces exactly one outcome row — "created N records", or "will create 0 records" with the reason — predicted in the practice run and confirmed after the run. The linking pass can be much longer than the table-write steps; the wait/progress view is still being hardened for that long phase. Maturity: Active. Live cold-import proof — a 2026-06-29 browser walk ran a fresh Coda import through the wizard and completed the final import into the workspace: 10 workspace tables, 10,080 records, and 29,696 relationships. The receipt led to browsable workspace tables. Maturity: Built for that import class; keep using the practice run and receipt for each new source because source shape still matters. Resolve a "nothing will import" stop from inside the wizard — when the practice run finds that your approved choices would bring in zero rows, Step 5 names the situation ("Nothing will import yet") and offers only the action it can honestly deliver for that cause, rather than a dead end: fix the conflicting columns (it deep-links you back to Step 3), return to the review queue, or align/restructure the flagged columns. You never lose your work — there is no new upload and no re-run from scratch. Maturity: Active. Keep non-standard values as-is (import as text) — when the source checks flagged a column only for advisory reasons (its values don't match the type or script the wizard expected, which can be intentional), Step 5 offers Import these as-is (keep non-standard values). The column is brought in as text with its values stored exactly as they appear — nothing is coerced or dropped. A DRY RUN card previews the change before you commit: the flagged column moves from skipped to kept, a note states the values are kept as text, a Won't touch list bounds what stays unchanged, and a seal states "No source rows are written until you run the import." This is offered only for advisory flags; a structural problem (a duplicate key, a missing column) must be corrected and is never offered as keep-as-is. If you later undo the decision, it is fully reversed — a subsequent normal approval will not silently re-apply it. Maturity: Active. Limit: a transformation history of the kept column and in-place cell correction are planned, not yet present. Import assistant chat — a chat control on each wizard step that knows where you are in the flow. It can explain what it sees and propose actions, but a proposed action is never executed until you confirm it. Each import session has a chat budget; when the budget runs out the chat pauses and every import control keeps working. Your environment's AI settings can turn the assistant off. Maturity: Active. AI refinement is optional — when no AI provider is configured for your platform, the wizard still works end to end: the structural reading produces the suggestions, and the import is marked that AI refinement was unavailable. To enable AI refinement, contact your platform operator. Maturity: Active. Efficiency tips (Step 3) — short tip cards can appear alongside suggestion cards when tips are enabled for your environment. Tips never block an action. See Efficiency Tips. Maturity: Active. Import telemetry — when capture is enabled, import steps emit operational counts that carry no source content: no rows, filenames, document or table names, credentials, or tokens. See Telemetry. Maturity: Active. Limit: collection runs in the platform; a dedicated screen for browsing these metrics is not yet available.

Start in the sidebar at Imports & AI → Imports. Step 1 shows the source choices, your recent imports, and your saved setups. The All imports list offers the same upload routes as toolbar buttons. Submit the source that matches your shape — Excel, database, CSV files, or Coda. Within the inline size limit, the wizard reads the source immediately and opens the review. Above it, choose the background option and follow the status page; it links to the wizard when the job completes. Walk the six steps. Review what was found (Step 2), decide on suggestions and set how involved you want to be (Step 3), answer the clarifying questions (Step 4), and read the practice run (Step 5). Approve in two steps. A reviewer approves each suggestion, then an administrator applies it. If the risk level shifted while the suggestion waited, read the new level and acknowledge it before applying. Start the import (Step 6). Once every suggestion is approved or rejected, Start import becomes available. If your source needs a credential to read rows at import time — a Coda key or a live database password — Step 6 asks for it again and uses it only for that request path. Read the receipt when the run completes, and use Open your workspace to see the results. If a run is interrupted, your setup, approvals, and practice run are kept; starting again resumes from the stopped table, and completed tables are not written twice. For a Coda import that already fetched its rows before being interrupted, retrying replays the saved copy of those rows and does not ask for the one-time key again; if that saved copy is unreadable, the wizard asks for the key rather than failing silently. Risk levels in plain terms: Level What it means What happens Low The change is additive — a new table meaning, a new field, or no change to anything that exists. Quick lane. Confident low-risk suggestions can move ahead for you, with undo, depending on your autonomy setting. Medium The change alters an existing setup that has no imported records yet. Held for review by default. At the two most hands-off autonomy settings, a confident structural reading at this level can also move ahead for you, with undo. High The change alters a setup that already has imported records, or removes or merges whole tables. Held for explicit confirmation even after reviewer approval. Never applied automatically. A second pair of eyes is expected.

Re-importing a source you have brought in before is a normal operation: The wizard recognizes the saved setup, carries your unchanged decisions forward, and asks only about what is new or changed. For refreshing the records themselves, the platform supports two behaviours. Edit-preserving refresh matches incoming rows to existing records by their source identity, refreshes the values the source manages, and keeps researcher edits to fields the source does not manage — the right default for routine re-runs. Full refresh wipes the existing rows and reloads from scratch — destructive to researcher edits, only for genuine start-over situations. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, check with your platform operator before running it.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The imports list is empty No imports have been started yet Start from Imports & AI → Imports, or use the upload buttons on the All imports toolbar. "Add" opened a bare form that does nothing useful The plain admin "Add" form does not read a source Close it and start from an upload route. The wizard only opens for imports created through an upload. The wizard says AI suggestions were unavailable No AI provider is configured for your platform The structural reading still produced suggestions — review them as usual. To enable AI refinement, contact your platform operator. A re-import overwrote researcher edits A full-refresh re-import replaced the rows instead of an edit-preserving refresh Contact your platform operator to restore from your environment's backup, then re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. An upload was refused as too large The file exceeds the inline limit for its source type Resubmit with the background option. Background limits: Excel 100 MB; MySQL dump 500 MB; CSV 50 MB per file and 250 MB total. Apply is blocked, asking you to acknowledge a risk change The risk level was re-assessed at apply time and differs from when the reviewer approved Read the new level and its reason. Acknowledge it to proceed, or reject the suggestion and revisit it. A Coda or saved-database re-import fails with a credential error The saved connection's secret reference could not be resolved Check the saved connection in your environment. If the secret is held in the platform's secret store, contact your platform operator. Several suggestion cards target the same finding Each finding should produce exactly one suggestion This should not happen. Contact your platform operator. The practice run says "Nothing will import yet" Your approved choices would bring in zero rows — a column collision, everything set aside, no importable rows, source values the checks flagged, or rows not yet attached Use the action the stop offers: fix the conflicting columns, return to review, align/restructure the flagged columns, or — for advisory flags — Import these as-is (keep non-standard values). Your work is preserved; no re-upload is needed. The final import looks paused or the wait area is blank while linking records The relationship pass can be much longer than the table-write steps on large, relationship-heavy sources, and the wait/progress view can fail to render even when backend progress data exists. Keep the page open or return later from the import list. Restart only after the run reports failure or your platform operator confirms the worker stopped. Imported workspace tables expose more columns than one source table had Table records are separated by source table, but field definitions can still be shared at the concept-family level. Review the table's visible columns and saved views before inviting researchers in. Hide irrelevant columns in the default view, and escalate if per-source-table field scoping is required.

For researchers: Adding and editing rows — what researchers see once imported data lands in the workspace. Environment admin companions: Voice and Vocabulary — the wizard's on-screen wording follows your environment's voice settings; Efficiency Tips — the Step 3 tip cards; Permissions Panel — who can review and who can apply; Telemetry — what import telemetry captures.

Tips are short, contextual suggestions the platform shows researchers while they work — in the review step of the import wizard and in the workspace — pointing out a faster way to do what they are already doing, or a field worth filling in. Tips are advisory: they never change data and never block anyone. As environment administrator, you decide whether tips appear in your environment at all, and the names tips use for your record types and fields come from your environment's vocabulary. Read this page when deciding whether to leave tips on at onboarding, when a researcher reports an unwanted or oddly worded suggestion, or when a kind of tip stops appearing.

Environment-wide tips switch — one setting turns tips on or off for your whole environment. It is on by default for new environments; off means no tips appear anywhere, regardless of any other setting. Maturity: Active. Tips during import review — when a researcher makes the same correction repeatedly while reviewing an import, a tip suggests fixing the underlying rule once instead of correcting the remaining rows by hand. Tip cards appear beside the correction cards in the review step. Maturity: Active. Tips in the workspace — when a selected record has noticeably fewer filled fields than similar records in your environment, a tip names a field worth adding. Maturity: Active. Confidence-tiered display — the most confident suggestions appear directly beside the researcher's work; middling ones wait under a collapsed "More suggestions" heading; anything below the confidence bar is not shown at all. Maturity: Active. Wording through your vocabulary — tip sentences are written by the platform, and the names they use for your record types and fields resolve through your environment's vocabulary. You adjust those names through vocabulary entries; you do not edit tip text directly. Maturity: Active. Per-family acceptance figures — the platform keeps aggregate figures per kind of tip — how often that kind was shown and how researchers responded — for your environment only, over a rolling 30-day window. Individual researcher actions are not reported. Maturity: Built; a self-service view of these figures is not yet available — contact your platform operator if you need them. Automatic quiet-down — a kind of tip your researchers consistently pass over can pause itself in your environment. The pause requires sustained low uptake (around four weeks) and a minimum number of researcher responses, so a quiet week does not silence a useful tip. Your platform operator is notified when a kind of tip pauses. Maturity: Built. Separate measurement switch — whether tip activity is measured is a separate per-environment setting from whether tips display, so tips can be shown without their activity being measured. When tips are off, nothing is shown, so there is no tip activity to measure. Measurement records which tips appeared and how researchers responded, without recording who. Maturity: Built. See Telemetry for what your environment records.

Decide at onboarding: tips are on by default for a new environment. Review how tips will read to your researchers — the record-type and field names come from your vocabulary (see Voice and Vocabulary) — and either leave tips on or have them switched off until your vocabulary is ready. Turn tips off for your environment: the environment-wide setting lives on your environment's platform record — contact your platform operator to change it. Once tips are off, no new tips are served anywhere; anything already on a researcher's screen clears the next time the page or wizard step loads. Change how a tip is worded: adjust the matching vocabulary entry, and the new name appears the next time the tip is shown. If the problem is in the sentence around the names rather than the names themselves, contact your platform operator. When a kind of tip goes quiet: this may be the automatic quiet-down. Re-enabling a quieted kind of tip is not self-service — contact your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Researchers see no tips even though tips are switched on No tip pattern currently applies — tips fire only after repeated same-shape corrections during import review, or when a record clearly lags similar records — or a kind of tip has been quieted Tips are deliberately conservative; silence usually means no pattern was found. If a kind of tip that used to appear has stopped, contact your platform operator to confirm whether it was quieted. The import review step shows no tips panel Nothing cleared the confidence bar for that session Nothing to fix — low-confidence suggestions are held back by design, and the panel does not render when there is nothing to show. A researcher reports an unwanted or oddly worded suggestion The tip draws your record-type and field names from your environment's vocabulary, and the entry it found reads poorly in context Adjust the matching vocabulary entry — see Voice and Vocabulary. If the wording problem is in the surrounding sentence, contact your platform operator. A kind of tip stopped appearing after weeks of normal use It may have paused automatically because researchers consistently passed it over Contact your platform operator to review and re-enable it. Consider whether different vocabulary wording would help it land better.

Researcher tier: Tips and guidance — what researchers see and how tips behave for them. Tenant admin companions: Voice and Vocabulary — controls the names tip wording draws on; Data Import Wizard — the review step is the main place tips appear; Telemetry — what your environment measures and records. For platform-side questions — switching tips or tip measurement on or off, re-enabling a quieted kind of tip, requesting your environment's acceptance figures, or anything affecting other environments — contact your platform operator.

The Entry Surface role configuration is the record that defines a public reading surface for your environment: which of your records become public pages, what the public route looks like, how the index is ordered, and what title each page carries. It is the configuration behind the readiness review — the readiness panel reviews the controls that would go public, while this record declares the surface itself. Read this when you want to understand what a public Entry role controls before asking your platform operator to change one, when you are reviewing why a record did or did not appear on the public surface, or when you need to read the meaning of the fields on the role configuration record. The companion review surface is Entry Surface Readiness.

The role configuration record lives in your environment's admin area and is owned by your environment — your platform operator's seeding never overwrites a role you have edited. Inspecting a role and understanding its settings is something you do yourself. Applying a change so that it takes effect on the public surface — launching a role, promoting public controls, or rebuilding published pages — is operator-mediated. Recording a readiness decision does not promote anything, and editing a role configuration does not by itself republish the public surface. The safe sequence is: understand the record (yourself), then ask your platform operator to apply and rebuild. The fields below are written so you can read and reason about a role before that conversation.
A single role configuration declares one public reading surface. Its fields fall into five groups, matching how they are arranged in the admin record.

Role key — the platform-stable name for the role, such as primary. It is internal and stable; it does not change when you rename the public-facing noun. Display noun — the reader-facing noun for what this role publishes (for example, "entry" or "record"). This is the word readers see, separate from the internal role key. Active — whether the role is in use. An inactive role declares no public surface.

The selector decides which of your records this role publishes, without reclassifying those records: Archetype — the record family (the kind of records, such as people or works) the role draws from. Canonical type — an optional narrowing to a single type within that family. Left empty, the role takes the whole family. Primary selector — marks this selector as the primary one for the role. Allow multiple primary selectors — when off, a role must have exactly one primary selector; turning it on lets a role publish from more than one primary selector. Blast radius of editing a live role's selector. A selector edit applies lazily. Already-published pages keep serving their last good version until the next publish or rebuild. At the next rebuild, any record the edited selector no longer matches is removed from the public surface — whether or not that record is itself still published. An invalid selector set fails before any pages are written, so a bad selector cannot silently corrupt the surface; it stops the rebuild instead. Because a selector edit can remove live public pages, treat selector changes as the change you most want to review with your platform operator before it is applied.

These three settings are dotted source paths (for example, data.title) that point at a value in each record. They derive the public-facing identity of each page: Slug source — derives the public route for each record. A record where the slug source resolves to nothing has no public identity and is skipped by the page builder — it will not get a public page. Sort key source — derives the value the public surface sorts records by. Index key source — derives the value the browsable public index is keyed on. The public route for a page takes the form /entry/<role key>/<route reference>, where the route reference comes from the slug source.

The rules group carries finer selector and display settings: Selector rules — additional selector and display rules. Two keys you will encounter: display_label_source sets which value becomes the public page title, and seed records how the default for the role was derived (it documents the starting point, so you can see whether a setting is a seeded default or your own edit). Route aliases — additional route segments the surface accepts for this role, for example an older path a reader might still have bookmarked. These are accepted routes only; they do not change which record family a record belongs to. Search engine — an optional search-engine choice for this role. Left as the default, the role uses your environment's search profile. The other choices select a specific search backend for this role only; the role key stays local to your environment.

Config version — bump this when the public Entry Surface behavior for the role changes. Changing it signals that stale published pages should rebuild at the next publish. Record version and content hash — read-only bookkeeping the platform maintains for the record.

Editing the role configuration record stores your intent; it does not redraw the public pages on its own. When a published surface is rebuilt, a change to the role's selector, public identity sources, display noun, route aliases, selector rules, config version, or active flag is what causes the builder to recompute the affected pages. A record whose slug source resolves to nothing is skipped; a record the selector no longer matches is removed. Your platform operator runs the rebuild — see the operator-mediated note above.
documents.s: How a change reaches the public surface

documents.t: For a selector change: confirm which records currently match and which would match after the edit, because records that stop matching are removed from the public surface at the next rebuild. For a public identity change: confirm the dotted source path resolves to a value on the records you expect to publish; a path that resolves empty means no public page for that record. For a route alias change: confirm you are adding a route a reader might use, not asserting a record type. Before launch: confirm the readiness review reads clean — see Entry Surface Readiness — then hand off to your platform operator to apply and rebuild.
documents.s: What to check before requesting a change

documents.t: Entry Surface Readiness — the companion review surface, where you review and record decisions about the public controls a role would expose. Public reader — what researchers and external readers see once a public Entry surface launches.

Before your environment exposes a public Entry surface — the published layer external readers will see — the readiness panel lets you review the filter ("facet") and autocomplete controls that would become public, record a decision about each one, and confirm or defer each candidate. Read this when preparing for a public launch, when a readiness report flags a compact-control warning, or when activating an additional public role. The panel is a review surface, not an apply surface. Recording a decision stores review state for your environment; promoting a public control or confirming your environment's search configuration is a separate, explicit step performed with your platform operator.

Readiness report — for every active public Entry role in your environment, the report lists the reviewed filter and autocomplete fields, candidate fields, compact-control warnings, blockers, and all stored decisions, along with how many records were sampled to produce it. Maturity: Active. Viewing the report requires admin access in your environment. Durable review decisions — each decision is stored with its action, your reason (required, up to 500 characters), your username, the time, and a snapshot of the evidence the report showed you. Maturity: Active. A decision is a review checkpoint; it does not change the public surface itself. Fixed decision actions — review candidate before promotion; choose shorter public label; defer candidate with reason; defer public control with reason; acknowledge long-value exclusion. The action list is fixed; the reason is free text. Maturity: Active. Environment isolation — the report and your decisions are always scoped to the environment you are signed in to. You cannot read another environment's report or record decisions for it. Maturity: Active. Refreshed report on every decision — recording a decision returns the updated report, including the newly stored decision, and confirms that your environment's search configuration was untouched. Maturity: Active.

Sign in with an account that has admin access. The Entry Surface readiness panel currently lives in the transitional standalone shell at /app/admin/; daily operations and configuration tasks remain in the Django admin area at /admin/. The readiness panel sits in the side column, next to the source-data refresh panel, and loads the current report as the page opens. The refresh button at the top of the panel re-runs the report at any time. The summary line shows the overall status — "Ready for scalar probe" once at least one public role has reviewed single-value filter fields, "Needs review" otherwise — along with the number of roles, warnings, and recorded decisions, and a "ratification unchanged" indicator confirming that review work never alters your environment's search configuration. Review compact-control warnings. The report flags fields where some values are too long to show in a compact public filter control. Each flagged field appears with a reason box and the actions that are valid for it; the panel shows up to three fields per role at a time. A field you have decided on stays in the list, now showing its stored decision with the action and reason you recorded. Record a deferral. When a candidate should not become public yet, defer it with a reason. The deferral is durable: the next report shows the stored decision, and the field stays deferred until you record a different decision. Walk the pre-launch checklist. Each role section lists its blockers, reviewed fields, candidates, and recorded decisions. Work through them row by row; every decision requires a reason. Hand off for launch. When the report reads clean and your environment is ready, your platform operator performs the public launch. Recording decisions is the review checkpoint that precedes the launch — it is not the launch itself. If the server rejects a decision — a missing reason, or an action that is not valid for that field — the panel shows the server's message inline.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The panel reports that readiness is unavailable, or you land on the sign-in page Your account does not have admin access in this environment Ask an existing environment administrator to grant admin access, or run the review from an admin account. Recording a decision fails with a validation message The reason is missing, or the chosen action is not valid for that field Read the message in the panel. Add a reason, or choose one of the actions the panel offers for that field. The panel reports no active public Entry roles Your environment does not have a public Entry role configured yet Public Entry roles are set up as part of preparing your environment for launch. Contact your platform operator. The report reads clean but the public Entry surface has not appeared Recording decisions does not promote public controls or launch the surface Confirm with your platform operator that the launch step was run. The panel is a review surface only. The "ratification unchanged" indicator worried you This is by design — recording decisions never changes your environment's search configuration Confirming the search configuration is a separate explicit operation performed with your platform operator. The indicator exists so you can verify nothing changed as a side effect of your review. You need to undo a recorded decision Decisions are durable review state Record a new decision for the same field. It replaces the earlier one; the report then shows the latest decision with its reason and time.
Public reader — what researchers and external readers see once your public Entry surface launches.

A small set of defaults live on your environment as a whole, rather than on any one import, field, or record. Each one shapes how a recurring activity starts out: how involved you are by default when new data arrives, how much AI assistance a single import-wizard session may use, and whether your environment's not-yet-reviewed vocabulary takes part in cross-environment summaries. Read this when you want to understand what these environment-wide defaults do, what their limits are, and who can change them today. These three settings are not edited from your own admin interface. They sit on the environment record that the platform operator manages, so changing any of them is an operator-mediated action — you decide what you want and ask your platform operator to apply it. The sections below mark each setting accordingly, so you know what to request and what to expect once it changes.

Default import autonomy — your environment carries a default answer to the import wizard's "How involved do you want to be?" question, used to pre-select the starting autonomy level for every new import. The four levels are Hands off, Stay informed, Ask if unsure, and Confirm everything; the environment default is Stay informed unless your operator sets it otherwise. The default only chooses the starting point — you can still change the level on any individual import, and your per-import choice always wins. Maturity: Active. Limit: this default is applied by your platform operator; there is no self-serve control for it in your admin interface today. AI chat session budget — the import wizard's assistant chat runs against a per-session token budget drawn from this environment-wide figure. The default is 50,000 tokens per session, and the platform allows a value up to 500,000. A value of zero means no cap — the chat is unbudgeted. When a session reaches the budget, the chat pauses for that session; every import control keeps working, so the pause never blocks the import itself. Maturity: Active. Limit: this budget governs the import-wizard assistant chat only; it is separate from the rolling budget that governs AI vocabulary-grounding suggestions, which is configured elsewhere. The figure is applied by your platform operator. Federation exposure for ungrounded vocabulary — by default, vocabulary values your environment has not yet reviewed can be included in future cross-environment summaries. Turning this off keeps your environment's not-yet-grounded values out of those summaries while your grounding work is still in progress, so only vocabulary you have reviewed represents your environment outside it. Maturity: Active. Limit: the control is on by default, applies to ungrounded values specifically, and is set by your platform operator.

None of these three settings is edited from the environment admin interface you work in day to day. To change one, decide the value you want and ask your platform operator to apply it on the environment record. Default import autonomy — if your team consistently overrides the per-import autonomy setting to the same level, that is the signal to change the environment default. Tell your operator which of the four levels you want as the starting point. The change affects only imports started afterward; imports already in progress keep the level they were given. For what each level does inside a single import, see Data Import Wizard. AI chat session budget — raise the figure if researchers report the wizard chat pausing before they are done in a session; lower it (or set zero for no cap) to suit your platform's posture. Because the budget is per session, a researcher who hits it can continue working immediately — only the chat pauses — and a fresh session starts again from the full budget. Confirm the new value with your operator. Federation exposure for ungrounded vocabulary — turn this off while your environment still has a meaningful queue of unreviewed vocabulary and you would rather that queue not represent you in cross-environment summaries. As your grounding work catches up, you can ask your operator to turn it back on. For the review work this setting interacts with, see Vocabulary Grounding.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A new import opened at an autonomy level you did not expect A new import starts at the environment default, not at the level you used last time Change the level on that import directly — your per-import choice always wins. If the default itself is wrong for your team, ask your platform operator to change the environment default. The wizard assistant chat keeps pausing before researchers finish The per-session token budget is being reached within a working session Researchers can continue — only the chat pauses, not the import. To allow more chat per session, ask your platform operator to raise the AI chat session budget (up to the platform maximum), or set it to zero to remove the cap. You cannot find a control for any of these settings in your admin interface These three settings live on the environment record managed by the platform operator, not in your admin surface Decide the value you want and ask your platform operator to apply it. There is no self-serve control for them today. Not-yet-reviewed vocabulary appears to be included in cross-environment summaries Federation exposure for ungrounded vocabulary is on by default Ask your platform operator to turn it off while your grounding work is in progress; turn it back on once your review queue is caught up.

Data Import Wizard — where the per-import autonomy setting and the assistant chat appear, and what each autonomy level does inside one import. Vocabulary Grounding — the review work that the federation-exposure setting interacts with, and the separate AI controls for grounding suggestions.

Every field in every table of your environment is described by one field definition: what kind of value the field holds, what it is called, where its data is read from, who can see it on published pages, how a connecting field finds the record it points to (its resolution rule — internally, a "resolver"), and how searches treat its script and accents. This page is the reference for those definitions. Read it when adding a field, choosing between a link and a lookup, restricting a field from published pages, or tuning accent behavior for a multilingual corpus. A field definition is configuration, not code. Renaming a field, reordering the field list, or restricting a field's visibility is an edit you make in the workspace, and it takes effect without platform changes.

A single definition drives the same field everywhere it appears · Maturity: Active. In the workspace — the definition is the column and the form field. Adding a definition adds a column to the table grid and a field to the editing form. The displayed name, the field description (the tooltip researchers see), and the field's position in the list all come from the definition. In editing — the field kind decides which editor control researchers get, and fields marked required gate the completion of a new row. Date fields use native date inputs in workspace editing surfaces and date-aware filtering in the table. In search matching — the definition's language settings (script, accent folding, language, multilingual) shape how searches match the field's values. Whether the field is searched, faceted, or suggested at all is a separate set of controls — see Making fields searchable. On published pages — the field's visibility level decides whether it appears on published pages; its display name and position carry over when it does.

Every field has exactly one kind · Maturity: Active. Kind Holds Plain text A text value Rich text Formatted text with a full text editor Number A numeric value, displayed per its numeric format Date A calendar date, edited with a native date input and filtered by calendar date Boolean Yes / no Select (single) One value from the field's option list Select (multi) Several values from the field's option list Relation A live link to one or more records in another table Lookup A read-only value pulled through a link field Media A reference to a media item The kind decides which detail settings apply (formats, roles, options — see below). Definitions are validated when saved: settings that do not fit the field's kind are rejected with a validation message rather than silently ignored. Changing a text-shaped timestamp column to Date does not bulk-convert every stored value. Existing text values remain raw until an explicit conversion or cleanup flow handles them. This avoids silently corrupting scholarly date forms that look parseable but carry project-specific meaning.

Source path — each ordinary field names the place its values are read from in your environment's record store (a path such as data.title). Fields added in the workspace default to a path derived from the field key. The source path belongs to your source: every re-import refreshes it, so a hand-edit to the path does not survive the next re-import. Maturity: Active. Field key and label — the field key is the field's stable identity. It survives source renames and label changes; renaming a field's displayed name never touches the key. Labels for imported fields default to your source's own column names, verbatim — your renames are then preserved. Maturity: Active. Imported or workspace-added — fields arrive through import or are added directly in the workspace. Field keys beginning with x_ mark a field as an environment extension. The table's Details view badges each field: capability badges (multilingual, linkable, script, lookup, rich text) and a scope badge distinguishing environment-wide fields, extension fields, and personal note fields. Maturity: Active. What a re-import can and cannot change — every setting on a definition falls into one of three behaviors · Maturity: Active: Refreshed from source — source path, storage layer (which internal store holds the field's values), and connection rules. The source is the truth; re-imports overwrite these. Filled once if empty — field kind, script, language, multilingual, position, and choice options. Detection and import fill blanks; they never overwrite a value that is already set. Yours after creation — display name, field description, required, accent folding, formats and roles, formula templates, link and lookup configuration, and standards declarations. No automatic process overwrites these; they survive every re-import.
documents.s: Where a field's data comes from

documents.t: When a field points at records in another table, its definition records how the connection is resolved — the rule the platform follows, each time a record is read, to turn the stored value into the connected record · Maturity: Active. Direct — no connection; the value is read as-is. The default for ordinary fields. Foreign-key walk — follows a true foreign-key relationship carried over from your source database. String match — for a soft foreign key: no declared relationship exists in the source, but a value in this field equals a value in a named column of the target table. The rule names the two columns. Composed — multi-step or computed matching, performed by a named function from the platform's function library with parameters — for example, matching the part of a value before a comma against a bibliography table. Choosing one for a soft foreign key: when two tables relate only by matching values, the rule is string match. When the match needs computation first — splitting, prefixes, normalization — it is a composed rule. Connection rules are established during import analysis. The analyzer detects candidate connections from your data's structure and from value overlap between tables; an AI assistant proposes a rule only where the analysis is uncertain; a person approves before anything is written. From then on the rule runs identically on every read — no AI is involved when records are read. Re-imports refresh these rules from the source's structure; correcting one by hand outside an import is operator-mediated.

Each field carries one of three visibility levels · Maturity: Active. Public — the field appears on published pages. This is the default for every field, so published pages are unchanged until you restrict something. Workspace — the field stays inside your environment's workspace and never reaches published pages. Private — the field is visible to its owner only. You set visibility per field on the workspace Publish view, with a three-way control next to each field. The choice saves per field as you set it; publishing changes then rebuilds every entry in the table, applying the current visibility. Because the filter is applied when entries are built for publication, a newly restricted field disappears from already-published pages when those entries are next published. The researcher-tier walkthrough is The Publish view.

Per-field language settings control how searches match the field's text · Maturity: Active. Script — the field's dominant writing system (for example latin, greek, arabic), detected automatically from content. Empty until detection has run; you can override it per field. Accent folding — on by default: searches match the field accent-insensitively, on both the stored text and what is typed. Turn it off for fields where a diacritic is part of the letter's identity — Scandinavian å versus a, Vietnamese tone marks, Turkish dotted and dotless i, or a critical edition whose polytonic accents distinguish words. Applies to text fields, plain and rich. Once you set it, the choice is yours; no automatic process overwrites it. Language — the field's language code (for example el, grc, ar), detected automatically. You can override it; while it is empty, the script setting stands in for language-based defaults.

A text field can be set to hold more than one value per record — one for each language, register, script, edition, or calendar (or a custom kind of your own) · Maturity: Built. All the values land in one searchable entry, so a search matches the record no matter which value carries the match. Two parts of the field definition govern this, and they are independent: Field definition (the schema window) ├─ This column's language & script ← ONE language + script for the whole column │ Language code: [ grc ] (a single-value modifier on the column) │ Script: [ greek ] │ └─ Multiple values ← the column keeps a SEPARATE value per entry [✓] This column holds more than one value A separate value for each: [ Language ▾ ] (Language / Register / Script / Edition / Calendar / Custom) Allowed languages: [ GK ✕ ] [ LA ✕ ] [ AR ✕ ] ← chips: the allowed values Add a language: [________] (Add) ← type a new one; normalized to a chip There is one control for this. When you turn on This column holds more than one value, two settings appear: A separate value for each — what the values are distinguished by: Language, Register, Script, Edition, Calendar, or Custom. This choice drives the wording of the next setting and of the per-record editor (Allowed registers, + Add register, and so on). Allowed languages (the label follows the choice above) — the set of values the field accepts, shown as chips. This is a controlled, extensible picker, not a free-text list: type a value and it is added as a chip; the × on a chip removes it. Drift normalization — a typed value is normalized to a canonical short form before it joins the set, so variant spellings of the same value fold together: typing greek yields a GK chip, and GREEK and GK collapse to one entry rather than splitting the data across two headings. Researchers entering per-record values pick from this same normalized set, with a + new affordance for a value the set does not yet offer. Researchers fill the per-record values in the table cell or the record's form — see the researcher walkthrough Working in multiple scripts and languages. Right-to-left values (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, Aramaic) render right-aligned in those editors. The researcher-facing wording avoids platform terms: the editor reads "Multiple values", "A separate value for each", and "Allowed languages", never "multikey", "key", or "kind". The kind labels (Language, Register, …) are the only domain terms shown.
documents.s: A field that holds several values

documents.t: Detail settings per kind · Maturity: Active: Number fields take a numeric format — integer, decimal, year, currency, percent, or duration — plus an optional decimal precision. The currency format requires an ISO currency code. Plain-text fields take a role: plain, URL, email, phone, or embed. Choice fields (single and multi select) carry their option list. Media fields declare which media kinds they accept: image, audio, video, file, or embed. Relation fields declare whether they hold one connection or many. Three field shapes derive their value rather than storing it directly: A link field (relation) holds live connections to records in other tables. The connections are stored as relationship records, not inside the record's own data. Its definition names which tables it may point to and which field of the connected record is shown as the link's display value. A lookup shows a value from the record on the other end of an existing link field. It is read-only: its definition names the link field it follows and which field on the connected record to show; nested paths and lists are supported. A lookup must always name its target field, and a field is either a link or a lookup, never both — both rules are enforced when the definition is saved. A formula field computes its value each time the record is read, from a template combining other fields of the same record. Empty components are dropped by default, so a missing part leaves no stray separators. Computed values are never stored, and a formula field cannot also be a link or a lookup. Lookup and formula columns are read-only in the grid. To change what they show, edit the fields or linked records they derive from.
documents.s: Formats, roles, and the link / lookup / formula distinction

documents.t: Field definitions are edited in the workspace; the edits require the administrator role in your environment. Add a field: use the add-column control at the end of the table grid, or the table Details view's add-field action. The dialog asks for the field key (required, the stable identity), the kind, and the kind's detail settings. Edit a field: open the column header menu on the field's column, or use the Details view's edit action. Changing the kind of a column that already holds data is a deliberate act — review the field's values first. Delete a field: from the same column header menu. Deleting removes the definition — the column and the form field — but not the stored values underneath. Re-adding a field with the same field key brings the values back. Set per-field visibility: open the Publish view, set each field's level (Public / Workspace / Private), then publish changes to rebuild the table's entries with the current visibility. Declare standards: a field definition can declare which standards its content conforms to, chosen from the platform's approved list — see Standards and Citations.

Admin-self-serve, in the workspace: Adding, editing, and deleting field definitions — kind, key, display name, field description, position, source path, language behavior, formats and roles, choice options, links, lookups, formulas, and standards declarations. Per-field visibility on the Publish view. Operator-mediated — contact your platform operator: Marking a field required or optional. There is no workspace control for this today. Correcting a connection rule by hand outside an import. Changing a field's storage layer.
documents.s: Which edits are self-serve, and which go through your operator

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix You edited a field's source path and a re-import reverted it The source path is refreshed from source on every re-import — the source is the truth for it Make the change in your source data or the import mapping; workspace edits to the source path do not survive re-import. A lookup or formula column cannot be edited row by row Lookup and formula values are derived, not stored Edit the linked record (for a lookup) or the fields the formula combines. You set a field to Workspace or Private, but it still shows on a published page Visibility is applied when entries are rebuilt for publication Open the Publish view and publish changes for the table; the rebuild applies the current visibility. You deleted a field and need its data back Deleting removes the definition only — the stored values remain in the record store Re-add a field with the same field key; the default source path matches and the values reappear. Searches ignore accent distinctions that matter in your material Accent folding is on by default Turn accent folding off for that field; its diacritics then count as letter identity in matching. A definition will not save A detail setting does not fit the field's kind — for example the currency format without a currency code, or a lookup without a target field Read the validation message; it names the setting to fix.

Researcher tier: The Publish view — field visibility and publishing changes as researchers experience them; Workspace walkthrough — the workspace these definitions shape. Companion pages: Making fields searchable — whether a field is searched, faceted, or suggested (this page covers how its text is matched); Data Import Wizard — where definitions are first created from your source; Standards and Citations — the standards declarations a field can carry; Voice and Vocabulary — environment-wide wording that composes with your field labels.

Reviewing a media artifact's attestations — confirming or correcting which part of the artifact maps to which term, adding bindings the automatic extractor missed, re-running the extractor, and pinning a working revision as a citable Edition — happens inside the workspace, on the media record's detail pane. Read this when reviewing a freshly ingested media artifact, when the extractor proposes bindings that look wrong, or when you are ready to pin a revision as an Edition. Two terms used throughout: an anchor is an addressable point inside the artifact (for a 3D model, a named node in the model file), and an attestation is the recorded link between an anchor and a term in your environment. The guarantees described in Citation Integrity rest on the review decisions you take here. The standalone admin review page (formerly at /admin/.../media-review/) has been retired — all of its review, re-extraction, and Edition-pinning actions now live on the workspace media detail pane described below. If you have an old bookmark to that page, open the record from the workspace Media view instead.

Open the Media view on a media table (it appears only on MEDIA tables), then open a record from the gallery. Its detail pane opens with the model rendered inline and a rail of tabs: Mesh→term — the review surface: each part of the model with the term it is matched to, a state chip, and per-part actions. Files — the artifact's stored files. Viewer (admins) — sets the model's opening camera framing as a live presentation default. Info — read-only record details. Version (admins) — pin a working revision as a citable, frozen Edition, or re-extract the mesh→term bindings. The researcher-facing walkthrough of the Mesh→term tab is in the See which mesh maps to which term help topic; tuning the camera is in Tune the 3D camera view.

Mesh→term review — the Mesh→term tab lists each part of the model with the term it is matched to and a state chip: auto (extracted, awaiting review), edited (you changed an existing binding), linked (you bound a previously-unmapped part), or unmapped — above counts of how many parts are mapped, edited, and auto. Selecting a part, in the list or in the model itself, highlights it on both sides and opens its card. Maturity: Active. Per-part Approve / Reassign / Strip — Approve confirms an auto binding as correct (shown only while the part is auto); Reassign / Assign term opens a picker to bind the part to a term (search the vocabulary by typing and choose a result by its display label, or paste a term record's id); Strip clears the term, leaving the part unmapped. Every action is recorded with your name and a timestamp. Maturity: Active. Strip is a recorded rejection, not a deletion: the decision is kept so a later re-extraction cannot silently re-propose the same binding. Manual attestation add — bind a part the extractor missed via the term picker: a typeahead searches the term records in your environment as you type, or paste a term record's id directly. Maturity: Active. The typeahead depends on search being activated for your environment; the paste path works regardless. Re-extraction dry run and apply — on the Version tab, re-run the extractor against the same artifact, first as a dry run that reports what would change without writing anything, then as an apply. The job runs in the background and the tab polls its status. Maturity: Active. The status is overall job status only — queued, running, succeeded, or failed — not step-by-step progress. Requires the Admin role. Re-extraction is refused once the version is a frozen Edition. Edition pinning — on the Version tab, pin a working revision as a citable Edition with an Edition label. Maturity: Active. Requires the Admin role. Once pinned, the Edition is frozen: the platform refuses any re-extraction against it. (Everyday citeability is automatic; pinning is the deliberate-permanence act.) Reviewer-decision preservation — approvals, reassignments, strips, and manual additions are all marked as reviewer decisions and survive re-extractions; the extractor never silently overwrites them. Maturity: Active.

Open the workspace, open a media table's Media view, and open a record from the gallery. Review actions and manual bindings require the Editor or Admin role in your environment; re-extraction and Edition pinning require Admin — the workspace hides the admin-only actions when your role cannot perform them, so you never dead-end on a permission error. The common review paths: Approve a correct binding: select the part, then Approve. The decision is recorded with your name and timestamp, and future re-extractions leave the binding alone. Reassign or bind a part: select the part, then Reassign / Assign term; search the term by typing and choose a match, or paste the term record's id. Strip a wrong binding: select the part, then Strip. Your rejection is recorded, and the extractor's next run will not re-propose the same binding. Re-extract: on the Version tab, dry run first — the job runs in the background and the tab polls its status until it succeeds or fails — compare the report against the current state, then apply (apply asks for confirmation, because it writes new anchors and attestations). Pin an Edition: on the Version tab, pin the working revision and enter the Edition label. After pinning the Edition is frozen — further extraction work requires a new working revision. The mesh→term counts refresh after each action, so the tiles always reflect the decisions you have taken so far.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The Media view does not appear on a table The table's records are not the MEDIA archetype The Media view appears only on MEDIA tables. Confirm the table holds media records. The model does not render in the detail pane The media record has no resolvable primary file The pane needs the artifact's stored primary file. Confirm the record was ingested completely; the rest of the pane still works for reviewing existing bindings. The re-extraction actions are disabled or refuse The current version is a frozen Edition, or the record has no resolvable source file Re-extraction is refused on a frozen Edition — start a new working revision by re-importing. If the record has no source file, add it. The term picker returns no matches for a term you know exists Search has not been activated for your environment, or the search found nothing for your query The picker shows a hint when this happens; paste the term record's id directly — the picker works regardless of search state. To get search activated for your environment, contact your platform operator. The Version tab's pin/re-extract actions are missing You do not have the Admin role Edition pinning and re-extraction require Admin. Review and binding actions are available to Editors. You stripped a binding but the next extraction proposed it again This should not happen — a strip is durable across re-extractions Contact your platform operator with the artifact id and the details of the stripped binding.

Citation Integrity — the structural guarantees behind Edition pinning. Permissions Panel — role assignment for Editor and Admin. Work with media in the workspace, See which mesh maps to which term, Tune the 3D camera view — the researcher-facing help topics for this surface.

The standard roles in your environment — and any custom role you compose — are built from one fixed set of permission building blocks. There are nine. Each block is a single capability: it is either granted or not. A role is a chosen combination of these blocks. This page names every block, says exactly what each one lets a contributor do, gives the default combination a new contributor starts from, and shows how the blocks combine into a reviewer, a supervisor, and an exporter. Read it when you are composing a custom role on the Permissions Panel and want to know precisely what each checkbox controls. The building blocks are fixed by the platform: you combine them, you cannot invent new ones. Composing roles and assigning them is yours to do as an administrator. Adding the contributor accounts those roles attach to is handled by your platform operator — see Onboarding a collaborator.

Each block below lists its name, what it gates, and its impact tier — low, medium, or high. The impact tier tells you how cautious to be when granting it; the three high-impact blocks are called out again in the next section.

Gates: reading and commenting on suggested changes before they are saved. A contributor with only this block can examine every proposed change and leave comments, but cannot save anything. Impact tier: medium.
Gates: saving additive changes — new records or new fields — that do not alter existing work. This is the lowest-impact save permission. Impact tier: low.
Gates: saving edits that change existing records. These are the everyday changes a working contributor makes, and they remain reviewable. Impact tier: medium.
Gates: running broad merges, deletes, and reorganizations — the changes that touch the most records at once. Impact tier: high.
Gates: reversing a just-saved change while the short undo window is still open. Without this block, a contributor can save but cannot self-reverse. Impact tier: low.
Gates: creating and updating the saved import setups the project reuses. Impact tier: medium.

Gates: changing the fields contributors use when they edit — which fields exist and how they behave. This reshapes the editing surface for everyone, which is why it sits in the high tier. Impact tier: high. See Field Configuration for what this controls.

Gates: inviting contributors into roles and deciding what each person can do — in other words, composing roles and assigning the other eight blocks. A contributor needs this block to open the role-management surfaces at all. Impact tier: high.
Gates: downloading aggregate metrics about suggestion quality and review patterns. The numbers are aggregate, never individual review text. Impact tier: medium.

When a contributor account first appears in your environment, it starts from a fixed default combination — the set the platform treats as a safe working baseline for a project team member. The five blocks below are on by default; the other four are off. Building block Default Review suggestions On Save additive changes On Save normal changes On Use the undo window On Manage import templates On Run high-impact changes Off Change field setup Off Manage roles Off Export suggestion metrics Off The default is a starting point, not a fixed role: from the Permissions Panel you assign a standard role or compose a custom one over it. The three high-impact blocks — run high-impact changes, change field setup, and manage roles — are off by default, and so is exporting metrics.

Three blocks are high-impact: run high-impact changes, change field setup, and manage roles. Granting one of these gives a contributor a capability that can affect a large share of the project's work, or affect what other contributors can do. These blocks decide who is allowed to make a high-impact change. They are separate from your environment's project rules, which decide how such a change is confirmed when it happens. The two work together: a block grants the capability; a project rule can require a second pair of hands before the change goes through. For example, your environment can require that a high-impact save is confirmed by a contributor who did not author it, and can require that destructive changes are confirmed either by two contributors or by a single contributor through an elevated confirmation step. So even a contributor who holds run high-impact changes is still subject to the project rules at the moment they apply a change. Granting the block does not bypass the rules; it only makes the contributor eligible to start the change. You set these rules on the Project rules tab — see the project rules described in the Permissions Panel. Manage roles is the one block that controls access to permission management itself. A contributor cannot open the role-management surfaces, or change anyone's permissions, without it.
documents.s: The high-impact blocks and the project rules

documents.t: These three shapes show how the blocks combine. They are illustrations, not extra preset roles — compose the equivalent as a custom role, or start from the matching standard role and adjust. A reviewer — someone who reads and comments but never saves. One block: Review suggestions Everything else is off. This shape can examine and annotate proposed changes and nothing more. A supervisor — a senior contributor who does the full editing job and can reorganize, but does not manage people or reshape the field setup. The save and undo blocks plus high-impact changes: Review suggestions Save additive changes Save normal changes Run high-impact changes Use the undo window Manage import templates Change field setup, manage roles, and export metrics stay off. This contributor can do every kind of save — including high-impact reorganizations — but reshaping the editing surface and managing other people's access remain with an administrator. An exporter — someone whose job is to pull aggregate metrics, with read access to the review stream but no save authority. Two blocks: Review suggestions Export suggestion metrics All save and management blocks stay off. This shape can read suggestions and download the aggregate quality and review-pattern metrics, without the ability to save changes or alter anyone's access.

Action Who Compose a custom role from the building blocks Administrator (self-serve, on the Permissions Panel) Assign a standard or custom role to a contributor Administrator (self-serve) Adjust a single contributor's blocks Administrator (self-serve) Add a new contributor account for a role to attach to Platform operator Add new building blocks beyond the nine Not available — the set is fixed by the platform

Permissions Panel — where you compose roles, assign them, and set the project rules these blocks work alongside. User and Access Management — the standard role set and how the four pre-loaded roles map onto these blocks. Field Configuration — what the change field setup block controls. Onboarding a collaborator — how a new contributor account is created before you assign a role to it.

The Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ is the single surface for who-can-do-what in your environment. Contributor roles, custom role composition, project safety rules, wording overrides, ownership hand-off, and the project-history lookup all live here. Read this when changing a contributor's role, composing a custom role, handing off project ownership, or answering "who reviewed that import, and when?".

Contributors tab — every contributor in your environment, with their assigned role and last activity. Change a contributor's role, adjust individual permissions, or narrow the scope of their assignment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the panel manages roles and permissions for existing contributors; contributor accounts are created by your platform operator — see User and Access Management. Roles tab with custom role composition — the standard roles come preloaded; custom roles are composed from a fixed set of permission building blocks. A standard role can be renamed inline; the new name is a display label only. Maturity: Active. Limit: the building blocks themselves are fixed by the platform. Role scoping — a role assignment (or a custom role) can be limited to specific record types or fields. Maturity: Active. Limit: a scope only narrows where the role applies; it cannot add permissions the role does not grant. Project rules tab — set your environment-wide review policy: whether high-impact saves need a reviewer who did not author the change, and how destructive changes are confirmed — by two contributors, or by a single contributor through an elevated confirmation step. Maturity: Active. Limit: the panel saves and displays these choices as your environment's declared policy; how each applied change was actually confirmed, and by whom, is shown on the Project history tab. Review learning setting — on the Project rules tab: opt in to record privacy-safe signals from your team's review decisions so future suggestions improve. Maturity: Active. Limit: off by default; switching it on requires acknowledging the privacy notice, and the change is recorded along with which admin made it. Wording tab — rename the permission-related labels shown in your environment, starting with role names. Maturity: Active. Limit: changes compose with your environment's voice and vocabulary settings; there is no separate translation table to maintain. Vocabulary review prompt — when the panel loads, it checks permission-related wording and flags entries that need review, with the reason and a link to edit each one. Maturity: Active. Limit: the check is read-only — it never changes anything; you act on a finding or dismiss it. Project history tab — look up the recorded history of an applied import proposal: its status, how it was confirmed, who reviewed it and when, the recorded reason, and the permissions that were in force at the moment it was applied. A record carries an "Edited after apply" marker when the applied content was changed afterwards. Maturity: Active. Limit: lookup is per proposal — you supply the proposal's ID from the import screens; records are read-only. Ownership hand-off — the current project owner can hand ownership to another contributor. The hand-off asks for explicit confirmation for both sides, completes as a single change, and is recorded. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the current owner can start a hand-off, and the new owner must be an active contributor holding the administrator role with permission management. Display density control — switch the panel between compact, cozy, and comfortable layouts. Maturity: Active. Limit: cosmetic only — it affects rendering, not permissions; the choice is remembered in the browser where you set it.

The panel's address is /admin/permissions/. It opens on the Contributors tab; the other tabs are Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. The active tab is kept in the page address, so a bookmark or a shared link opens the panel on that tab. Change a contributor's role: Contributors tab, open the contributor's row, pick the role. To limit where the role applies, set a scope on the same row. Compose a custom role: Roles tab, combine the permission building blocks, name the role. Rename any role's display label inline with the edit control; the underlying building blocks stay fixed. Set project rules: Project rules tab. Switch the separate-reviewer requirement on or off, choose the destructive-change policy, and save. Enable review learning: Project rules tab. Switch the setting on, acknowledge the privacy notice, and save. The decision is recorded along with who made it. Hand off ownership: as the current project owner, use the "Hand off ownership" control, choose the new owner, and confirm for both sides. Look up an import's history: Project history tab, enter the proposal's ID, and load the history. The record shows the review decision and the permission snapshot from the moment of apply. Review flagged wording: when the vocabulary check finds entries needing review, a notice appears. Open the Wording tab, follow each flagged entry's edit link, or dismiss the finding.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A notice says permission wording needs review The load-time vocabulary check flagged entries Open the Wording tab. The check is read-only; follow the edit link on each flagged entry, or dismiss the finding. See Voice and Vocabulary. Renaming a standard role did not change what it allows A rename sets a display label only; the role's permission building blocks are fixed This is the intended behavior. Compose a custom role if you need a different set of building blocks. A contributor cannot act on content their role should allow Their role assignment carries a scope that excludes that content Open the contributor's row and check the scope. Widen it or remove it. The ownership hand-off will not complete Only the current owner can hand off, and the new owner must be an active contributor holding the administrator role with permission management Give the intended new owner the administrator role with permission management first, then run the hand-off again. Review learning is on, but suggestions do not seem to improve Signals accumulate gradually and stay within your environment This is expected early on. The setting records your team's review decisions over time; it does not change behavior immediately.

Companion pages: Voice and Vocabulary — the wording system the panel's overrides plug into; User and Access Management — the standard role set and how contributor accounts are created; Telemetry — what the review-learning setting records. Platform-level operations — cross-environment concerns such as incident response and platform-wide data-protection records are handled outside this panel. Contact your platform operator.

This page is the reference for the configuration records that decide how a published record is laid out on the public reader: which field becomes the page title, which becomes the description, which carries the citation, which drives the page's web address and its position in an index. Those decisions live in a public stream profile and its field bindings. Read this when a published page shows the wrong field in a heading, when a record's citation or evidence is missing from the public layout, when you are reviewing what an import seeded for a new collection, or when planning a change to how a public page is composed.

The public reader's layout is governed almost entirely by records the platform seeds and maintains. A dedicated environment-admin editor for these records does not exist yet, so changes today are made for you by your platform operator. Admin-readable. You can read every stream profile and its field bindings, see which fields fill each part of the public page, and tell apart a binding the platform seeded from one that was authored by hand. This page is written to let you read and verify those records confidently. Operator-mediated. Creating a profile, adding or changing a field binding, editing a route alias, or switching a profile off is done with your platform operator. Bring them the specific change — "the title should come from this field, not that one" — and they apply it in the platform's administration records. Platform-maintained. Most profiles and bindings are seeded automatically when imported data is materialized, derived from your environment's public roles and collection metadata. A re-seed refreshes only the parts it owns; any binding authored by hand is reported and never overwritten.
documents.s: What you change yourself, and what the platform maintains

documents.t: Stream profiles — one profile defines a single public stream: a presentation contract that turns your data into a public-reader page. A profile carries a stream key (its unique name), an optional public role it presents, an optional concept family and record-type narrowing that scope which records it serves, an active flag, and the contracts described below. Most environments need only the seeded default; an environment can have more than one stream. Maturity: Active. Limit: the stream key is unique per environment, so a second stream needs its own key. Field bindings — each binding maps one part of a public page to where its content comes from in your data. A profile has many bindings — one for the title, one for the description, one for each citation part, and so on. A binding names the part it fills (its semantic role, below), how it resolves the value, and the value itself or the path to it. Maturity: Active. Limit: a profile allows at most one binding per field key, so two parts cannot claim the same key. Semantic roles — the named parts of a page — every binding declares which part of the public page it fills. The available parts cover the page's structure: the main display label and a secondary label; a description, with shorter and longer variants; a translation set and a transliteration set for multi-script records; the citation label and the citation quote; locators, including a page locator and a line locator; author and treatise facets; media links; the page's route reference, sort key, and index key; an active flag; and a passthrough for content carried through unchanged. Maturity: Active. Limit: the role list is fixed by the platform; a binding chooses from it rather than inventing a new part. How a binding resolves its value — a binding draws its content one of five ways: from a single field, from a path inside a record's stored data, from a fixed constant, from a computed value, or by composing several inputs into one. The resolution kind decides what the binding's payload must contain, and the platform checks the payload before a public page is built from it. Maturity: Active. Seed evidence on every binding — each binding records whether it was seeded by the platform or authored by hand, the strategy that last produced it, the share of sampled records that strategy covered (from none to all), and the machine-readable reasons from the last seeding attempt. This is how you tell an automatically derived binding from a hand-authored one, and how you judge whether a seeded binding fit your data well. Maturity: Active. Identity, projection, and adapter contracts — a profile carries three contract blocks. The identity contract holds the public-facing semantics of the page — its route, label, sort, and index behavior. The projection contract is the shape the platform's page assemblers consume. The adapter contract is temporary compatibility data for transitional readers, not a permanent part of how a page is described; it exists to bridge older reading surfaces during the move to the public reader. Maturity: Active. Limit: the adapter contract is transitional and is not treated as the authoritative description of the page. Route aliases — extra web-address segments a stream will answer to, alongside its primary route. Useful when an environment has published a record under more than one path and wants old links to keep resolving. Maturity: Active. Limit: editing a profile's identity or selector changes which records the stream can serve; pages already published keep their last good content until the platform rebuilds them. Active flag and provenance retention — switching a profile or a binding off removes it from the public build without deleting it. An inactive record is kept for provenance and ignored by the page loaders. Maturity: Active.

Public stream profiles live in your environment's administration records. Each profile lists its stream key, the role and concept family it presents, whether it is seeded or hand-authored, its active flag, and how many field bindings it carries. Opening a profile shows its three contract blocks and its bindings together, so you can read the whole page composition in one place.
