Because a dedicated environment-admin editor does not exist yet, the steps below describe what you read and verify yourself, and what to bring to your platform operator to apply. Read what fills each part of a page. Open the profile and read its bindings. Each binding's part name (its semantic role) and field key tell you which piece of data fills the title, the description, the citation, and so on. A profile with a title binding, a description binding, and citation bindings composes a standard reading page. Tell a seeded binding from a hand-authored one. Read each binding's seed evidence. A binding marked seeded was derived automatically; its coverage figure tells you how much of your data the strategy fit. A binding marked manual was authored by hand and will survive any re-seed. Check why a part is missing or wrong. If a public page shows the wrong field in a heading, find the binding for that part and read its field key — it points at the data the platform is pulling. If a coverage figure is low, the seeded strategy fit only some records, which is the likely reason a part is blank on others. Plan a layout change. Decide the exact change in terms of parts and data — "the description should come from this field" — and bring it to your platform operator. They edit the binding (or add one) in the administration records; the public page picks up the change on the next rebuild, not instantly. Verify after a change applies. Confirm the binding now names the field you intended, that the profile is active, and then preview a published record to see the part filled correctly. The published page reflects the change only after its snapshot rebuilds. Changing a profile's identity or selector changes which records a stream can serve going forward. Records already published keep their last good content until the platform rebuilds and reindexes them — a layout change is never instantly retroactive.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A published page shows the wrong field in its heading or description. The binding for that part names a different field key than you expect. Open the profile, find the binding for that part, and read its field key. Bring the corrected field to your platform operator to apply, then preview a record to confirm. A part of the page (citation, description, locator) is blank on some records but not others. A seeded binding's strategy fit only part of your data — its coverage figure is below full. Read the binding's seed evidence. A low coverage figure means the part is expected to be blank where the strategy did not apply; supplying the missing data, or a hand-authored binding from your operator, fills it. A binding I expected the platform to keep was changed after a re-seed. Only seeded bindings are refreshed by re-seeding; a binding must be marked manual to survive. Read the binding's seed-evidence flag. If a binding should never be overwritten, ask your platform operator to author it as a manual binding. An old public link stopped resolving after a layout change. The profile's route changed, and the old path is not listed as a route alias. Ask your platform operator to add the old path to the profile's route aliases so old links keep resolving. A profile was switched off but its records still appear published. Switching a profile off removes it from future builds; pages already published keep their last good content until the platform rebuilds. The change takes effect on the next rebuild and reindex, which your platform operator runs. Confirm with them when the rebuild has completed. Two parts of a page seem to fight over the same content. A profile allows only one binding per field key; the conflict is in how the bindings are composed. Read the bindings and their parts. Bring the intended single source for each part to your platform operator to resolve.

Companion pages: Entry surface configuration: the record behind the readiness review — the role configuration that decides which records reach the public layer, paired with the readiness review; Entry Surface Readiness — the review surface for the public filter and autocomplete controls; Field configuration: kinds, scopes, resolvers, and language behavior — the per-field settings, including publish scope, that decide what content a binding can draw on. What readers see — The public reader describes the reading-facing page these profiles compose, from a researcher's point of view.

Every field in your environment carries its own search settings: whether the field's text is matched by search, whether the field can become a filter ("facet") control, and whether its values feed suggest-as-you-type. The settings live on each field's configuration record, are filled automatically when the field is created, and are exactly the configuration the Entry Surface readiness review reads. Read this page when a field matches (or fails to match) in search unexpectedly, when you are deciding which fields should become public filter controls, or when preparing your environment for a public launch.

Per-field search settings — each field carries three eligibility settings: searchable (text matching), filter ("facet") eligibility, and autocomplete eligibility. Maturity: Active. Limit: the admin screens do not currently include a control for editing a stored value — changing one is done with your platform operator. Automatic defaults from the field's type — when a field is created during an import, the platform fills the three settings from a fixed per-type table, the same for every environment. The platform never infers them from the content of your data. Maturity: Active. Limit: the automatic value fills a blank only; an explicitly chosen value is never overwritten, including by re-imports. Searchable fields define the search index — when a record is written to your environment's search index, only its searchable-marked fields contribute text. The search your team uses inside the environment reads this index. Maturity: Active. Limit: fields created before automatic defaults existed fall back to built-in platform rules until explicit values are stored for them. Filter ("facet") eligibility — a facet-eligible field can produce filter buckets, and the readiness review lists it as a reviewed filter field. Maturity: Active. Limit: a public filter control additionally requires a simple single-value field, your review, and promotion into the public configuration — eligibility alone does not create a public control. Autocomplete eligibility — an autocomplete-eligible field feeds suggest-as-you-type. Maturity: Active. Limit: a public suggestion source has the same additional requirements as a public filter: a simple single-value field and review. Search boost (reserved) — a field's configuration can record a weighting value for ranking its matches. Maturity: Built. Limit: the value is stored and preserved as yours, but no search engine consults it — it has no effect on results today. Leave it unset.

The settings sit on the field's configuration record, next to its label, type, and ordering. You do not set them by hand at creation time: the moment a field is created, the platform writes all three eligibility values from the field's type. Field type Searchable Filter-eligible Suggestions Short text Yes No Yes Long-form (rich) text Yes No No Single-choice list Yes Yes Yes Multiple-choice list Yes Yes No Link to another record Yes Yes No Looked-up value Yes No No Number, date, yes/no No No No Media No No No Three rows deserve a note. A link field is matched through the linked record's display text, which is why it is searchable even though it stores no text of its own. Number, date, and yes/no fields start with everything off — an opt-in you record explicitly is preserved and never reverted by the platform. A media field itself carries no searchable text; the descriptive fields on a media record (title, creator, and so on) are ordinary text and choice fields and follow their own rows in this table.
documents.s: Where the settings live, and what fills them

documents.t: You can do yourself: read each field's stored eligibility values and sampled evidence in the Entry Surface readiness report, and record review decisions there — including deferring a filter or suggestion candidate with a reason. A recorded deferral is read by the public surface: the deferred control is reported unavailable, with a reason citing your review. Performed with your platform operator: editing a stored searchable, filter, or autocomplete value on a field (the admin screens have no control for this today); refreshing the search index after a change so existing records reflect it; promoting reviewed fields into the public Entry configuration; and enabling your environment's search engine in the first place. Whichever path sets a value, the same protection applies: an explicit value is yours. Re-importing your source data fills blanks with automatic defaults but never overwrites a value that was chosen deliberately.
documents.s: Changing a setting — what is self-serve and what runs through your operator

documents.t: Hiding works the same way in reverse. A field whose searchable setting is off contributes no text to the search index, so its values stop matching once the index is refreshed. A field explicitly marked not filter-eligible also leaves the readiness review's candidate list — the review stops proposing it.

The readiness report classifies every field of the public role's record type by its stored settings: A field marked filter-eligible appears as a reviewed filter field — listed with the reviewed single-value filter fields when its values are simple single values, or flagged separately when its shape is complex (multi-value, linked, looked-up, media). A field marked autocomplete-eligible with simple single values appears as a reviewed autocomplete field. A simple single-value field with no explicit eligibility appears as a candidate, with the review actions the panel offers (review before promotion, choose a shorter label, defer with reason). Each row carries evidence sampled from your records: how many records carry a value, how many distinct values exist, and warnings where values are too long for a compact public control. The report is the place to confirm a setting change landed — see Entry Surface Readiness for the panel itself.
documents.s: How the settings feed the readiness review

documents.t: Inside your environment, the workspace search matches against the search index, so only searchable-marked fields produce hits. If your environment's search engine has not yet been enabled, a search request is refused with a plain message that search is not enabled for the workspace yet — enablement is an operator step. On the public Entry surface, a filter or suggestion control reaches readers only when the field is explicitly eligible, holds simple single values, has passed your review, and was promoted into the public configuration. A control that does not meet all of these is reported with an unavailable status and a short reason, one of four kinds: the field is not part of that public role's configuration; the control was deferred by a review decision you recorded; the field has not yet been reviewed and promoted; the field's value shape (multi-value, linked, looked-up, or media) has no public control of this kind. An automatic default alone never creates a public control: a field the platform seeded but nobody reviewed stays review evidence, not a public promise.
documents.s: What researchers and public readers see

documents.t: Open the Entry Surface readiness panel and refresh the report. Find the field's row and confirm its stored eligibility values and classification moved as expected — into the reviewed lists, into the candidates, or out of the candidates entirely. For a searchable change, ask your operator to confirm the index refresh ran, then search for a value that occurs only in that field and confirm it now matches (or no longer matches).

Symptom Likely cause Fix A field's text never matches in search The field is not marked searchable, or the index has not been refreshed since the setting changed Check the field's evidence in the readiness report. Have your platform operator set the field searchable and refresh the search index. Search reports it is not enabled for the workspace Your environment's search engine has not been enabled and confirmed Engine enablement is performed with your platform operator. A field you expect as a public filter is reported unavailable Not yet reviewed and promoted; deferred by a recorded review decision; or a multi-value, linked, or media field, which has no public filter control Open the readiness report and read the field's row. Record or revise the decision; promotion into the public configuration is performed with your platform operator. Suggestions never include a field's values The field is not autocomplete-eligible — long-form text, multiple-choice, and link fields do not feed suggestions by default If the field is short text or a single-choice list and should suggest, have your operator mark it autocomplete-eligible and refresh the index. You recorded a search boost and rankings did not change The boost value is stored but not consulted by any search engine This is current behavior, not an error. Leave the value unset. A re-import changed a search setting you chose It does not: automatic values fill blanks only If a value looks wrong, check the field's evidence in the readiness report — an explicitly stored value survives re-imports; only fields that never had one receive the per-type default.

Entry Surface Readiness — the review panel that reads these settings and records your decisions. Data Import Wizard — where fields enter your environment; their search settings are filled at that moment. Searching as a public reader — the reader-side companion to this page. Public reader — what external readers see once your public Entry surface launches.

This page is the environment administrator's working view of the platform's standards support. It tells you which standards-backed capabilities your environment inherits without configuring anything, what you can configure on top, what published entries expose to the outside world, and what stays your environment's own interpretation. Read this when an institutional reviewer asks "what standards does our knowledge environment comply with?", when a federation partner asks whether a specific export format is supported, or when you are deciding which standards a field in your environment should declare conformance with. The cross-audience overview is the Standards & Compliance Overview; this page is for someone running an environment.

These capabilities ship with every environment. None of them require per-environment engineering, custom code, or a separate contract. Each carries a maturity tag; the standards overview records the audited maturity of every standard the platform engages with. Stable, citable identity for published artifacts — a published artifact carries a stable public identity that an external identifier service (your library's DOI minter, for example) can target. The platform does not mint DOIs itself, and data cited against a frozen Edition cannot silently change · Maturity: Active · See Citation Integrity for the guarantees in detail. Citation framework built on Citation Style Language (CSL) — citations render through CSL styles, the same open format reference managers and journals use. A catalog of more than seventy standard styles ships with the platform (Chicago and APA among them), and each environment holds its own active styles · Maturity: Built · Limit: a style that is not in the catalog can be installed on request — contact your platform operator. Per-entry citation export in CSL JSON — every published entry's citation is available in CSL JSON, the interchange format reference managers read · Maturity: Built. Media locators that follow IIIF and W3C Web Annotation conventions — a cited region of an image, audio/video segment, or 3D model is addressed by the artifact's own natural self-description (an image region selector, a 3D-model node name, a text passage identifier), never a platform-invented code · Maturity: Built · Limit: locator support ships today; dedicated standard viewers are not yet integrated. See Citation Integrity. Vocabulary review backed by shared authorities — vocabulary values first seen in your imported data queue for review rather than being guessed at, and AI suggestions (when enabled) can reference public authority records: Wikidata for entities and concepts, PeriodO for historical periods. Suggestions are advisory only — a reviewer declares or rejects every value · Maturity: Active (the review queue); the authority-backed AI suggestions are Built · See Vocabulary Grounding. Typed, self-describing API — integrations read published data through a documented GraphQL API: a typed contract a partner can inspect, not an undocumented internal surface · Maturity: Built. Privacy-aware telemetry — activity records are redacted before they are stored and kept in a tamper-evident chain, supporting a defensible data-protection posture under GDPR · Maturity: Active · See Telemetry. Accessibility controls in the reading interface — readers can adjust font size, line height, color presets, and font family. The platform targets WCAG 2.2 AA; a full audit against that target has not yet been recorded · Maturity: Active. Capability-to-standard quick reference: Capability Backing standard(s) Stable citable identity for published artifacts DOI (minted externally against platform-held identity) Deep-linkable image / AV / 3D regions IIIF, W3C Web Annotation Citations consumed by reference managers CSL Vocabulary review informed by shared authorities Wikidata, PeriodO Typed API for integrations GraphQL Accessible reading interface WCAG 2.2 AA (target) Defensible data-protection posture GDPR

Citation style — per environment and per entry type. Adopt a style from the shipped catalog, or refine one through the review workflow described below. Applying a style requires the administrator role; styles are versioned, and the platform refreshes published citations after a style is applied · Maturity: Active. Vocabulary grounding — declare or reject queued vocabulary values through the Vocabulary Grounding workflow, with a display label of your choosing and optional links to standards from the platform's recognized list · Maturity: Active. Field standards declarations — a field definition in your environment can declare which standards its content conforms to, chosen from the platform's approved standards list. Declarations are validated when you save the field definition — a standard outside the list is rejected with a validation message — and the declarations are visible through the API · Maturity: Active. Voice and vocabulary substitution — independent of standards but composes with them: your wording is yours, the structural conformance underneath is the platform's. See Voice and Vocabulary · Maturity: Active. Reference evidence and citation rules — declared once per published entry type; described in the next section · Maturity: Active. How often you touch each of these: Citation style — once at environment setup; revisit when you adopt a new venue's or institution's style guide. Vocabulary grounding — during onboarding, and after any import that brings in vocabulary values your environment has not seen before. Field standards declarations — when designing or revising a field definition. They are part of the field's definition, not a day-to-day switch. Voice substitution — whenever the platform's default wording feels foreign to your researchers. Reference evidence and citation rules — once per published entry type, when deciding how its References section should read.
documents.s: What you can configure on top

documents.t: When a published entry shows a References section — one row per piece of evidence, each with a scholarly citation — two declarations on the entry type produce it. Both are configuration, not code: the platform supplies the machinery, your environment supplies the meaning. The evidence declaration — where your evidence lives and how it joins. You declare which record type holds the occurrences of an entry (the passages, witnesses, specimens, or find records), which link connects them to the entry, and which of your columns carry the locators (page, chapter, line, quote) and the source details (author, work, editor). Every column name in the declaration is your environment's vocabulary; the platform never assumes any of it. Citation rules — how citations are built and styled. You declare which of your columns map to the standard citation fields (author, title, editor, date, page), and which CSL style renders them. The result is a formatted citation per evidence row, plus standalone source citations beneath the evidence list. Two behaviors worth knowing when designing the declarations: Editions are optional. An occurrence with no published edition — a researcher's own catalogued manuscript or fragment — still appears as a full evidence row. Evidence is never gated on the existence of a published edition. Paired-edition bridging. When an occurrence is catalogued against more than one edition — say a modern critical edition and an early printed one — the row bridges them in the classics convention: the modern citation first, then = volume.page (abbreviated editor) for the paired edition. The abbreviations and locators are your data; the bridge composition is the platform's. Citation appearance (punctuation, abbreviated author forms, locale) is managed through CSL styles, not by editing rendered text. If a citation looks rough, the fix is a style refinement — see the review workflow below and the troubleshooting table.
documents.s: Reference evidence and citations on published entries

documents.t: When your environment publishes entries, the outside world can rely on: A rendered citation on each published entry, produced against your active CSL style · Maturity: Built. The same citation in CSL JSON at a stable address per entry, ready for import into reference managers · Maturity: Built. Typed API access through which an integration partner reads published data under the same visibility rules as the reading interface · Maturity: Built. Machine-readable semantic export formats — JSON-LD representations of published entries and research-object packaging for archival hand-off — are committed in the platform's architecture but not yet available. The standards overview records the current maturity of each format; point a federation partner there rather than promising a format ahead of its maturity tag. Exports are produced by the platform; your environment does not build or maintain a custom export pipeline. What is yours is the data, the wording, and the entry-type design — not the export machinery.

The day-to-day operator paths: Pick a citation style at environment setup: the platform's citation-style service lets you browse the shipped catalog and adopt a style per entry type. A dedicated configuration screen is not yet available — the service is operated through the platform's administrative citation endpoints, and your platform operator can run the selection with you. A style that is not in the catalog can be installed on request. Declare a field's standards conformance: edit the field definition and choose from the platform's approved standards list. A declaration outside the list is rejected with a validation message when you save. Review new vocabulary values: work the review queue through the Vocabulary Grounding workflow. When AI suggestions are enabled, a suggestion can reference a matching Wikidata or PeriodO record to inform your decision. Answer "what standards does our knowledge environment comply with?": point the asker to the standards overview. It is written for exactly that conversation, and its maturity tags distinguish what ships today from what is committed but still on the way.

When the active style renders roughly for your material, a style is refined through a three-step review path, so no one person silently changes how every citation reads: Propose. A proposed style (or a refinement of the active one) is generated from sample citations you want to match. The proposal is measured against your environment's pinned citation test cases and assigned a risk class (low / medium / high) based on how many existing citations it would change. Scholar review. A scholar reviews the proposed style, its differences from the active style, and its risk class before approving. Admin apply. Once scholar-approved, an administrator applies it. The style is stored in your environment — no code change is involved — and the platform refreshes published citations after the style is applied. Styles are versioned and never auto-applied by the platform; AI assistance never changes a published citation directly. The workflow runs through the platform's administrative citation endpoints today; a dedicated review screen is not yet available. Your platform operator can walk the three steps with you.
documents.s: Refining a citation style (the review workflow)

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A published entry shows no References section The entry type has no evidence declaration — the platform does not guess where evidence lives Declare it on the entry type: the occurrence record type, the connecting link, and the locator and source columns. Evidence rows appear but without formatted citations No citation rules declared for the entry type, or the chosen citation style was not found Add citation rules mapping your columns to the standard citation fields, and confirm the style name matches an installed style exactly. Citations render with awkward punctuation or separators The active CSL style has not been refined for your material Refine the style through the review workflow (scholar reviews, admin applies). Do not hand-edit rendered text — the next refresh would overwrite it. An internal reference code appears inside a rendered row A locator or source-detail declaration points at a linking column rather than a plain-text column Re-point the declaration at the human-readable column; linking columns belong only in the join declaration. A style your researchers need is not pre-loaded CSL is an open standard; the style file is portable XML Contact your platform operator to install it. Provide the CSL file or a published style URL. A standards declaration is rejected when you save a field definition The declared standard is not on the platform's approved list Choose a standard from the list, or ask your platform operator to evaluate adding the one you need. The list is deliberately narrow: every entry on it is one the platform can stand behind. A vocabulary value cannot be declared or rejected from the review queue The acting account lacks the review permission for grounding decisions Ask an environment administrator to take the decision, or to grant your role the review permission — see Permissions Panel. A federation partner needs a machine-readable export format Semantic export formats are committed but not yet available Point the partner at the maturity tags in the standards overview, and raise the need with your platform operator. Neither you nor the partner should have to take a conformance claim on faith.

Cross-audience parent: Standards & Compliance Overview. Tenant admin companions: Citation Integrity — the published-citation guarantees in detail; Vocabulary Grounding — the Wikidata / PeriodO workflow; Voice and Vocabulary — your wording on platform surfaces; Telemetry — what the platform records and how it is protected.

The platform collects a deliberately small set of operational signals about how it runs — never a copy of your research content. This page tells you what those signals are, where they live, how long they are kept, what you control, and what to tell an institutional DPO or IRB. Read it when onboarding under a Data Processing Agreement, when an institution's information-security team asks the standard onboarding questions, or before enabling any optional capture. The default posture is capture-off: AI-call, import-run, and review-decision capture record nothing until switched on for your environment. The one exception is tip-activity capture, which starts on — with its own off switch — so that unhelpful tip categories can pause automatically.

AI-call records — for each AI call the platform makes on your environment's behalf, a structured record: the task, the model and its version, token counts, latency, a refusal or escalation flag, and the verdict of a prompt-injection screening check. The record carries one-way hashes of the prompt and response — never the raw text. A call whose prompt matches a high-risk personal-data pattern (such as an identification number) is dropped entirely: no record, no hash, no count. Maturity: Active. Import-run records — for each import run: the source format, entity counts before and after, error categories (never error values), and duration. By construction these records contain no personal data: raw source rows, filenames, staged file paths, document and table names, and credential references are deliberately not recorded. Maturity: Active. Review-decision records — structured signals from suggestion review: reject, undo, edit-after-apply, and feedback-button events, each with a structured reason code. The record carries a keyed fingerprint of the suggestion's shape, not its content, and never records free-form reviewer comments. Maturity: Active. Tip-activity records — which efficiency tips surfaced and whether they were accepted, aggregated into acceptance ratios that drive the automatic pausing of unhelpful tip categories. Tip records carry no researcher identity at all — which tip appeared and what happened to it, never who. Automatic pausing acts on a tip category only once it has at least five recorded responses (the default minimum sample), so it never reacts to a single researcher's actions. Supports the Efficiency Tips surface. Maturity: Active. Search-quality records — planned aggregate measures of search health (zero-result rates, hashed query patterns with small-count suppression). This signal class is not capturing yet: today the platform stores no search-query telemetry at all, raw or hashed. Maturity: Deferred. Per-environment capture switches — capture is controlled per signal class for each environment, and every switch starts off except the tip-activity pair, which starts on. Enabling review-decision capture additionally requires a recorded privacy acknowledgment (who acknowledged, when, and which version of the privacy notice) before the switch will take effect. Maturity: Active. Environment telemetry panel — a dashboard showing your environment's own signals: counts per signal class, a suggestion-quality summary, and any automatically paused suggestion categories. It reads only your environment's records and never displays raw source rows, filenames, file paths, credentials, or tokens. Maturity: Active. Telemetry export for access requests — a self-service, audit-grade export of your environment's telemetry is planned but not yet available. Today, your platform operator produces the export for you on request. Maturity: Deferred.

Read what is happening in your environment: open /admin/monitoring/telemetry/. The panel shows your environment's signal counts by class, the suggestion-quality summary, and any paused automatic-suggestion categories. It is scoped to your environment only; cross-environment comparisons exist only on the platform operator's side. Turn capture on or off: capture switches live on your environment's platform record and are changed through the platform's administrative console — contact your platform operator to change your capture posture. Each signal class is switched independently; everything except tip-activity capture starts off. Enable review-decision capture: this switch requires a privacy acknowledgment to be recorded first. The acknowledgment (person, timestamp, notice version) is stored with your environment's record and is enforced — the switch cannot be turned on without it. Control efficiency-tip capture: tip surfacing and tip-event capture each have their own switch on your environment's record. Both are currently on by default. Tip-event capture continues while both switches are on, even where other capture classes are off — this keeps the automatic pausing of unhelpful tips working. See Efficiency Tips. Honor a data-access request (GDPR Article 15): contact your platform operator, who produces a telemetry export scoped to your environment. Honor an erasure request (GDPR Article 17): see the right-by-right table below; route the request through your platform operator. The configurable settings, summarized: Setting What it does Default Per-signal capture switches Turn each telemetry class (AI calls, import runs, review decisions) on or off for your environment. Changed by your platform operator. Off Review-decision privacy acknowledgment Required before review-decision capture can be enabled; records who acknowledged, when, and which notice version. Not acknowledged Tip surfacing Whether efficiency tips appear at all in your environment. On Tip-event capture Whether tip surface/acceptance events are recorded, independently of other capture classes. On Minimum sample for automatic tip pausing The number of recorded tip responses a category needs before automatic pausing will act on it, so the mechanism never reacts to a single researcher's actions. Changing it is a platform-level change — ask your platform operator. 5

Each environment's data lives in its own separate compartment of the database — its own database schema. The database itself enforces that isolation, and telemetry honors it: telemetry tables refuse to be read from outside an environment's schema. Data Where it lives Who can read it AI-call records (structure and hashes) Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only, for support) Import-run records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Review-decision records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Tip-activity records Your environment's schema You; platform team (read-only) Cross-environment operational metrics (cost, latency, model name) Platform-level storage; never your content Platform team only Cross-environment metric rows identify an environment by an internal identifier and carry model name, token counts, cost, and latency — never content.

The platform's default retention policy per data class: Data Default retention AI-call records (structured shape) 30 days verbatim, then 12 months as hashed aggregate Import-run records 12 months Validation and abuse audit records (security-relevant) 2 years (GDPR Art. 17(3)(e) — defence of legal claims) Confirmed prompt-injection material (quarantined) 90 days; extendable under legal hold for specific incidents These defaults are calibrated against ICO and EDPB operational-log guidance, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control A.8.15, and EU AI Act logging requirements. For retention questions beyond this table — including shorter environment-specific retention — contact your platform operator.

Right How the platform handles it Access (Art. 15) Your platform operator produces a telemetry export scoped to your environment, with an accompanying manifest. Rectification (Art. 16) Not applicable to operational telemetry. For environment content, rectification flows through the standard editing surfaces. Erasure (Art. 17) User-identifying telemetry rows are pseudonymized in place. Small-count-suppressed aggregates are retained as anonymous data (Art. 17(3)(d)). Restriction (Art. 18) Verbatim capture for a specific person can be suppressed on request while anonymous aggregates continue. Portability (Art. 20) Same export format as Article 15. Object (Art. 21) Per-person suppression on request; an environment-level objection turns the signal class off entirely. Automated decision-making (Art. 22) The platform does not make automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on data subjects. AI output is advisory; researcher review gates any change to your data. Lawful basis is Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f)), with a documented assessment per signal class available from your platform operator. A data-protection impact assessment precedes production capture and is refreshed annually; environment-specific documentation is available on request.

Third party What they see AI model vendor Under the platform's standard routing, AI calls run inside a cloud provider's hosted model service, and the model vendor does not receive your data. Confirm the routing in force for your environment with your platform operator. Cloud provider hosting the model service Runs the model on each call; provider-side invocation logging is kept off, so the provider retains only the call envelope (model, role, timing) — not prompts or responses. Platform team Read-only access to your environment's schema for support; access to platform-level operational metrics (cost, latency — never your content). Anyone else Nothing. No third-party analytics, advertising, or telemetry services.

When an environment offboards, its database schema is dropped — all telemetry payload in it is deleted, including every aggregate stored there. Cross-environment operational metrics (cost and latency at the platform level) are retained for cost-history continuity; they identify the environment only by an internal identifier and contain no content. On request, that metric trail can be deleted too; the trade-off is the loss of platform-level cost-trend history for the periods your environment participated in.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The telemetry panel shows no signals Capture is off — the default for every signal class except tip activity. Search-quality telemetry is not capturing yet for anyone. Ask your platform operator to enable the signal classes you need. Review-decision capture also requires the privacy acknowledgment to be recorded first. An import run reports that a stored service credential could not be retrieved The stored credential for that import source is missing, expired, or unreachable Check the import source's connection settings, or contact your platform operator. The telemetry row records the outcome only — no credential material is ever in a telemetry record. A DPO asks for the legitimate-interest assessment per signal class The assessment is maintained per signal class as platform documentation Contact your platform operator, who supplies the documented assessment for the signal classes in question. A researcher exercises the right to be forgotten Handling depends on the data class User-identifying telemetry rows are pseudonymized in place; anonymous aggregates are retained as anonymous data. Route the request through your platform operator. You want to verify no raw search queries are stored Raw query text is not captured at all in the current platform — the search-quality signal class is not yet capturing in any form Nothing to configure. When search-quality telemetry ships, it will store hashed, small-count-suppressed aggregates, not raw queries.

For researchers: Privacy and safety. Environment admin companions: Permissions Panel — the Project history tab records who reviewed what, and when; Efficiency Tips — the tip-capture switches. For platform-level monitoring, data-protection impact assessment records, or residency requirements, contact your platform operator.

When your records bring in vocabulary the platform does not already recognize — today, calendar names appearing in your data and standard identifiers declared on your field definitions — the platform collects each new value in a review queue instead of guessing what it means. Grounding is that review step: you decide, value by value, whether each one becomes a recognized part of your environment's vocabulary, with a label of your choosing and optional links to recognized scholarly and data standards. Read this when you are working through the review queue after an import, when you want AI help proposing matches against public reference sources, or when a researcher reports that a vocabulary value was reviewed incorrectly.

Vocabulary review queue — every watched vocabulary value first seen in your data appears in a review list, with its category, how often it occurs, and its review status (shown as Ungrounded, Tenant-declared, Promoted, or Rejected). Maturity: Active. Limit: the platform currently watches two categories — calendar names in your records and standard identifiers on your field definitions; queue rows are created by the platform from your data, and you cannot add rows by hand. Declare a value — accept a value into your environment's vocabulary, with an optional display label (leave it blank to use the value itself) and optional links to standards from the platform's recognized list (TEI, CIDOC-CRM, IIIF, CSL, and others). Maturity: Active. Limit: within one vocabulary category, two declared values cannot share the same label. Reject a value — mark a value as not belonging to your vocabulary, with an optional reason kept for the audit record. Maturity: Active. AI grounding suggestions — when enabled for your environment, the platform can propose a grounding for a queued value: a suggested label, suggested standards, and — where a match exists — a reference to a public authority record. Wikidata supplies candidates for entities and concepts; PeriodO supplies candidates for historical periods, including each period's time range and regional coverage as the authority describes them. Maturity: Built. Limit: suggestions cover common reference-data categories only (calendars, standards, place types, period types, media kinds, languages, scripts); there is not yet a button in the review queue for requesting one — suggestions are requested through the platform's administrative API, and the review queue shows a notice when suggestions are available but not yet switched on for your environment. Privacy screening for external lookups — before any value is sent to an external reference source, the platform classifies it. Only values that are clearly public reference data are looked up externally; values that resemble personal or private data are never sent outside your environment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the screen is deliberately cautious — a blocked lookup costs you a manual check, never a data leak. Decision capture on AI suggestions — each decision you take on an AI suggestion (accepted as-is, edited before applying, rejected) is recorded as a structured signal for audit and quality measurement. Maturity: Active. Limit: these records stay within your environment. AI usage controls — AI suggestions are switched off by default for each environment, and usage is capped by a rolling token budget. When the budget runs out, suggestions pause and manual review continues unaffected. Maturity: Active. Limit: the budget has a platform-defined maximum. AI availability notice — a fixed, platform-written notice on the review queue tells you when AI suggestions are available but switched off for your environment. Administrators who manage permissions see a link to the settings page; other reviewers see guidance to ask their administrator. Maturity: Active. Limit: the wording is platform-controlled and cannot be customized.

The review queue lives in your environment's admin interface, alongside the other vocabulary surfaces. Work the queue after an import: open the ungrounded vocabulary list. Filter by category or by review status to focus on what is new. Each row shows the value, its category, and how many times it occurs in your data. Declare one or more values: select the rows, choose the declare action, and confirm on the follow-up page. You can set a shared label (or leave it blank so each value becomes its own label) and pick any standards the values comply with from the provided list. Declared values stop appearing as unreviewed in future imports. Reject values that do not belong: select the rows, choose the reject action, and optionally record a reason on the follow-up page. The reason is kept with the audit record. Turn AI suggestions on: AI suggestions are off until enabled for your environment. When the feature is available, the notice at the top of the review queue links administrators with permission-management access to the settings page; see Permissions Panel. Enabling AI suggestions and adjusting the token budget are administrator-only actions; if you do not find these controls on the settings page, contact your platform operator. Trust re-imports: re-importing your data never resets a review decision. A value you have already declared or rejected keeps its status; the platform only updates how often it occurs. Every grounding decision — declare or reject, manual or AI-assisted — is written to the platform audit log with the acting administrator, the value, and the outcome.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The declare action refuses your label Another declared value in the same vocabulary category already uses that label (capitalization does not matter) Choose a different label, or leave the label blank so each value is labeled as itself. A standard you want to link is not offered in the list The standards list is platform-managed; only recognized standards can be attached Declare the value with the standards available now. To request an addition to the list, contact your platform operator. An AI suggestion arrives without an external reference, or marked as reduced confidence The privacy screen blocked the external lookup, or the public source returned no match — the suggestion was produced from the value alone The suggestion is still usable. Review it manually before accepting, or reject it and declare the value yourself. AI suggestions stop arriving partway through a session Your environment's rolling token budget is used up, or AI suggestions were switched off — either in your environment's settings or platform-wide Manual review keeps working. Check your environment's AI settings; if the feature is unavailable platform-wide, contact your platform operator. A value you already reviewed shows as unreviewed after a re-import This should not happen — re-imports never reset review decisions Contact your platform operator with the affected value and the import date. You want to change the wording of the AI availability notice The notice is platform-controlled and cannot be edited per environment Share environment-specific guidance with your reviewers through your own channels rather than working around the notice.

Voice and Vocabulary — configuring the wording your researchers see across the platform. AI-Assisted Bootstrap — the one-pass onboarding path that can run alongside grounding review. Standards overview — which scholarly and data standards the platform recognizes and what each enables.

The platform talks to your researchers constantly — page headers, button labels, confirmation phrases, tips, chat copy. Voice and vocabulary is how you make that text speak your environment's language instead of generic platform English. Read this when onboarding a new environment, when a researcher asks "why does it say X?", or when a platform phrase needs to use your wording. Wording configuration is an environment-admin concern; researchers see the result but do not edit it. It applies only to text the platform itself emits — researcher-authored content is never reworded.

Per-environment wording entries — every platform-emitted phrase resolves through a wording table scoped to your environment, one entry per phrase. Surface families displayed today: import wizard pages, workspace headers and toolbar labels, assistant chat copy, permission and role wording, and telemetry panel labels. Maturity: Active. Limit: an entry only takes effect where the platform actually asks for that phrase. Built-in baseline with your labels substituted — every environment starts with a complete neutral-English baseline, and the platform automatically substitutes the names you gave your concept families (the categories your records belong to — "Person", "Place", "Text") into those phrases. A fresh environment already speaks in its own category names before anyone writes a wording entry. Maturity: Active. Layered resolution — for each phrase, the platform uses the most specific wording available: an explicit override set for your environment, then an AI suggestion you accepted during onboarding, then wording seeded during setup, then the baseline. Maturity: Active. Visible failure instead of blank text — if a phrase has no entry and no baseline, the platform renders the phrase's internal dotted key (for example wizard.stage3.match_card.header) rather than showing nothing. A raw key on screen is a signal, not your configuration error. Maturity: Active. Permission wording overrides — role names and permission labels can be renamed from the Permissions Panel. Renaming changes the displayed wording only, never what the role can do. Maturity: Active. AI suggestion provenance — a wording entry that came from an accepted AI suggestion carries a tamper-evident reference to the suggestion it came from. Maturity: Active. Limit: tamper-evident, not hidden — it proves origin, it does not encrypt anything. Two further families prepared, not yet displayed — the wording table also holds confirmation phrases for high-impact actions and review-history labels. Both are seeded with baseline wording, but no screen displays either family yet, so entries for them have no visible effect today. Having or lacking your own phrasing for these never blocks an action or locks any part of onboarding. Maturity: Built.

The highest-leverage move is naming your concept families well. Most of what researchers read is the baseline with those names substituted in, so a good set of category labels improves hundreds of phrases at once. Name your concept families: set the display label for each category of record your environment manages. This normally happens while you confirm an import; the labels can also be edited afterwards in your environment's admin area. Every platform phrase that mentions the category updates. Rename roles and permission wording: open the Permissions Panel and edit the role's displayed name inline. The underlying permissions are unchanged. Accept AI wording suggestions at onboarding: see AI-Assisted Bootstrap for the assisted onboarding path that proposes environment-specific phrasings for you to accept or reject. Act on the wording review notice: the Permissions Panel shows a read-only review notice when concept-family labels are missing or look machine-generated. Fix the flagged labels; the notice can also be dismissed, but it returns if your labels change again. Override a specific phrase: there is currently no self-service screen for editing an individual wording entry. If a specific platform phrase needs different wording and the paths above do not cover it, contact your platform operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A platform phrase shows generic wording in your environment No environment-specific wording exists for that phrase, so the baseline is rendering Check that the concept family the phrase mentions has a display label — that fixes most generic-sounding phrases. For a specific phrase that still needs different wording, contact your platform operator. A page shows a raw dotted key like wizard.stage3.match_card.header instead of readable text The phrase has no wording entry and no baseline — the platform deliberately shows the key so the gap is visible This indicates a platform-side gap, not an error in your configuration. Contact your platform operator. The wording review notice in the Permissions Panel returns after you dismissed it Dismissal applies to the labels as they were; the notice reappears when your labels change Fix the flagged labels rather than re-dismissing. The notice is read-only and never changes anything itself. You renamed a role but its permissions did not change Renaming a role changes its displayed wording only This is the intended behaviour. To change what a role can do, compose a custom role in the Permissions Panel.

Researcher tier: Workspace walkthrough — what researchers see (your wording in action). Tenant admin companions: AI-Assisted Bootstrap — assisted onboarding wording suggestions; Vocabulary Grounding — a different surface: grounding the research vocabulary in your data against external authorities; Permissions Panel — role renaming and the wording review notice.

This page is the reference for the configuration records that shape what researchers see in the workspace: the table records behind every entry in the workspace sidebar, the display field that names each record, the default column set, the ontology entries that label your environment's concept families, and the environment-wide saved views. Read it after an import has landed a new table, when renaming or reordering tables, when record labels look wrong, or when curating the views your whole team shares.

Admin-self-serve. Renaming a table, changing its icon, hiding it, reordering the sidebar, setting the display field, choosing default columns, and curating saved views are all yours to change in the administration interface. Re-importing source data never reverts a table's label, icon, or order once you have edited them. Import-maintained. Workspace table records and ontology entries are created automatically when imported data is applied — you do not create them by hand for imported sources. The import also maintains a read-only record of which display column the source itself declared, and refreshes the ontology entries (including the anchor) each time an import is applied. Operator-mediated. Environments configured from a declaration file rather than through the import wizard receive their initial tables, labels, and anchor from a seeding run performed by your platform operator. Re-running that seeding converges on the declared file — if you change those values by hand, tell your operator so the declaration is updated to match.
documents.s: What you change yourself, and what the platform maintains

documents.t: Workspace table records — one record per table in the researcher workspace. Each record carries the table's label, an icon name from the Material icon set, an active flag, and a sidebar position (lower numbers appear first). Switching the active flag off hides the table from the sidebar without deleting anything. Maturity: Active. Limit: deleting a table record deletes its saved views with it — hide rather than delete unless you mean to discard the views too. Record labels from the display field — the display field is the data column shown as each record's name in the table, in search results, and on linked-record chips. It is written as a data path to one of the table's columns, in the form data.<column name>. It is set from the source's declared display column at import and refreshed on re-import only while you have not edited it — your edit always wins. A second, read-only field records what the source declared at the most recent import, so the platform can tell your edit apart from an import-written value. When the display field is blank, records show a visible placeholder rather than a guessed column. Maturity: Active. Default visible columns — an optional list of field names that render as the table's columns by default; leaving it empty shows all fields. This is the environment's default for the table; researchers' own column arrangements and saved views sit on top of it. Maturity: Active. Limit: the underlying field definitions can still be shared across a concept family, so two source tables that share one concept family may expose a broader shared field set until their views hide irrelevant columns. Table scoping — each table shows the records of one concept family (the configuration forms call this an archetype), optionally narrowed to a single record type and a single source table. Two source tables that share a record type stay two distinct tables rather than merging. When a source renames a table while keeping its stable identity, the platform reuses the existing record so saved views survive, leaves your label untouched, and adds a warning suggesting you review it. Maturity: Active. Limit: table records are scoped per source table, but field-definition scoping is not yet as narrow as table identity in every import shape; curate the default view after large cold imports. Advanced filter setting — a reserved setting on each table record for filtering a table beyond its record type. The workspace does not yet apply it to the rows researchers see; the import writes its own source-table scope into it, and that is the only shape in use. Maturity: Deferred. Limit: entering a custom value today makes the table's scope ambiguous, which switches off in-table record creation, relation editing, and table publishing for that table — leave it as the import wrote it. Ontology entries — each entry pairs a platform concept family with the label your environment uses for it, an optional record type that narrows it, and an anchor flag. The anchor marks the concept family your environment is organized around; the platform allows at most one. Maturity: Active. Limit: these entries are import-maintained — applying an import refreshes the labels and recomputes the anchor from the approved import decisions, so treat this list as something you read and verify; raise a lasting change with your platform operator. Environment-wide saved views — named views attached to a table, each storing filter conditions, sort order, column arrangement (order, visibility, pinning, sizing), row density (compact, cozy, or comfortable), and row color rules, plus the view mode it opens: Table, Details, Relations, or Publish. A view can be pinned to the primary tab row, and one view per table can be the default. Every saved view is shared with everyone working in the environment. Maturity: Active. Limit: the database allows at most one default view per table.

The records on this page live in your environment's administration interface. The administration sidebar lists each active workspace table by its label — these entries open the researcher workspace itself, with a badge showing the record count — and ends with + Add table, which opens the form for a new table record. The Tenant Ontology entry in the same sidebar section opens the ontology list. Rename a table, change its icon, or reorder the sidebar. Open the table record and edit the label; the icon, sidebar position, and active flag can also be changed directly in the list of table records. Researchers see the new label and order in their workspace sidebar. A later re-import does not undo these edits. Hide a table without deleting it. Switch the active flag off. The record, its configuration, and its saved views all remain, and the table returns intact when you switch the flag back on. Deleting the record instead removes its saved views permanently. Set which column names each record. In the table record's display section, set the display field to a data path such as data.<column name>, pointing at a column every record fills. The read-only companion field beside it shows which column the source declared — if you prefer the source's choice after editing, copy that value back in. Clearing the display field makes records show a placeholder instead of a name. Choose the default columns. Fill the default-columns list with the field names to show; leave it empty to show every field. Researchers can still arrange their own columns, and saved views carry their own column arrangement. Curate first views after import. After a cold import with several source tables under one concept family, open each workspace table before researchers begin using it. If a table shows fields that belong to a neighboring source table, hide those fields in the default saved view and keep the table label source-specific so researchers can tell the tables apart. Read the ontology. The ontology list shows each concept family's label, its optional record type, and which one is the anchor. Verify it after an import; a label that needs to change durably should go through your import decisions or your platform operator, because the next import apply refreshes this list. Curate saved views. Saved views and the views researchers create in the workspace are the same records — there is no separate admin-only kind, and every view is visible to the whole environment. The administration list shows each view's name, table, stable address key (the segment workspace addresses use), view mode, density, order, pinned flag, and default flag; the pinned and default flags and the ordering can be edited directly in the list. A view's stored state — filters, sort, column arrangement, color rules — is easiest to shape by arranging the view in the workspace itself, where changes are stored as you work; the form exposes the same state for inspection and repair. Set the default view. Mark one view per table as the default; it is what the table opens with, for everyone. The database enforces at most one default per table, so clear the current default before assigning a new one.

Symptom Likely cause Fix An import created two similar-looking tables Two source tables share one record type; each source table becomes its own workspace table by design Rename the labels so researchers can tell them apart, or hide the one not in use. A table shows columns from a related source table The table record is scoped per source table, but the field definitions can still be shared at the concept-family level Hide the irrelevant columns in the table's default saved view. Escalate if the field set itself must be separated by source table. Records show a placeholder instead of a name The table's display field is blank — the source declared no display column — or it points at a column many records leave empty Set the display field to a data.<column name> path for a column every record fills. A re-import did not pick up the source's new display column You edited the display field, and your edit always wins over the import Compare with the read-only companion field showing what the source declared, and copy that value in if you want the source's choice. Creating records or editing relations is unavailable in one table, or the table cannot be published The table record carries a custom advanced-filter value, which makes its scope ambiguous Remove the custom additions from the advanced filter, keeping only what the import wrote. Marking a second view as the default fails A table can have at most one default view; the database enforces it Clear the default flag on the current default and save, then mark the new view. Saved views disappeared after a table was removed Deleting a table record deletes its saved views with it Restore from your environment's backup if available. Going forward, hide tables with the active flag instead of deleting them. Your ontology label edits were reverted Applying an import refreshes ontology entries, including labels and the anchor Make the label change part of your import decisions, or ask your platform operator to update the environment's declaration.

Same tree: Data Import Wizard — the import flow that creates these table records and maintains the source-declared display column. Researcher tier: Save your table arrangement as a view — how researchers create, duplicate, and share the same saved views you curate here; Workspace Walkthrough — what researchers see once these records are in place.

A new person is joining your environment mid-project — a research assistant, a co-investigator, a visiting scholar, or a short-term contributor who needs access for a few weeks. This page is the start-to-finish sequence for getting them from "no account" to "working in the right tables with the right role." It also marks clearly which steps are yours to do and which only your platform operator can do, so you know where to wait and where to act. Read this when someone new is arriving. For the new collaborator's own first session, hand them the researcher tutorial — Getting started — once their access is ready.

Onboarding has two owners. The account itself is created by your platform operator; everything about what the collaborator can do inside your environment is yours to configure on the Permissions Panel. Step Who does it Where 1. Decide the role and scope You Plan ahead — no UI yet 2. Request the account You ask; operator creates Outside your environment 3. Assign the role You Permissions Panel → Contributors 4. Prepare the workspace You Workspace views and sidebar 5. Brief the collaborator You Point them at the researcher tutorial 6. Verify their access You and the collaborator Permissions Panel + a check from their side You can do steps 1, 3, and 4 yourself. Step 2 depends on your platform operator. Steps 5 and 6 involve the collaborator directly.

Decide what the person should be able to do before the account exists, so you can assign a role the moment they appear in your Contributors list. Every environment ships with a standard role catalog: Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin. Match the person to the closest standard role: A reviewing scholar who reads and comments but should not save changes → Reviewer. A guest from outside the project making small additive changes in one area → External collaborator. A team researcher doing routine editing → Researcher contributor. A co-director who needs configuration and role-management authority → Project admin. If no standard role fits, compose a custom one from the platform's fixed set of permission building blocks on the Permissions Panel's Roles tab, and name it. You combine existing permissions; you cannot define new ones. See User and Access Management for the standard catalog and Permissions Panel for composition. A new contributor starts with a baseline set of permissions: they can review suggestions, save routine (low- and medium-impact) changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups. They do not start with the ability to apply high-impact changes, configure fields, or manage permissions — those are granted deliberately, by assigning a role that includes them. Keep this in mind when matching a visiting or temporary collaborator to a role: the safe default already withholds the high-authority actions. You can also narrow where a role applies. A role assignment — or a custom role — can be scoped to specific record types or fields, so a collaborator working on one collection does not gain reach across the whole environment. This is the right tool for a visiting scholar who should touch one area only.
documents.s: 1. Choose or compose the role before they arrive

documents.t: Contributor accounts are created by your platform operator, not from inside your environment. Send the operator the person's details and ask them to create the account. This is the one step you cannot complete yourself; until the operator finishes, the person will not appear in your Contributors list.

Once the operator confirms the account exists, the person appears in the Contributors tab of the Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/. Open their row, pick the standard or custom role you decided on in step 1, and — if appropriate — set a scope on the same row to limit the role to specific record types or fields. If your environment has a project rule requiring a second contributor to confirm high-impact changes, that rule already applies to the new collaborator; you do not configure it per person. Project rules are environment-wide and sit on top of every role.

Make the collaborator's first session land them somewhere useful rather than on a raw table. Shared default view. Each table has one default view — the view that opens when anyone first visits that table. If your team has agreed on a working view (its filters, sort, and columns), set it as the default so the new person sees the same starting point as everyone else. The default is shared across the team, so this one action prepares the workspace for the collaborator without any per-person setup. See Save a view. Sidebar organization. The sidebar lists your environment's tables. If your environment groups or orders tables for clarity, that organization is already in place for the new collaborator; there is nothing per-person to configure.

Tell the collaborator three things and then let the product teach the rest: Their work is safe to explore — drafts do not publish by accident, and recent changes can be undone. Reading comes before writing — they can search and read existing records before editing anything. Help is built in — the contextual help is available without leaving the workspace. For everything beyond that, point them at the researcher tutorial: Getting started. It walks a new researcher through their first week — signing in, finding the team's default view, reading, and making safe first edits — so you do not have to write your own orientation.
documents.s: 5. Brief the collaborator on day one

documents.t: Confirm two things before you consider onboarding done. From your side: on the Permissions Panel's Contributors tab, the collaborator shows the role you assigned, with the scope you intended. From their side: ask the collaborator to open the search and reading area and look for a note about hidden collections. The platform shows a banner — "N collections are hidden — they require a review capability you don't hold" — whenever a person's role does not include the review capability some collections require. If the collaborator sees that banner and you intended them to have full access, their role is too narrow; widen it on the Contributors tab. If you intended to restrict them, the banner confirms the restriction is working. This from-their-side check catches scope mismatches that the Contributors tab alone can hide.
documents.s: 6. Verify their access — including a check from their side

documents.t: A visiting or short-term collaborator is onboarded the same way, with two adjustments: Prefer a scoped role. Limit the role to the record types or fields they need rather than granting environment-wide reach. The baseline new-contributor permissions already withhold high-impact actions; a scope narrows reach further. Plan the wind-down. When the visit ends, change or remove their role on the Contributors tab. Removing the account itself is a platform-operator action, like creating it — ask the operator to deactivate or remove the account when access should end entirely.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The new person does not appear in the Contributors tab The account has not been created yet Contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Confirm the operator has created the account; until then there is no row to assign a role to. You assigned a role but the collaborator cannot act on content they should Their role assignment carries a scope that excludes that content Open their row on the Contributors tab and check the scope. Widen it or remove it. The collaborator sees a "collections are hidden" note Their role does not include the review capability some collections require If they should have access, assign or compose a role that includes that capability. If the restriction is intended, this is working as configured. See Permissions Panel. No standard role matches what the collaborator needs The standard catalog is fixed Compose a custom role from the available permission building blocks on the Roles tab. If the permission you need does not exist in the platform's set at all, contact your platform operator. You need to remove a departing collaborator's account entirely Account removal is a platform-operator action Change or remove their role on the Contributors tab to cut access immediately, and ask your platform operator to deactivate or remove the account itself.

Where you do the work: Permissions Panel — assigning roles, composing custom roles, and scoping assignments. The role model in one page: User and Access Management — the standard role catalog and how contributor accounts are created. For the collaborator: Getting started — the researcher tutorial to hand off on day one. Preparing the workspace: Save a view — setting the shared default view a new collaborator lands on.

A re-import brings a refreshed copy of source data you have imported before into your environment. Most re-imports are routine: the source gained a few rows, corrected some values, or grew a new column, and you want the environment to reflect that. This page is for the planning that happens before you press start — checking what would change, choosing how records are refreshed, and reading the practice run — so a refresh updates your data without quietly overwriting work your researchers have done. Read this before re-running a source you have imported once already, especially if researchers have been editing those records in the workspace since the first import. This page covers the planning and the choices. For the wizard's screens, size limits, and step-by-step controls, see Data Import Wizard. For what your researchers see afterwards, see the cross-links at the end.

A re-import is routine when: The source gained rows, or corrected values in fields the source manages. The source grew a new column you want as a new field. Nobody has hand-edited the affected records inside the workspace, so there are no researcher edits to protect. A re-import deserves a careful plan when: Researchers have edited records in the workspace since the last import — added notes, set field labels, marked fields required, or filled in fields the source does not manage. The source dropped or renamed columns that your researchers rely on. You are not certain which refresh behaviour a planned run will use. The wizard itself never publishes anything and writes nothing to your environment until you press Start import in the final step. The risk is not in opening the wizard. It is in choosing the wrong refresh behaviour for a source whose records carry researcher edits.
documents.s: When a re-import is routine, and when it is risky

documents.t: Researcher edits are the thing a re-import can put at risk, so locate them before you plan the run. Open the affected tables in the workspace and look for records that have been worked on since the last import — filled-in fields the source does not provide, renamed field labels, required flags, or notes. Field configuration you set — labels, required flags, field-level settings — is preserved across a re-import regardless of refresh behaviour. It is the record values that researchers entered into fields the source does not manage that depend on which behaviour you choose. If researchers have been working in these tables and you cannot tell what they changed, treat the run as risky and plan for the edit-preserving behaviour described below.
documents.s: Before you run: check for researcher edits

documents.t: The platform supports two behaviours for refreshing the records themselves. The difference is what happens to anything a researcher added that the source does not manage. Behaviour What it keeps What it replaces When to use Edit-preserving refresh Researcher edits to fields the source does not manage, on records it can match Only the values the source manages, refreshed from the new data The right default for routine re-runs Full refresh Nothing from the prior records Everything — the existing rows are removed and reloaded from scratch Only a genuine "start over", when you intend to discard prior records and their researcher edits Edit-preserving refresh matches each incoming row to an existing record by the record's source identity — the stable identifier carried from the first import — then refreshes the source-managed values and leaves everything else alone. Where there is no match, it creates a new record. Full refresh does not match at all: it removes the existing rows and reloads, which discards any researcher edit those rows held. This choice is made by your platform operator, not in the wizard. Edit-preserving refresh and full refresh are run as platform commands, not as buttons inside the wizard. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, confirm it with your platform operator before the run — this is the single most important step in planning a safe re-import. State plainly which one you want and why.

When you re-import a source you have brought in before, the wizard works for you rather than starting over: It recognizes the saved setup from the earlier import. It carries your unchanged decisions forward instead of re-asking them, so you review only what is new, changed, or ambiguous. Anything new, changed, or genuinely uncertain goes back to review. Uncertainty always routes to review — it is never carried forward silently. This carry-forward is about the structural decisions you made (how a table is read, what a column becomes). It is separate from the record-refresh behaviour above, which governs the record values themselves.
documents.s: What the wizard does on a re-import

documents.t: The wizard's practice run is a full dry run that happens before anything is written. It is your last and best check on a re-import plan. It reports how many records will be created, updated, or skipped, and how many are blocked by unresolved review items. Issues are grouped by cause rather than scattered by row, with a good / warning / error breakdown, and each group links back to the review queue. For a re-import of mostly unchanged data, the practice run should show nearly all records ready rather than blocked, because carried-forward decisions are already accounted for. Read the practice run as a forecast of the real run. If the numbers do not match what you expect — far more records updated than rows changed, or a table predicted to create nothing — stop and find out why before pressing start. The practice run is also where the wizard predicts each table's outcome, so the final receipt should confirm what the practice run forecast.
documents.s: Reading the practice run before you commit

documents.t: A re-import surfaces to researchers as a delta — a summary of only what is new, changed, carried forward, removed, or restored since their last import. It does not ask them to re-review decisions already made. Point researchers at these entries so they can read their side of a re-import: Understand what changed after a re-import — how the delta reads, and the reassurance that their own edits and labels are not overwritten by an edit-preserving refresh. What happens to saved views after a re-import — how a saved view adapts when a field it referenced is removed in the new source, and how it is restored if that field returns.

The safe direction is to plan so that nothing needs undoing. But if a re-import has already written records you wish it had not: Records written by an import cannot be undone from inside the wizard. The wizard's undo applies to review decisions before the final run; it does not reverse records written when you press start. The verified recovery path is to restore the affected records from your environment's backup, then re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your platform operator runs imports for you, ask them to restore from backup and use the edit-preserving behaviour. This is operator-mediated work, not something you reverse yourself.
