A re-import that was interrupted mid-run — rather than completed wrongly — is a different case: the setup, approvals, and practice run are kept, and starting again resumes from the stopped table without writing completed tables twice. A run that did not finish cleanly is reconciled by your platform operator before the next attempt; it is not something to force past. The honest statement is that a full refresh over records with researcher edits is destructive and the records themselves are recovered only from backup, not from within the platform. Plan the behaviour choice carefully and you avoid needing recovery at all.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A re-import replaced researcher edits with source values The run used a full refresh, which removes and reloads rows, instead of an edit-preserving refresh Restore the affected records from your environment's backup, then re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your platform operator runs imports for you, ask them to use the edit-preserving behaviour. The wizard re-asked every decision as if this were a first import The earlier import was never completed through the final step, so there is no carried-forward baseline Check that the previous import finished through the wizard's last step. Only completed imports produce a baseline for carry-forward. The practice run shows far more records updated than rows actually changed in the source The run may be matching on an identity that shifts between imports, so records are not recognized as the same record Stop before pressing start. Confirm with your platform operator that the source identity used to match records is stable across imports. You are unsure which refresh behaviour a planned run will use The behaviour is chosen at run time by your platform operator, not in the wizard Ask your platform operator which behaviour the run will use, and state which one you want and why, before the run. A new re-import is blocked, citing a previous run that did not finish A prior run was interrupted and left in an unfinished state Do not force the run. Your platform operator reconciles the unfinished run first, then a new run can proceed.

The wizard itself: Data Import Wizard — the screens, size limits, six-step flow, and the autonomy setting. Who reviews and who applies: Permissions Panel — the two-step approval a re-import's suggestions pass through. For researchers: Understand what changed after a re-import and What happens to saved views after a re-import — the researcher's side of a re-import.

This tutorial walks a new environment from empty to its first published records. It sequences the work — what to do first, what can wait, and which steps your platform operator performs for you — and hands you off to the feature page for each task when you are ready to act. Follow it once, in order, when you are standing up a fresh environment. Each later visit, you will go straight to the feature page you need. The platform ships generic. Setup is how you make one environment speak your domain's language, decide who can do what, bring in your data under review, and put your first records in front of readers.

You need an environment that already exists and an account in it that holds the administrator role with permission management. Creating the environment and your first administrator account is platform-operator work, not something you do from inside the environment. If you are reading this without an environment to sign in to, that is the step to request first. Two divisions of labor recur throughout this tutorial, so it helps to name them now: Admin self-serve — you do it yourself from your environment's admin area. Operator-mediated — you prepare and review the work, but your platform operator runs the step that takes effect. This is true for creating contributor accounts, applying a citation style, and launching the public surface. The tutorial flags which kind each step is as you reach it.

Stage What you do Self-serve or operator-mediated 1. Voice and vocabulary Name your concept families; review the vocabulary arriving in your data Self-serve 2. Roles and contributors Compose the roles your team needs; invite the people You compose roles; the operator creates the accounts 3. First import Practice-run a source, choose an autonomy level, review proposals Self-serve 4. First published records Run the entry-surface readiness review, then launch You review; the operator launches Stages 1 and 2 can overlap — you can name concept families and compose roles in either order. Stage 3 depends on having concept families named, because the import wizard works in your category names. Stage 4 depends on having records to publish, so it comes last.

The single highest-leverage move in setup is naming your concept families — the categories your records belong to, such as Person, Place, or Text. Most of what a researcher reads is the platform's standard wording with those category names substituted into it, so a good set of labels improves hundreds of phrases at once before you write a single custom phrase. A fresh environment already speaks in neutral English and substitutes your category names into its phrases automatically. You do not start from blank screens; you start from a working baseline and shape it. Name your concept families. This normally happens while you confirm your first import (Stage 3), and the labels can also be edited afterwards in your environment's admin area. If you are setting up before you have data to import, you can still set the labels directly. Watch for the wording review notice. When concept-family labels are missing or look machine-generated, the Permissions Panel shows a read-only notice with the flagged labels. Fix them; the notice returns if your labels change again, so treat it as a running check rather than a one-time gate. Full detail on how wording resolves, role renaming, and the one phrase you cannot edit yourself (an individual platform phrase, which is operator-mediated today): Voice and Vocabulary.

Separate from the platform's own wording, your records bring in vocabulary the platform does not recognize — today, calendar names appearing in your data and standard identifiers declared on your field definitions. The platform collects each new value in a review queue rather than guessing. Grounding is where you decide, value by value, whether each becomes a recognized part of your environment's vocabulary, with a label you choose and optional links to recognized scholarly and data standards. You do not need to ground anything to keep working — the queue is there when you are ready, usually after your first import. AI grounding suggestions, which can propose a label and a match against public reference sources, are switched off by default and turned on per environment; only the tenant administrator role can confirm a grounding. When to come back to this: after Stage 3, once an import has populated the queue. Full detail: Vocabulary Grounding.

Decide who can do what before people arrive, so a new contributor lands in a role that already fits. Every environment ships with four standard roles — Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin — and you compose custom roles from a fixed set of permission building blocks when the standard roles do not fit. Renaming a standard role changes its displayed label only, never what it allows. Open the Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/. It opens on the Contributors tab; the other tabs are Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. Compose the roles your team needs. On the Roles tab, combine the permission building blocks and name the role. A role assignment can be narrowed to specific record types or fields, so a guest collaborator can be scoped to one part of your project. Set your project rules. On the Project rules tab, decide whether high-impact saves need a reviewer who did not author the change, and how destructive changes are confirmed. These rules tighten what a role allows; they never grant more. Invite your contributors — operator-mediated. Contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Once a person appears in the Contributors section, you assign their role there. So the sequence is: prepare the role, ask the operator to create the account, then assign the role when the person shows up in the panel. A new contributor's account starts able to review proposals, apply low- and medium-risk changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups — but not apply high-risk changes, configure fields, or manage permissions. Adjust from there with a role or a scoped assignment. Full detail: Permissions Panel for composing and assigning; User and Access Management for the standard role catalog and how accounts are created.

The Data Import Wizard is the supported path for getting data into an environment. It reads your source, proposes how each table and column should land, routes every proposal through a two-step approval, and writes records only when you press Start import in the final step. Nothing reaches your environment before that. Treat the first run as a practice run. The wizard's fifth step is a full dry run that writes nothing, so you can see exactly what would happen before committing. Start in the sidebar at Imports & AI → Imports. The wizard accepts an Excel workbook, a MySQL dump or live connection, a set of CSV files, or a Coda document. Start from an upload route — the plain admin "Add" form does not read a source. Choose how involved you want to be. Step 3 asks the autonomy question — Hands off, Stay informed, Ask if unsure, or Confirm everything — saved per import. For a first import you do not yet know well, a more involved setting holds more suggestions for your decision. High-risk and restructure suggestions wait for explicit review whatever the setting, and every automatic decision comes with an undo window. Read the practice run (Step 5). Issues are grouped by cause rather than by row, with a good/warning/error breakdown. This is where a misread table or a field you did not expect surfaces — before any record is written. Approve in two steps. A reviewer approves each suggestion, then an administrator applies it. If a suggestion's risk level shifted while it waited for review, the apply step blocks until you acknowledge the new level. Start the import (Step 6) once every suggestion is approved or rejected. Watch the per-table progress, read the completion receipt, and use Open your workspace to see the results. Naming your concept families (Stage 1) happens naturally here: confirming an import is the usual moment you give each category its display label. Full detail, including the four source types, background imports for large files, and re-import behavior: Data Import Wizard.

Once your data is in and your researchers have a working set of records, the last setup stage prepares the public surface external readers will see. Before your environment exposes a public Entry surface, the readiness panel lets you review the filter and autocomplete controls that would become public, record a decision about each one, and confirm or defer each candidate. It is a review surface, not an apply surface: recording decisions stores your review state and never changes the public surface by itself. Open the readiness panel. Sign in with an account that has admin access. The Entry Surface readiness panel currently lives in the transitional standalone shell at /app/admin/; daily operations and configuration tasks remain in the Django admin area at /admin/. The panel sits in the side column and loads the current report as the page opens. Work through each role's checklist. The report lists blockers, reviewed fields, candidate fields, and compact-control warnings — fields whose values are too long to show well in a compact public filter. Each decision requires a reason, and the decision is durable: the next report shows it. Hand off for launch — operator-mediated. When the report reads clean, your platform operator performs the public launch. The "ratification unchanged" indicator in the panel confirms that your review work never altered your environment's search configuration as a side effect; confirming that configuration and launching the surface are separate, explicit steps run with your operator. Full detail: Entry Surface Readiness, and Public reader for what readers see once the surface launches.
documents.s: Stage 4 — First published records and the readiness review

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A researcher-facing phrase still shows generic platform wording The concept family the phrase mentions has no display label, or no entry exists for that phrase Set the concept-family label first — it fixes most generic-sounding phrases. For a specific phrase that still needs different wording, contact your platform operator. See Voice and Vocabulary. A new contributor cannot be assigned a role Their account has not been created yet Contributor accounts are operator-mediated. Ask your platform operator to create the account; assign the role once the person appears in the Contributors tab. The "Add" form in the import area opened a bare form that does nothing The plain admin "Add" form does not read a source Close it and start from an upload route at Imports & AI → Imports. A re-import overwrote a researcher's manual edits The run replaced the rows instead of doing an edit-preserving refresh Restore from your environment's backup and re-run as an edit-preserving refresh. If your operator runs imports for you, ask them to use the edit-preserving mode. See Data Import Wizard. The readiness report reads clean but the public surface has not appeared Recording decisions does not launch the surface The launch is a separate step. Confirm with your platform operator that it was run. See Entry Surface Readiness. A vocabulary value you reviewed shows as unreviewed after a re-import A re-import should never reset a review decision This should not happen — contact your platform operator with the affected value and the import date.

Stage 1 — Voice and vocabulary (self-serve): name your concept families; act on the wording review notice; plan to work the grounding queue after your first import. → Voice and Vocabulary, Vocabulary Grounding Stage 2 — Roles and contributors (roles self-serve; accounts operator-mediated): compose the roles your team needs, set project rules, then have accounts created and assign roles. → Permissions Panel, User and Access Management Stage 3 — First import (self-serve): start from an upload route, choose an autonomy level, read the practice run, approve in two steps, then start the import. → Data Import Wizard Stage 4 — First published records (review self-serve; launch operator-mediated): work the readiness review per role, then hand off to your operator for launch. → Entry Surface Readiness

Environment administration home: Environment Administration — the reference index for every configuration surface this tutorial touches. Assisted wording onboarding: AI-Assisted Bootstrap — a one-pass path that proposes domain-specific wording; note its review screen is not yet available, so concept-family naming is the live wording path today. Researcher tier: Researcher guide — what your contributors see in the workspace and public reader once setup is done.

This page covers team membership and the standard role set. It is the lightweight overview; the live source of truth for contributors, roles, project rules, ownership transfers, and project history is the Permissions Panel. Read this if you want a one-page summary of the role model; go to the Permissions Panel page when you are about to make a change.

Standard role catalog — four pre-loaded roles every environment ships with: Reviewer, External collaborator, Researcher contributor, and Project admin. Maturity: Built. Limit: the permissions behind a standard role are fixed by the platform; renaming a standard role changes its label only. Custom role composition — build a role by combining permissions from the platform's fixed permission set. Maturity: Active. Limit: you combine existing permissions; you cannot define new ones. Project rules — environment-wide safety rules that sit on top of roles, such as requiring a second contributor to confirm high-impact changes. Maturity: Active. Limit: rules tighten what a role allows; they never grant more. Ownership transfer — moves ownership of the environment from the current owner to another contributor. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the current owner can start a transfer; both the owner and the receiving contributor must confirm; every transfer is recorded.

The Permissions Panel at /admin/permissions/ is where you do this day-to-day. The panel has five sections: Contributors, Roles, Project rules, Wording, and Project history. Role names follow your environment's wording settings, so the role names you see may differ from the standard names used on this page. Assign or change a role: Contributors section. Pick the contributor and choose a standard or custom role. A role assignment can also be limited to specific record types or fields. Compose a custom role: Roles section. Combine permissions from the platform's set and name the role. Roles can be renamed at any time; a rename changes the label your team sees, never the permissions. Set project rules: Project rules section — for example, require that high-impact changes are confirmed by a second contributor. Transfer ownership: available to the current owner only. The owner starts the transfer, both sides confirm, and the transfer is recorded. Add a new contributor: contributor accounts are created by your platform operator. Once the person appears in the Contributors section, you assign their role there. Standard role summary: Role What it allows Typical contributor Reviewer Read and review suggested changes; cannot save changes. External reviewers, students. External collaborator Review and save small additive changes in a focused area, without broader project authority. Guest collaborators from outside the project. Researcher contributor Review suggestions, save routine changes, undo recent changes, and manage saved import setups. Project team researchers. Project admin Everything, including high-impact changes, field setup, role management, and review metrics. Project directors, principal investigators.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A contributor cannot open the Permissions Panel Their account does not have administrator access Ask a contributor with the Project admin role to check their role in the Contributors section. If no one in your environment can resolve it, contact your platform operator. You need a permission shape no standard role provides The standard catalog is fixed Compose a custom role from the available permissions. If the permission you need does not exist in the platform's set at all, contact your platform operator. Renaming a standard role did not change what it allows Renaming changes the label only This is the intended behavior. Compose a custom role if you need a different set of permissions. A contributor can review changes but cannot save them Their role does not include saving (for example, Reviewer), or a project rule requires a second contributor for that kind of change Check the contributor's role in the Contributors section and the rules in the Project rules section. An ownership transfer will not complete Transfers must be started by the current owner; both sides must confirm; and the receiving contributor must be an active contributor holding the Project admin role with role management Confirm on both sides, and check the receiving contributor's role in the Contributors section. If the transfer was not started by the current owner, ask the owner to start it.
Live source of truth: Permissions Panel.

You are a scholar, student, archivist, or editor working in a knowledge environment built on this platform. You sign in, read, search, edit drafts, and cite records. You do not run the system; you use it. This guide is the entry point for everything researcher-facing. Read it when you join a new environment, when a control is not behaving as you expect, or when you want to know what the platform will and will not do for you. If you configure the environment — turning columns on or off, choosing which fields are searchable, managing other researchers' permissions — see the environment administration guide instead.

The researcher surface gives you eight capabilities, ordered by how often you will reach for them. Workspace table view — the main table of records for each record type, with a toolbar, a Manage columns panel, filters, a row-density toggle, cell and selected-row clipboard actions, and a Details panel for reading a full record. Maturity: Active. Limit: which controls appear for each record type is configured per environment; if a control you need is missing, your environment administrator can expose it. Inline editing and drafts — edit a field directly in the table: double-click a cell to open it and press Enter to save, while longer and multilingual fields open an editor with its own Save and Cancel buttons. Date fields use a date picker; text fields that merely look like timestamps stay text until their type is changed or converted. + New row opens a drawer where your draft is saved as you work and becomes a full row when you choose Activate row. Maturity: Active. Limit: on a brand-new row, fields that link to other records become editable after the first save creates the draft. Search across scripts — a quick search finds records across the collections you can access, a full Search & Read page filters and reads results in place, and the toolbar box narrows the rows already in front of you. Search matches the scripts your records carry — original script, transliteration, and translation — for fields marked searchable. Maturity: Active. Limit: only fields your environment marks searchable are covered. Media and citations — records can carry images, audio, video, and 3D models, and each media item carries a citation in your project's citation style, ready to copy. Maturity: Active. Limit: which media a record carries depends on what your project attached. Public reader and draft preview — a stable read-only view of published records, with an in-workspace preview that shows a record as a reader outside the project would see it. Maturity: Active. Limit: which records reach the reader depends on your project's review and publish workflow. Tips and guidance — small suggestions that appear in the workspace and in multi-step wizards. You can dismiss a single tip or mute a whole family of tips. A tip only suggests; acting on it is always your choice. Maturity: Active. Accessibility — keyboard navigation, visible focus indicators, the row-density toggle, and controls for font size, line height, font family, and color presets. Maturity: Active. Limit: screen-reader announcement coverage continues to improve. Privacy — the platform records usage as aggregate counts and timings, not transcripts of what you typed, and masks sensitive text before anything is stored. Privacy and safety explains exactly what is recorded and what is not. Maturity: Active.

Start with whichever matches what you want to do. New to the workspace, or unsure where a control lives → Workspace walkthrough. Creating a new record, picking up an abandoned draft, or editing an existing record → Adding and editing rows. Hunting for a record across scripts, opening media, or reading citations → Searching and reading. Curious about the small suggestions appearing beside the form or the table → Tips and guidance. Driving the platform from the keyboard, or adjusting display settings → Accessibility. Wondering what the platform records about you and what it does not → Privacy and safety. Wanting to know what a reader outside the project sees, and how to preview it → Public reader. Stuck on one specific task, or after a quick answer in the moment → the in-product Help page (/app/workspace/help) groups short task-shaped guides by topic, and a ? beside a control opens the matching guide in a drawer. Browse the same guides in the help topics (see find help on a topic). A few conventions across all walkthroughs: Bold marks an on-screen control name — for example, + New row, Add filter, Activate row. A code-style font marks a path, URL fragment, or literal value. Examples use abstract content ("historical figures", "manuscript editions") rather than your specific project's records. The mechanics are the same regardless.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A column you expected is missing from the table. Either hidden in the current view, or not exposed in your environment's configuration. Open Manage columns in the toolbar; if the column is not listed there, ask your environment administrator to expose it. Your environment administrator. A field is read-only when you expected to edit it. Permissions on your account, or a workflow rule for that record type. Confirm your role with your environment administrator; if the restriction is intended, request edit permission for that record type. Your environment administrator. A draft will not activate. A required field is still empty. The drawer highlights the required fields that are still empty — fill them, then choose Activate row again. See Adding and editing rows. Your environment administrator, if the message is unclear. Search returns nothing for a record you know exists. The relevant field is not marked searchable in your environment's configuration. Open the record directly through its Details panel; ask your environment administrator to mark the field searchable. Your environment administrator.
Environment administration guide — the companion guide for the person who configures your environment. Help topics — the same short, task-shaped guides that the in-product Help page shows.

Your knowledge environment is built to work with keyboard navigation, screen readers, and adjustable display settings. This page walks through what is available, where to find it, and what is still on the way. Read it when you want to drive the workspace without a mouse, when you need to adjust how text is displayed, or when a control is not reachable or readable the way you expected.

Workspace keyboard navigation — Tab / Shift+Tab, Enter, Escape, arrow keys, and Space cover the workspace's interactive controls. The combinations follow common conventions. Active. Visible focus rings (keyboard-only) — a clear outline on the focused element, drawn when you navigate with the keyboard and suppressed for mouse clicks, so the screen stays quiet for mouse users. Active. Inline editing with the keyboard — Tab into a field, type, Tab out; your change is saved when the field loses focus. Enter saves it too. Dropdown fields respond to arrow keys and Enter. Active. Hints on fields that are not editable yet — a field whose editing surface has not shipped shows a hint in place of an editor. The hint is part of the keyboard tab order and is announced as disabled to screen readers, so you know the field exists and is intentionally not interactive yet. Active. Named workspace form controls — toolbar filters, column-header menus, Details fields, and New-row fields expose stable labels and form identities to browsers and assistive technology. Active. Row density control — three row heights (Compact, Cozy, Comfortable); your choice is saved with the view you are working in. Active. Accessibility control panel — font size, line height, font family, and a small set of background color presets, remembered by your browser. Available on your environment's reading and browsing pages; the workspace does not include it yet. Active. Finer-grained color customization is Deferred. Accessible inline tips — the tip panel that appears alongside your work is screen-reader-friendly and keeps focus stable when its content updates. Active.

Tab / Shift+Tab moves through interactive controls — toolbar buttons, filter controls, the search box, table cells, drawer fields. Arrow keys move within the table grid, the saved-views menu, and the row density control. In the column manager, the arrow keys on a column's reorder handle move that column up or down the list. Space selects the focused row. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on Mac) with Space to add a row to the selection or remove it. Shift + Up/Down arrow extends the selection across a range of rows. Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on Mac) opens the focused row's details. Enter activates the focused button or saves an edit in a focused field. Escape closes the active drawer, panel, or dialog. Focused elements show a visible focus ring — a clear outline marking where you are. The ring is keyboard-only by default; clicking a control with the mouse does not draw it.
documents.s: Driving the workspace from the keyboard

documents.t: Tab into a field, type, then Tab out — your change is saved as soon as the field loses focus. Pressing Enter saves it too. For dropdown fields, arrow keys move through the options and Enter selects one. For related-record lookups, type to search, then Tab to a result and press Enter to link it. Escape closes the panel when you are done.

Some fields show a "not editable yet" hint instead of an editor. These hints are deliberately part of the keyboard tab order and are announced as disabled to your screen reader, so it is clear the field exists and is intentionally not yet interactive. They are not skipped, not invisible, and they do not pretend to be editable.
documents.s: Fields that are not editable yet

documents.t: The table toolbar has a row density control with three settings — Compact, Cozy, and Comfortable. Pick whichever works for your eyes and workflow; your choice is saved with the view you are working in, so it is there when you come back. On your environment's reading and browsing pages, the accessibility control panel adjusts how text is displayed. Open it from the accessibility button in the page header — announced to screen readers as "Open accessibility settings" — or press Alt+A. The panel is not available inside the workspace yet. It lets you adjust: Font size — make all text larger or smaller as a percentage of the base size. Line height — increase line spacing for easier reading; particularly helpful for dyslexia and low vision. Font family — switch between the default font and alternatives. Background color — a small set of page background presets, useful for contrast and reducing glare. A Reset to defaults button restores the standard settings. These settings are remembered by your browser on the device where you set them. If you sign in from a different device or browser, set them again there.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A control is not reachable with Tab. A gap in the focus order. Try Shift+Tab from a nearby control that is reachable. If the control still cannot be reached, contact your environment administrator — an unreachable control is a bug, not a setting. Your screen reader skips a "not editable yet" field. Your screen reader is set to skip disabled controls, or the hint did not load. Turn on your screen reader's setting for reading disabled controls. If the field is still skipped, contact your environment administrator. No focus ring appears after pressing Tab. You last interacted with the mouse — the ring is keyboard-only — or the page styling is interfering. Press Tab once more. If the ring still does not appear, contact your environment administrator. Font size resets after you sign out. Display settings are stored in your browser; the browser's stored data was cleared, or you are in a different browser or a private window. Re-apply the setting in the accessibility control panel. These settings do not follow your account across devices. You cannot find the accessibility control panel in the workspace. The panel lives on the reading and browsing pages; the workspace does not include it yet. Open a reading page and use the accessibility button in the page header, or press Alt+A there. Inside the workspace, use the row density control and your browser's own zoom. Your row density choice does not stick. The choice saves to the view you have open; the save may not have completed. Set the density again with the view open. If it still resets, contact your environment administrator. The highest-contrast preset is still not enough for your needs. The preset set is deliberately small for now; finer color customization is deferred. Use the preset closest to your needs and tell your environment administrator about the gap — reports shape what gets built next. An inline edit does not save when you Tab out. The field is read-only for your role, or the value failed validation (look for an inline error). Correct the value if there is an error shown. For a permissions question, contact your environment administrator.

Workspace keyboard navigation: Active. Visible focus rings: Active. Row density control: Active. Accessibility control panel on the reading and browsing pages (font size, line height, font family, background color presets): Active. Inline editing with the keyboard: Active. Discoverable hints on fields that are not editable yet: Active. Accessible inline tips: Active. Screen-reader announcement coverage — for example, a spoken confirmation when an edit saves — is still expanding.
documents.s: What is there, what is still arriving

documents.t: Accessibility problems are bugs, not configuration questions. If a control cannot be reached from the keyboard, a screen reader misreads a field, or poor contrast makes text unreadable, contact your environment administrator so the problem reaches the people who can fix it.
documents.s: If something is not working for you

documents.t: Workspace walkthrough — the controls keyboard navigation moves through. Adding and editing rows — the draft drawer and its keyboard behavior. Tips and guidance — how the inline tip panel behaves.

This page covers creating new records and editing existing ones in your workspace. The model is: a new row is created as a draft the moment you ask for one, every edit saves as you finish each field, and your draft stays in the table until you complete it. There is no Save button to forget. Read this when you create your first record, when you want to know what "draft" means for a new row, or when an edit is not behaving as you expect.

Create a row from the toolbar — one click adds a draft row to the current table and opens it for editing. Active. Insert and duplicate — insert a row directly below an existing one, or duplicate a row to start a new one from its values. Active. Autosave editing — every change saves when you finish the field. There is no Save button. Active. Draft stage for new rows — a new row starts as a draft: visible to your project, never shown to public readers, and not yet linkable to other records. Active. Editing in two places — the table cells and the Details panel edit the same record; a change made in one shows in the other. Active. Linked-record fields — search the related record type and pick a match, directly inside the field. Active for records past the draft stage. Row deletion from the workspace — not yet available. Deferred.

Open the table you want to add to. New rows always belong to the table you are looking at. Click + New row in the toolbar. Your environment may label this button differently. The row is created right away as a draft: a notice confirms Draft row created, with a Review row button that takes you to it, and the row joins your table and opens for editing. Fill in the fields. Each field saves when you finish it — click out of a text field or press Enter, and the value is stored. Choices and checkboxes save the moment you pick them. Leave and return whenever you like. Your draft is a row in your table. Close the panel, navigate away, come back another day — your values are saved. Click the row to continue where you left off. Required fields can stay empty while you draft. They must be filled before the row can leave the draft stage. Two more ways to start a row: Insert row below — right-click an existing row and choose Insert row below. In views you order by hand, the new row lands directly below that one; in sorted or filtered views, the active sort and filters decide where it appears. Duplicate row — right-click a row and choose Duplicate row. This creates a new draft with that row's directly editable values copied in; derived and linked fields are skipped. If + New row is unavailable, the button itself tells you why. Some views cannot accept new rows — for example, a view that combines or filters records rather than showing a single stored table.

A new row begins as a draft: Your project sees it. Draft rows appear in the workspace table alongside everything else. Public readers never see it. Only records that have been completed and published reach the public reading site. It cannot be linked yet. The platform declines attempts to link a draft row to another record — the link is refused with a message rather than saved. Required fields may wait. A draft saves with required fields empty; the row cannot become an active record until every required field has a value. Once every required field is filled and the row passes its checks, it can leave the draft stage and become an active record — after that, links to other records save normally.

You can edit in two places, and they stay in step: In the table — edit a cell directly. The change saves when you confirm it or move on to another cell. In the Details panel — click a row to open its Details panel. Click into a field, change the value, then leave the field or press Enter. The panel header shows Saving… and then Saved. A value you did not change is not re-saved. Date fields use your browser's date picker in table cells, new-row fields, and the Details panel. Choosing a date stores the date itself, such as 2025-10-19; the workspace does not add a time or timezone. A field that only looks like a timestamp but is configured as Text remains a text field until its type is changed or a future conversion workflow is used. Not every field takes typed input: Fields marked with a Read badge are not editable in place. These are derived fields (computed from other fields), media fields, and field types that do not have an in-place editor yet. To change a derived value, edit the fields it is computed from. Relation fields show the linked-records editor instead: existing links appear as removable chips, and a search box lets you type part of a related record's name and pick a match to add a link. Click the × on a chip to remove a link. If a save fails, an error message tells you what went wrong. The field returns to its stored value — re-enter your change after fixing the problem.
Removing rows from the workspace is not yet available — the row menu shows Delete row as unavailable. If you created a row by mistake or need a record removed, contact your environment administrator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix + New row is unavailable. No table is selected, or the current view cannot accept new rows. Hover over the button to see the reason, or switch to a regular table view. Creating or editing a row fails with a permission message. Your role includes read access but not edit access. Contact your environment administrator. A field will not accept your edit and shows a Read badge. The field is derived from other fields, holds media, or has no in-place editor yet. Edit the fields it is computed from. If you believe the field should be directly editable, contact your environment administrator. You cannot link another record from a new row. The row is still a draft. Records cannot be linked while either side is a draft. Fill in the required fields and complete the row first. If linking stays unavailable afterwards, contact your environment administrator. A change did not save. The value failed a check, or the field never lost focus. Look for an error message near the field or panel. Click outside the field or press Enter to confirm the save, then re-enter the value if it reverted. You need a row deleted. Row deletion from the workspace is not yet available. Contact your environment administrator. A field you expected is missing from the form. The field is hidden in the current view, or it is not configured for this record type. Check the view's hidden fields first. Otherwise, ask your environment administrator to add the field.

What you can do in the workspace reflects your role in the project. Members with read access browse, search, and view Details; adding and editing rows requires edit access. If your role does not include editing, the platform declines the change with a permission message. Roles are assigned by your environment administrator; the permissions panel page describes what each role covers.

Workspace walkthrough — the table and Details panel. Searching and reading — how records surface in search. Public reader — how completed and published records reach public readers. Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a row is complete. Accessibility — keyboard-first editing and screen-reader support.

You are about to cite something from your knowledge environment in a paper — a published record, a passage, a region of an image, a named part of a 3D model. This page explains what the platform guarantees about that citation: what stays fixed once you have cited it, what an Edition is and why it matters before anything goes to a peer-reviewed venue, and what a citation style is — including how a style gets changed when the active one does not suit your venue. Read it before a platform citation goes into print, or when you want to understand why a citation reads the way it does. For the steps of actually copying a citation, see Copy a citation for a record or media item.

Stable web addresses for published records — every published record keeps a stable address that stays valid even if your project later reorganizes its pages. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Frozen, citable Editions for media items — a media item's version is either a working copy that can still change, or an Edition: frozen and safe to cite in print. Maturity: Active. Limit: freezing a version as an Edition is a deliberate administrator action, never automatic. Refusal of re-processing against an Edition — an automatic re-processing run that would change an Edition's data is refused outright; it stops before anything is touched. Maturity: Active. Rejections that stay rejected — when a reviewer in your project rejects a wrong label that automatic processing proposed, the rejection is recorded permanently; later re-processing does not bring the label back. Maturity: Active. Citations rendered in your project's citation style — published entries carry citations rendered in the style your project has adopted, ready to select and copy. Maturity: Active. Limit: how complete a citation reads depends on the fields your project has filled in. A shipped catalog of standard styles — more than seventy standard citation styles ship with the platform, Chicago and APA among them; different collections within a project can use different styles. Maturity: Built. Limit: a style outside the catalog can be installed on request through your environment administrator. Reviewed style changes — a style change passes through three steps: a proposal built from sample citations, a scholar's review, and a deliberate apply by an environment administrator. No proposal takes effect without the review. Maturity: Active. Citations readable by reference managers — every published entry's citation is also available in Citation Style Language JSON, the format reference managers such as Zotero read. Maturity: Built.

Nothing changes underneath your citation by accident. The address you cite keeps resolving, and a published record's content changes only when someone in your project changes the record — no background run rewrites published content on its own. For media items, the guarantee is stronger still: data frozen as an Edition cannot change at all, and the platform enforces that refusal itself rather than relying on anyone's caution.

A published record's stable web address is one half of citable identity. The other half matters when you cite a media item — a 3D model, an image, an audio or video segment. The platform can propose labels connecting your project's terms to regions of a media item — a named part of a 3D model, a region of an image. Reviewers in your project approve, amend, or reject each one. That reviewed state lives on a version of the media item, and a version is one of two things: A working copy — annotation on it can still change as your project reviews and refines. An Edition — frozen. Once an environment administrator promotes a version to an Edition, its data is protected: the platform refuses any re-processing run that would alter it. Before a media citation goes to a peer-reviewed venue, the version you cite should be an Edition. If your venue or repository needs a DOI, that DOI is minted by your institution's library or repository service against the Edition's stable identity — the platform itself does not mint DOIs, it provides the stable target. A citation never exposes the platform's internal identifiers; locations are described in the item's own terms, such as the name of a model part or a region of an image. In the references rows of a published entry, "edition" usually means a published edition of a source text — a different thing. The Edition on this page is a frozen, citable version of a media item held on the platform.
documents.s: What "Edition" and stable identity mean before you cite

documents.t: Three things hold after you cite: File updates do not touch your citation. When the underlying model or image file is updated, the new file comes in as a new working copy under its own version label. The Edition you cited — and any DOI adopted for it — keeps its data intact. The new version earns its own review and can become its own Edition later. Automatic re-processing cannot alter an Edition. A re-processing run against an Edition is refused before any data changes. This is not a warning someone could click past; the platform stops the run. Review decisions survive re-processing. A rejection a reviewer made is recorded permanently and is not re-proposed by later runs. Labels a reviewer has approved or amended are likewise preserved — even while the version is still a working copy. Every review action keeps a record of who acted and when, stored with the data.
documents.s: What stays fixed across model updates and re-processing

documents.t: A citation style is the set of rules for how a citation reads: the order of author, title, and date; the punctuation; the abbreviations. The platform defines styles in Citation Style Language — an open format used by reference managers such as Zotero and by thousands of journals — so a style is data your environment holds, not something hand-edited into each record. A catalog of more than seventy standard styles ships with the platform, and different collections within your project can use different styles. To tell whether the active style suits your venue, read a rendered citation against the venue's style guide or a recent issue: open a published entry, or its draft preview, and compare. The preview shows the same rendering before anything goes public — if a citation will read roughly in print, it reads roughly in the preview. If you are unsure which style is active for a collection, ask your environment administrator; the active style and its version are recorded in your environment.

Style changes run on the administrative side — there is no self-service style control in your workspace. Your part is the request and the evidence: Collect sample citations formatted the way your venue requires — real examples covering the kinds of material you typically cite. Send them to your environment administrator with the request. For a standard venue, the administrator may adopt a matching style straight from the shipped catalog. A proposal is drafted from your samples and measured against your environment's pinned example citations. The proposal carries a count of existing citations it would change and a risk level, so reviewers see the consequences before anything is decided. A proposal may be drafted with machine assistance, but no proposal — machine-drafted or not — takes effect on its own. A scholar reviews the proposal. The platform refuses to apply a proposal that has not passed this review. An environment administrator applies the reviewed style. Styles are versioned, the record of who applied which version is kept, and published citations render in the applied style — you do not edit any record to pick up the change.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A citation reads wrong for your venue — punctuation, ordering, or abbreviations are off. The active style does not match the venue, or no style has been adopted yet for that collection. Collect sample citations in the form the venue requires and send them to your environment administrator with a request to adopt or refine the style. A citation shows placeholder text or is missing pieces. The fields the citation draws on are incomplete on that record or media item. Complete those fields on the record — see Copy a citation for a record or media item for the details. You want to cite a 3D model or image in print and worry a later update will change it. The version you are citing may still be a working copy. Ask your environment administrator to confirm the version is an Edition — or to freeze one — before the citation goes to press. A wrong label your project rejected has reappeared after re-processing. This should not happen — a recorded rejection is permanent across re-processing. Report it to your environment administrator, naming the media item and the label. A recurrence is a platform defect, not something you mis-clicked. Your venue or repository asks for a DOI. The platform does not mint DOIs itself. Ask your environment administrator — DOI minting is handled by your institution's library or repository service against the frozen Edition's identity.

Copy a citation for a record or media item — the short task-shaped steps. Read the references section on a published entry — what each evidence row in the References area means. Public reader — stable addresses, the draft preview, and what readers see. Citation integrity (for environment admins) — the same guarantees in administrative detail, including Editions and DOI safety. Standards and citations (for environment admins) — the style catalog and the review workflow from the administrator's side. Standards overview — the platform's standards posture for institutional readers.

Some environments pair their records with interactive 3D models — an anatomical structure, a scanned artifact, a molecular form. The model viewer lets you and your readers turn a model, name its parts, and open the scholarly entry behind each part. This page walks through opening a model, reading what a part means, shaping the view so you see what matters, working through a model group by group, and what to expect from attachments that have no built-in viewer.

When a table holds media, a Media view joins Table / Details / Relations / Publish in the view bar. It appears only on media tables. The Media view shows your media records as a gallery of cards — each card carries the record's title and a media-type badge (for example 3D model). Opening a 3D-model card renders the model right there in a detail pane, where you can orbit and zoom to inspect it, alongside a rail of tabs for the model's parts, files, viewer framing, info, and versions. Maturity: Active. From the Mesh→term tab you review which part of the model is matched to which term and approve, reassign, or strip those matches; environment admins use the Viewer tab to set the framing the model opens at. Two researcher how-to guides cover this in the workspace: See which mesh maps to which term and Tune the 3D camera view. The reader experience below — the public viewer your readers see — is described separately in this page.
documents.s: In your workspace — the Media view

documents.t: Click a part, read its entry — hovering over the model names the part under your pointer; clicking it opens a panel with the entry's headword, translations, transliteration, description, and a link to the full entry. Maturity: Active. Limit: a part shows entry details only where your project has linked that part to an entry. View shaping, part by part — fade, hide, isolate, or zoom to any part. Every shaping action raises an on-screen bar with its own undo, and one control resets the whole view. Maturity: Active. Group-by-group exploration — a strip labeled LAYERS lists the model's groups; each group opens a list of its parts with individual show/hide toggles. Maturity: Active. View controls — on-screen orbit, zoom, and pan controls plus a reset; scroll-wheel zoom and middle-button pan with the mouse; touch gestures on phones and tablets. Maturity: Active. Built-in walkthrough — a short guided tour starts on its own the first time you open a model in a browser, and can be rerun from the Help button. Maturity: Active. Typed attachment cards — a record page lists its attachments as labeled cards (3D model, Image, Audio, Video, Molecular). A 3D model card opens this viewer; cards of other types open only when the attachment carries its own viewing address. Maturity: Active. Limit: the built-in viewer exists for 3D models today; other media types display as cards and rely on the address the attachment provides.

Open a record that has a 3D model attached. Its attachments appear as a strip of cards, each labeled with its type. Select the card labeled 3D model. The viewer opens with the model's name in the top bar. To leave, use the back arrow beside the model's name — it returns you to the page you came from, or to the reading site's opening page if you arrived by direct link. Your environment's reading site may also feature its models directly — for example on its opening page — and selecting a model there opens the same viewer. Beside the model's name sits Model Info. If the model carries an overview, it unfolds in place, with a Read Full Model Info link to the model's full information page; if there is no overview, the button takes you straight to that page. The overview folds away when you select a part. If the model includes an animation, a play/pause control appears near the top of the view.

Hover over the model (on a computer): the part under your pointer is highlighted and its name appears beside it. Click a part: a detail panel opens. The heading is the entry's headword, with its translations in parentheses; the transliteration sits underneath; below come the description and the part's place in the model's structure, from the largest group down to the part itself. Full Details, at the bottom of the panel, opens the part's full entry page in a new tab. Click empty space to close the panel and clear the selection, or use the panel's close control. When a part has not been linked to an entry, the panel falls back to the part's name as written in the model, and a notice reports that no entry details were found for it. Linking parts to entries is part of how your project prepares its models — if a part you need is unlinked, tell your environment administrator.

Right-click a part (on a computer) to open a circular menu around your pointer. On a touch screen, tap the part: a small card names it, offers See Details, and unfolds the same actions from its menu control. The menu offers four ways to shape the view, each marked with its keyboard letter: Fade (F) — the part turns translucent, so you can see past it while keeping it in place. Hide (H) — the part is removed from view. Isolate (I) — the part is shown on its own. Zoom (Z) — the camera moves in on the part. Each state raises a bar at the edge of the model area naming the affected part: A faded part's bar reads Part Faded, with Invert — the faded part returns to full strength and everything else fades instead — and Reset. With several parts faded, the bar shows their count and their names, with Invert All and Reset All. A hidden part's bar reads Part Hidden, with Unhide. With several hidden, the bar shows the count and a list; picking a part from the list brings it back, and Unhide All brings back everything. An isolated part's bar reads Isolated, with Exit. A zoomed part's bar reads Zoom, with Exit. To start over entirely, use the round Reset the view control among the view controls, or press Alt+R. The circular menu also carries the part's name — selecting it opens the detail panel — and Cite, which opens the page's citation form.
documents.s: Shaping the view: fade, hide, isolate, zoom

documents.t: On a computer, the pointer is reserved for parts — hovering names them, clicking selects them — so moving the view goes through dedicated controls: The round controls at the edge of the model area: Orbit the view (two turn buttons; press and hold to keep turning), Zoom in/out in the view (press and hold to keep zooming), Pan the view (four direction arrows), and Reset the view. The mouse: scroll to zoom; drag with the middle button to pan. On a touch screen, drag with one finger to turn the model, pinch with two fingers to zoom, and drag with two fingers to pan.

The strip along the bottom of the screen, labeled LAYERS, lists the model's groups. Select a group: its parts light up and a list opens showing every part in the group, each with an eye toggle. Toggle a part's eye to show or hide that part. Hide all / Show all at the top of the list switches the whole group at once. Moving the pointer away from the strip clears the group highlight. This is the steady way through a dense model: open a group, hide what is in the way, study what remains, then move to the next group.
documents.s: Working through the model in groups

documents.t: The first time you open a model in a given browser, a short walkthrough starts on its own once the model has loaded. It tours navigation, part selection, the view-shaping menu, the groups strip, the model information, and the page's cite, help, and feedback buttons. To run it again, use the round Help button at the edge of the page. The walkthrough is remembered per browser, not per account — on a new device or browser it introduces itself again. The neighboring round buttons offer Cite — a citation for the page, formatted in common styles (APA, MLA, Chicago) and ready to copy — and Feedback, which opens a form for sending your impressions to the team behind the site.

With a part selected, four shortcuts act on it: F fades, H hides, I isolates, Z zooms. Alt+R resets the view at any time. Two honest limits: Selecting a part requires a pointer — a mouse click or a tap. There is no keyboard-only way to move through the model's parts, so the shortcuts extend pointer work rather than replace it. The model area itself is not part of the keyboard tab order. If a keyboard-only path matters to your work, tell your environment administrator — an accessibility gap is a bug to report, not a setting to find. The model view follows the background color chosen in the accessibility settings on your environment's reading pages: a dark background there gives the model a dark backdrop here.

A record's attachments appear as cards in a strip, each labeled with its type — 3D model, Image, Audio, Video, Molecular, or the type name your project recorded. A card shows the attachment's image where one is catalogued (a type placeholder otherwise), its title, and its creator where catalogued. A 3D model card opens this viewer. A card of any other type opens only when the attachment carries its own viewing address; selecting it then leads to that address. A card with no viewing address is a labeled reference: it tells you the attachment exists and what it is, without leading anywhere.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Clicking a part shows its name, but a notice says no entry details were found. The part is not yet linked to an entry. The rest of the model still works. Ask your environment administrator to link the part if you need its entry. Parts of the model seem to be missing. Parts are hidden, or one part is isolated. Check the bars at the edge of the model area — Unhide All or Exit — or reset the view with the Reset the view control or Alt+R. Dragging with the mouse does not turn the model. On a computer, the pointer selects parts; turning the model goes through the view controls. Use the Orbit the view control; scroll to zoom; drag with the middle button to pan. On a touch screen, a one-finger drag turns the model. The keyboard shortcuts (F, H, I, Z) do nothing. No part is selected — the shortcuts act on the selected part. Click a part first, then press the shortcut. The walkthrough did not appear. It starts on its own only on your first visit in a given browser, and only once the model has loaded. Use the Help button at the edge of the page after the model finishes loading. An Image, Audio, or Video card on a record page does not open anything. The attachment carries no viewing address of its own; only 3D model cards have a built-in viewer. The card still documents the attachment. If it should open somewhere, ask your environment administrator to add a viewing address to the attachment. The model never finishes loading. A large model file, or a connection problem. Wait — larger models take longer — then reload the page. If the problem persists, contact your environment administrator.

Public reader — the reading layer where published records and their models live. Accessibility — display settings and keyboard behavior across your environment. Searching and reading — finding the records a model is attached to.

The task guides answer "how do I do this one thing." This page answers the questions that cross several of them — the ones that come up when something behaves in a way no single step explains. Each answer is short, and points you to the guide with the full steps.

Two reasons are common. If the record is still a draft, only you see it in the table — a draft becomes part of the shared workspace only once you Activate it. If it is activated but your colleague is looking at the public reader, that is a separate step again: activating makes a record part of your team's workspace, while publishing makes it visible to the world. To finish a draft, see Finish a new row in the drawer; to put a record on the public site, see Publish a record.
documents.s: Why can't my colleague see the record I created?

documents.t: The public page keeps the version it was last published with — your edits sit in the workspace until the next publish, they do not flow out automatically. The same is true for a field's visibility setting or a renamed label: the public page catches up only when you publish again. Open the Publish view and select Publish changes to push the current version live. To see the steps, see The Publish view.
documents.s: I edited a published record, so why does the public page still show the old version?

documents.t: Publishing is controlled by your role, not by the record's stage — anyone whose role includes publish access can publish any activated record, reviewed or not. The platform has no separate sign-off gate that holds a record back until a reviewer approves it. If your team needs review to come before publishing, ask your environment administrator to arrange roles so that only reviewers hold publish access. For how reviewing works today, see Reviewing your team's work.
documents.s: Who can publish in my project, and why can a colleague publish work I have not finished reviewing?

documents.t: Saved views are shared. When you change the filters, columns, or sort on a view, everyone working in that collection sees the change immediately, and deleting a view removes it for everyone. If you want to experiment without disturbing your team, Duplicate the view first and work in the copy. For the full behavior, see Save your table arrangement as a view.
documents.s: Are my saved views private, or does the whole team see them?

documents.t: A shared search link reproduces your exact search, filters, and result page, but results always respect the person opening them — they see only the collections and records their own access allows. So fewer results for your colleague usually means they lack access to a collection you can see, not that the link is broken. If they need that collection, ask your environment administrator. To copy a link that reproduces your search, see Share a search.
documents.s: I sent a colleague a search link, so why do they see fewer results than I do?

documents.t: They are still there if the run used an edit-preserving refresh: the platform matches incoming source rows to existing records, refreshes source-managed values, and keeps the fields your team owns. Field labels and field settings you changed are also yours and are not reset by the re-import. A full refresh is different: it reloads rows from scratch and is destructive to researcher edits, so it should be planned with your environment administrator before it runs. A re-import shows you a delta: only what is new, changed, or removed since your last import, so you are not asked to re-decide settled structure. To read the delta, see Understand what changed after a re-import.
documents.s: Where did my changes go after I re-imported my source?

documents.t: Your label is yours, and a re-import is not supposed to bring the source name back. One case looks like that but is not: in the delta view, changed items are listed under their source-side names until you confirm them, after which your label reappears in the workspace. That label guarantee is separate from record value refresh behavior: edit-preserving refresh protects researcher-owned values, while full refresh is destructive. If your label is genuinely overwritten in the workspace itself after a re-import, that is a defect worth reporting. See Rename a field label and Understand what changed after a re-import.
documents.s: A field I renamed is showing its old source name again after a re-import — is that a bug?

documents.t: The most common cause is a renamed column in your source. When a column's name changes, the platform sees the old name disappear and a new name arrive, so the delta lists one removed field and one new field for what is really the same column. Approve the new one and your label carries over to it. Your saved views adapt to a removed field rather than breaking — see What happens to saved views after a re-import.
documents.s: A field I know is in my source shows as "removed" after a re-import — why?

documents.t: When two columns in your source would map to one field, the import stops before writing anything and lists every collision at once, so you can fix them together rather than one error at a time. Give the clashing columns distinct names in your source and re-import. For the full walkthrough, see Fix colliding column names during import.
documents.s: My import stopped with a message that two columns would become the same field — what do I do?

documents.t: Search and the table look at different things. The toolbar filter box narrows only the rows already loaded in the active table, while search looks across collections — but only at the fields your environment has marked searchable. So a record can sit in your table yet stay out of search because the word you typed lives in a field that search does not cover. Try a word from a different field, or use full search across collections. See Find a record when search returns nothing and Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read.
documents.s: Why can search find a record I can see right in front of me in the table?

documents.t: Searching across a collection requires a review capability for that kind of record, and the note counts the collections your access does not cover. The records are not gone — they are held back from your search until your access includes the capability that covers them. Ask your environment administrator for the capability you need. See See why some collections are hidden in Search & Read.
documents.s: Why does the search results panel say some collections are hidden?

documents.t: A collection needs a display field — the field that names each record — for results to read as names. When no display field is set, the result falls back to an internal identifier, which is the string of letters and numbers you are seeing. This is set per collection by your environment administrator; ask them to set a display field for that collection. For how search reads across your data, see Searching and reading.
documents.s: Why do some search results show strings of letters and numbers instead of a name?

documents.t: Two different reasons. For Greek, breathings are set aside in matching but the acute accent still counts — a term typed without its acute accent can miss a record whose stored form carries it. For transliteration, the match works only if the transliteration field actually holds a value and is marked searchable; if it is empty on that record, the native-script form will still find it. See Working in multiple scripts and languages and Find a record when search returns nothing.
documents.s: Why does my search miss a Greek term, or a transliteration that I know is there?

documents.t: Some fields are not edited directly. A field that is computed from other fields, holds media, or links to other records shows as read-only; you change it by editing the fields it is built from, or by adding links and media after the record exists. A field can also be read-only because your role has read access but not edit access. To tell the cases apart and act on each, see Adding and editing rows.
documents.s: Why can't I edit this field — it has no editor or shows a "Read" badge?

documents.t: A link can only point to an active record, and a brand-new row is a draft until you activate it — so the relation field stays unavailable while either side is still a draft. Fill in the required fields, activate the row, and the link becomes available. To finish the draft, see Finish a new row in the drawer; to add the link, see The Relations view.
documents.s: Why can't I link my new record to another record yet?

documents.t: Your table layout — column order, sort, filters — is stored on the active view, and views are shared, so a layout can change because a collaborator adjusted the same view, or because you are looking at a different view tab than before. The sidebar is the exception: its width and collapsed state are remembered per browser, while your pins and groups follow your sign-in. For what is remembered where, see What the workspace remembers, and how undo works.
documents.s: My column arrangement reverted, or a colleague's looks different from mine — why?

documents.t: The column's field type decides how the workspace treats the value. A Date field shows a readable date in the table and uses a date picker when you edit it. A Text field that happens to contain a timestamp stays text, so it still shows the full stored string until someone changes or converts the field type. See Adding and editing rows and Table layout: sorting, column controls, and the column manager.
documents.s: Why does one date look friendly while another still shows the full timestamp?

documents.t: Copying a focused cell copies one field value. Copying selected rows copies the visible columns for those rows, with column-label headers, so it can paste into a spreadsheet as a small table. A cell range copies only the rectangular cells you selected, without row headers. When you paste one copied value while several rows are selected, the workspace can fill that same column for the selected rows on editable tables; when a cell range is active, paste targets that rectangle. For the full distinction, see Copy and paste table values.
documents.s: Why are there several copy actions in the table?

documents.t: A table-wide publish includes every activated record, and a withdrawn record is still activated — so publishing the whole table can put it back. Withdrawal is held by your environment's administrators, not by the workspace publishing controls. If a record must stay out of public view, agree with whoever publishes that it stays out of table-wide publishes. See Withdrawing a published record.
documents.s: I withdrew a published record, so why is it back on the public site?

documents.t: It depends on which it is. Placeholder text means the fields the citation draws on are incomplete on that record, and completing those fields fixes it on the next publish. Rough punctuation or ordering means the collection's citation style is not the right one yet, or is still being refined — that is set by your environment administrator, not on the record. See Copy a citation for a record or media item and Citations you can trust.
documents.s: A citation looks rough or shows placeholder text — is that mine to fix?

documents.t: You have just joined a knowledge environment. This page is a guided first week — a sequence to follow, not a reference to memorize. By the end you will have signed in, found your bearings, read a few records, made a safe first edit, previewed it as a reader would see it, and learned where to turn next. Every step links to the page that covers it in full; this tutorial puts those pages in order so nothing surprises you. Work through it once, in order. After that, the Researcher Guide is your map back to any single piece.

When your environment administrator gives you access, you sign in and land in your workspace. The screen has a stable shape you will see everywhere: a left sidebar listing the tables you can work with — figures, terms, manuscript editions, whatever your project tracks; a top bar with a search control and a command palette; a toolbar of table controls; and view tabs that switch between Table, Details, Relations, and Publish. Media tables also show a Media view. Click a table in the sidebar. You land in that table's workspace at an address like /app/workspace/<record-type>/, and you can bookmark or share that address. If your project has several record types, each has its own workspace. Do not try to set anything up yet. Just open two or three tables and notice that they all open into the same shell. The full tour of every control is in the Workspace walkthrough — read it when you are ready, but you do not need it to keep going here. What you are looking at is your team's shared workspace. Other researchers see the same tables; you are not alone in here.
documents.s: Day 1: sign in and look around

documents.t: Above the table sit view tabs. A view is a saved arrangement — which filters are on, how the rows are sorted, which columns show, how tall the rows are, and which view kind opens first. Your environment may have set one view as the default: the shared view and view kind the table opens with when you do not follow a link to another view. For now, stay on whichever view opens first. Look at the columns and ask yourself what each record represents. You are reading the shape of your team's data — what a "record" is here, and what fields describe it. You will arrange your own views later; Workspace walkthrough covers saving and switching them when you get there.
documents.s: Find the view your team starts from

documents.t: The instinct on a new project is to start adding records. Resist it for a day. Reading first tells you the conventions your team already follows. You have two ways to find records: Quick search, for jumping to one record. Click Search database… in the top bar (or press Ctrl+Shift+F, ⌘⇧F on Mac), type a term, and pick a result. Results group by collection and show which field matched. This is the right tool for "find this person, source, or term, wherever it lives." Search & Read, for dwelling among many records. From the quick search panel, choose Open full Search & Read — your typed term carries over — or pick Search & Read from the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K). The full page lets you filter, page through results, and open a record in a reading pane beside the list. Its address encodes your whole search, so you can bookmark or share it. Search matches across the scripts your records carry — original script, transliteration, and translation — for the fields your environment marks searchable. The full behavior, including how diacritics are handled, is in Searching and reading. For now, search for something you expect to exist, open it, and read its fields.

You do not have to come back to these pages to get help. The platform carries the same guidance inside the workspace, in two places. A small ? sits beside many controls. Click it and a help drawer opens beside your work, showing the guide for that exact control — so you can read it without losing your place. Inside the drawer, Related guides are one click away, and a breadcrumb with a Back button lets you return to where you started. Press Escape to close it. The Help page at /app/workspace/help lists every guide grouped by topic. Open one to read it in place. When a guide is tied to a control that is always on screen, its Show me where button jumps you to the workspace and highlights the matching ? spot. When you are stuck mid-task, reach for the nearest ? first; when you want to browse, open the Help page. Find help on a topic covers both.
documents.s: Find help without leaving your work

documents.t: Editing here is built so you cannot lose work or publish by accident. Three things are true before you touch anything: A new row is a draft the moment you create it. Click + New row in the toolbar and the row joins your table immediately as a draft. Drafts are visible to your project and never shown to public readers. Every change saves as you finish each field. There is no Save button to forget. Click out of a text field or press Enter, and the value is stored; choices and checkboxes save the moment you pick them. You can leave and come back another day — your draft waits in the table. Undo exists. The toolbar's Undo and Redo step your view changes — filters, sort, columns, density — backward and forward. Required fields can stay empty while you draft; they only need filling before the row can leave the draft stage and become an active record. Nothing reaches the public reading site until a record is completed and published, and that is a deliberate step you take, never an accident. The full lifecycle — drafts, activation, linking, and what each badge means — is in Adding and editing rows. Make one small edit to a draft you create yourself and watch it save. If you want to practice Undo, change the view instead — hide a column, change density, or add a harmless filter — then use Undo view change. Record-value edits are fixed by editing the value again, not by the view Undo button.

Now string the pieces together into one loop you will repeat for the rest of the project: Search for the area you are working in — a person, a source, a term. Read a few neighbouring records to learn the conventions. Edit or add a draft, letting each field save as you finish it. Preview the record. Open its Details panel: alongside the fields, a reader-preview pane renders the record exactly as a reader outside your project would see it — same layout, same fonts, same citations — without publishing anything.
