Read it, spot anything wrong, and fix it in the fields beside it. That loop — search, read, edit, preview — is the daily rhythm of the workspace. Searching and reading covers the search and preview ends of it; Adding and editing rows covers the editing end.
documents.s: A first full session, end to end

documents.t: You now have the loop. Here is the map for everything around it. The whole workspace, control by control → Workspace walkthrough. The draft-to-record lifecycle in full → Adding and editing rows. Search behaviour, media, and citations → Searching and reading. Working across scripts and languages → Working in multiple scripts and languages. What a reader outside the project sees, and how to preview it → Public reader. Driving the platform by keyboard, and display settings → Accessibility. What the platform records about you → Privacy and safety. The small suggestions beside the form and the table → Tips and guidance. One specific task, right now → the in-product Help page (/app/workspace/help), or browse the help topics — start with find help on a topic. If a control is missing, grayed out, or behaving unexpectedly, that almost always traces back to how your environment is configured, and your environment administrator is the person to ask. The Researcher Guide troubleshooting table lists the common cases.

Researcher Guide — the entry point and map for everything researcher-facing. Workspace walkthrough — the full tour this tutorial sequences. Adding and editing rows — the draft lifecycle your first edits rely on. Searching and reading — search, reading, and the reader preview. Find help on a topic — the in-product help page and the contextual ? buttons.

These pages give short answers to everyday questions about doing your work in your knowledge environment — finding and sharing material, shaping your fields and records, bringing in your source data, and publishing your entries. Each page covers one task, so you can read what you need and get back to your research.

Find help on a topic

When you add a row to a table, the platform creates it as a draft right away — no Save button needed. Every field you fill in saves the moment you leave it. Your draft is a real row in your table; you can close the panel and come back to it another day. When every required field is filled, the row can leave the draft stage and become an active record.

Open the table you want to add to. Click + New row in the toolbar. Your environment may label this button differently. A confirmation notice appears — Draft row created — and the row opens for editing. Fill in the fields. Each value saves when you click out of the field, press Enter, or make a choice. There is no Save button to forget. Leave and return whenever you like. Your values are stored. Click the row in the table to pick up where you left off. Required fields can stay empty while you draft. They must be filled before the row can be activated. Two more ways to start a row: Insert row below — right-click an existing row and choose Insert row below. Duplicate row — right-click a row and choose Duplicate row. The new draft starts with that row's editable values already filled in — a useful way to create a second entry that shares most of the same details. If + New row is unavailable, hover over it to see why. Some views cannot accept new rows — for example, a view that combines or filters records rather than showing a single stored table.

A new row begins as a draft: Your project sees it. Draft rows appear in the workspace table alongside every other row. Public readers never see it. Only records that have been activated and then published reach the public reading site. It cannot be linked yet. If you try to link a draft row to another record, the platform declines with a message. Finish the draft first. Required fields may wait. A draft saves even if required fields are empty. The row cannot be activated until every required field has a value.

Once you have filled in every required field and the row passes its checks, it can leave the draft stage and become an active record. After activation, the row is no longer a draft — it is a full record in your collection, and links to and from other records work normally. Activation is not the same as publication. An activated record is visible to your project but not yet public. A separate publish step sends it to the public reading site. See Preview an entry before publishing.

Symptom Likely cause Fix + New row is unavailable or greyed out. The current view cannot accept new rows. Hover over the button to see the reason, or switch to a regular table view. Creating a row fails with a permission message. Your role includes read access but not edit access. Contact your environment administrator. A field did not save after you typed a value. The field may not have lost focus, or the value failed a check. Click outside the field or press Enter. Look for an error message near the field, then re-enter the value if it reverted. You cannot link another record from a new row. The row is still a draft. Links to other records are not accepted until the row is activated. Fill in the required fields so the row can leave the draft stage, then try again. The row stays in the draft stage. One or more required fields are still empty. Look for a message near any empty field, fill in every required field, and try again. The row you added has disappeared from the table. It may have been filtered out of the current view. Remove or adjust any active filters, or switch to a view that shows all rows.

Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a row can be activated. Preview an entry before publishing — checking how a record will look to public readers before you publish it. Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — creating the collections and fields that hold your records.

When a column is set up to hold several values — one for each language, register, script, edition, or calendar — you fill those values in per record, in the table cell or in the record's form. Every value here is one you enter. The platform never translates a value into another language or fills one in from another field.
documents.s: Add a value in another language

documents.t: Open the record, either by editing the cell in the table or by opening the record's form. You see one row per value the record already has — each row pairs the value with the language (or register, script, edition, or calendar) it belongs to. To add a value, click + Add language (the wording follows the column's setup — + Add register, + Add script, and so on). A new row appears. Choose the language for the new row from the dropdown. It lists the values the column allows; if the one you need is not there, click + new and type it. Type the value beside it. Keep the changes: in the table cell, click Save; in the record's form, your edits save on their own. Either way, a row left blank is dropped.
When a row's language is Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, or Aramaic, its value box writes from right to left, so the text reads correctly as you type. Other languages write from left to right.

The language for each row is a dropdown of the values the column allows — not a box you type into freely. This keeps every record's values lining up under the same set of languages. When you genuinely need a value the list does not offer, + new lets you add one, and it is tidied into the same standard short form the rest of the column uses. Which languages a column allows is set on the column itself — see Let a column hold several values.
documents.s: Choosing the language is a pick, not free typing

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Arabic or Hebrew text writes left to right. The row's language is not set to a right-to-left language. Pick the right-to-left language from the dropdown; the value box switches direction. The language you need is not in the dropdown. It is not yet in the column's allowed list. Click + new and type it, or ask whoever set up the column to add it (see Let a column hold several values). A blank row disappeared. Empty rows are dropped when your changes are kept. Fill in both the language and the value.
Let a column hold several values — setting up the column and its allowed languages. Add a new record — creating a record and filling its fields.
Alongside search, a published environment offers an index — a browsable, alphabetised list of every entry. It is the way to explore the whole corpus when you are not looking for one specific item.

A project can publish more than one index, and you switch between them from the controls at the top of the list. For a multilingual corpus that often means browsing the same entries by transliteration or by original script — the same entries, ordered and bucketed by whichever index you pick. The available indexes are chosen by your project; you see only the ones it publishes.
Each row in the index can show more than a bare headword — typically the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together — so you can recognise an entry without opening it.

A character rail runs alongside the index. Click a letter to jump straight to that bucket; the list pages as you scroll, so even a very large corpus stays responsive. Which index is the default, and what each row shows, are set by your project when the environment is published — different projects will offer different index choices.
You do not need a spreadsheet or data file to start. You can create collections, define their fields, and wire up relations between them directly in the workspace — no import wizard required.
documents.s: Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing

documents.t: A knowledge environment is made of: Collections — the types of things you are keeping track of (people, manuscripts, events, places — whatever is relevant to your project). Fields — the pieces of information you record for each item in a collection (a person's name, a manuscript's date, a place's region). Relations — links between collections that let you say "this person wrote this manuscript" or "this event happened in this place." All three are created the same way whether you are starting from scratch or refining a set that an import created.

Open the workspace. In the sidebar, use Add table. This opens the administration form for a new workspace table. Give the table a label — for example, "People" or "Manuscripts". Choose the concept family that best describes the things in this collection (person, document, place, event, and so on). This helps the platform apply sensible defaults for search and display. Confirm. The empty table appears in your sidebar after it is saved and active. It has no project-specific fields yet; you add them next.

Open the collection. Use the Add column header at the end of the table, or choose Insert column... from an existing column's header menu. The column editor opens. Give the field a label — the name as you want it to appear in the table (for example, "Full name", "Date of composition", "Language"). Choose the field type: text, number, date, select (a list of options), or other types your project supports. Save. Repeat for as many fields as the collection needs. You can always add more fields later. When you create a field this way, the label you type is the only name it ever has. There is no source column name to fall back on — what you typed is exactly what appears everywhere.

A relation lets a record in one collection point to a record in another. For example, a field on "Manuscripts" that points to a "People" record for the author. Open the collection where the relation field will live (e.g., "Manuscripts"). Use Add column or Insert column... from a column header menu. Give it a label (e.g., "Author"). Choose the field type Relation (or Link to collection). Select the collection this field points to (e.g., "People"). Save. When you open a Manuscripts record, the "Author" field shows a picker that lets you search and select a People record. The link is live — clicking the linked record opens that person.
documents.s: Creating a relation between two collections

documents.t: You can mix import and manual. Start with a skeleton you build by hand, then import data later. Or import first and add extra fields by hand. The rules are the same either way. Relations you create manually are immediately active. Unlike some imported relations that go through a review queue, manually created relations are ready to use as soon as you save. Your labels are your labels. Every field you create from scratch is researcher-owned from birth — no import will ever overwrite the label you gave it (see Rename a field label). Removing a field. If you later decide a field is not needed, use the column header menu and choose Delete column. Deleting removes the field definition from the table and form, but it does not erase the stored values underneath; re-adding a field with the same field key restores them.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Add collection is not visible in the sidebar. Your role may not have permission to create collections. Ask a project administrator. The concept family I need is not in the list. Only the concept families enabled for your project are listed. Ask an administrator to enable the one you need. A relation field I created is not showing the picker when I open a record. The relation may need a moment to become active, or the target collection has no records yet. Refresh the record; if the target collection is empty, add a record there first. I created a field but it does not appear in the table columns. New fields may not be visible in all views by default. Open the Column manager (from the toolbar) and enable the field.

Make a field required — requiring a value for any field. Rename a field label — how labels work and what you own. What changed after re-import — if you later import source data into a hand-built collection.

A row color rule belongs to one column. You pick a value and a color, and every row whose field holds exactly that value shows a stripe of that color at the left edge of the row, next to the row number. The row itself is unchanged — the stripe lets your eye pick out the matching rows while every column stays readable. You can give several values of the same field their own colors — "Reviewed" in moss green, "Needs attention" in rose — and set rules on more than one column at the same time.

Click the ⋯ (Column actions) button on the column's header. Right-clicking the header opens the same menu. Select Conditional format. Under Color rows where value is, pick the value you want to highlight. For a choice field, the list offers the field's options; for other fields, it offers values found in the rows already loaded in the table. Select a color: Rose, Amber, Moss, Steel, Violet, or Graphite. The stripes appear on the matching rows, and Saved with view shows next to the panel title. To color another value of the same field, pick it in the same list and choose its color.

The stripes themselves: a colored edge on a row means at least one rule matches it. In a column's menu, the Conditional format entry reads Saved when that column has a rule. Inside the Conditional format panel, the color marked with a check is the one assigned to the value shown in the list. Rules are kept per column, so to review them, open each column's menu. A row shows one stripe color even when it matches rules on more than one column.

Open Conditional format on the column: Clear value removes the color from the value currently shown in the list. Clear this column's rules removes every value and color on that column. The button is there only while the column has a rule. Changing or clearing color rules is a view change like any other: the Undo view change arrow in the toolbar restores what you cleared, and Redo view change re-applies it.

Color rules are part of the view, alongside filters, sort order, and column layout. They are stored on whichever view is active as you work, and they are waiting for you when you return. Duplicating a view copies its color rules; each view keeps its own set. See Save your table arrangement as a view. Views are shared with everyone working in your environment. A color rule you add or clear on a view reaches your collaborators too — to highlight rows for your own work without changing what your team sees, duplicate the view first and set the rules in the copy.
documents.s: Rules are remembered by your views

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The value I want to color is not in the list. The list offers a choice field's options plus values found in rows already loaded in this table. A value no loaded row holds does not appear, and when a column holds many distinct values, the list offers only the first ones found. Check that at least one row in the table holds the value, then reopen the column menu. The panel says no values are loaded yet. The column has no data in the rows loaded for this table. The value list appears once the column has data in the active table. A row I expect to be colored shows no stripe. The rule matches the value exactly as it is displayed. The row's value may differ — a different option, extra wording, or another spelling. Compare the row's value with the value named in the rule, and add a rule for the variant if both forms are in use. I colored a value, but a row shows a different color. The row also matches a rule on another column — a row shows one stripe color even when several rules match. Open the other columns' menus and clear the rule you no longer want. My rules disappeared after switching view tabs. Each view keeps its own color rules. Switch back to the view where you set them, or set rules on the view that is now active. My rule changes are not kept when I come back. Changes are stored on the active view — if your role is read-only on this table, the view cannot be changed. Ask your environment administrator for editing access.

Save your table arrangement as a view — views remember your color rules along with filters, sort, and columns. Narrow the current table with filters — hide the rows you don't need instead of coloring the ones you do.

When you open a published entry — or its draft preview — the reading view shows the entry's citations rendered in your project's citation style. Select and copy the text to paste it into a bibliography, footnote, or document. Citations sit in the entry's References area. Rows of evidence carry their citations, and when your project has set up a citation for the record itself, it appears as its own row there too. Read the references section on a published entry explains what each row means.
documents.s: Copy a citation for a record or media item

documents.t: A media item attached to a record can carry its own citation details — separate from the record's citation. When your project has given a media item full citation details, its citation appears among the entry's references, rendered in your project's style and ready to copy.

Your project's citation style is set by your environment administrator. It is defined in Citation Style Language — the same format reference managers such as Zotero use. Different collections within your project can use different styles.
documents.s: What citation style your project uses

documents.t: The draft preview shows an entry exactly as a reader will see it, references and citations included, so you can copy a citation before anything goes live — see Preview an entry before publishing.
documents.s: Copying before an entry is public

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A citation shows placeholder text or looks incomplete. The fields the citation draws on are missing or only partly filled in on that record or media item. Open the record in your workspace and complete those fields. The citation updates on the next publish; the draft preview shows the result first. If the needed fields are not clear, ask your environment administrator. The citation style looks wrong for your field. Your project has not yet declared a citation style for that collection, or the style is still being refined. Contact your environment administrator. Citation styles are set per collection; the citations update once a style is applied. A citation renders roughly — punctuation or ordering looks off. The collection's citation style is a proposed draft that has not yet been reviewed and applied. Raise it with your environment administrator. A reviewed and applied style replaces the rough rendering on the next publish. No citation appears for a media item. The media item's citation details are missing, or your project has not set up citations for media items in that collection. Complete the citation fields on the media item's record, or ask your environment administrator whether media citations are set up for that collection.
The workspace table has separate clipboard paths for cells, cell ranges, and full selected rows. Use the one that matches what you want to paste next.

Focus the cell whose value you want. Press Ctrl+C on Windows or Linux, or Cmd+C on Mac. Move to the cell where the value should go and paste with Ctrl/Cmd+V. When several rows are selected and the focused column is editable, pasting one copied value fills that same column for each selected row. Read-only fields, derived fields, and fields your role cannot edit are skipped rather than silently changed.

Use a cell range when you want a rectangle of cells, not entire records. Click the first cell in the rectangle. Shift-click the opposite corner, or hold Shift and use the arrow keys to extend the range. The status line shows the range size, such as Cell range: 3 x 3. Press Ctrl/Cmd+C to copy the range as tab-separated values, without row headers. Paste while the range is active to target that rectangle. A single copied value fills the editable cells in the rectangle. Tabular data follows the visible row and column order; cells that cannot be written are skipped and reported. Press Escape to clear the cell range. Clearing a cell range does not clear selected rows.
documents.s: Copy or fill a cell range

documents.t: Use row copy when you want rows as a small table, usually to paste into a spreadsheet. Focus a row and press Space to select it. Use Ctrl/Cmd+Space to add or remove another focused row, or Shift with the arrow keys to extend the selection. Select Copy TSV in the selection toolbar. The copied text includes the visible columns and a header row with the column labels. It is different from copying cells or a cell range: row copy gives another tool enough structure to paste whole records and columns.

If you copied rows from a spreadsheet or from another workspace view, focus the top-left editable target cell and paste. The table lines up pasted columns by header label when the copied data includes headers, otherwise it starts at the focused column. Pasted rows update rows already visible in the table; extra rows are reported as skipped instead of being created by accident.
documents.s: Paste tabular data into existing rows

documents.t: On a persisted table where row creation is available, the table can show a Paste rows here target. Use it when your clipboard contains full tabular rows and you want the workspace to create draft records from them. The paste creates only fields that can be edited directly in a new draft. Derived fields, linked fields that cannot be set during draft creation, hidden or unknown columns, and values your role cannot write are skipped with a summary. Large pastes ask for confirmation before creating rows. If New row is unavailable for the current table, paste-as-new-rows is also unavailable. This happens on views that are not backed by one persisted workspace table.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Pasting one copied value changed only the last focused cell. No cell range was active, the destination rows were not selected in the table grid, or focus was not in the editable column to fill. Use a cell range for a rectangle of cells, or select the target rows and focus the column to update. A copied range pasted with some cells skipped. Some target fields were read-only, derived, hidden, unknown, or not editable by your role. Check the paste summary, then edit those fields manually if the table offers an editor. A browser permission prompt or copy failure appears. The browser blocked clipboard access for this site. Allow clipboard access for your environment and retry. Some pasted fields were skipped. The pasted columns include read-only, derived, hidden, unknown, or not-yet-editable fields. Check the paste summary, then edit those fields manually if the table offers an editor. The table did not create new rows from extra pasted lines. Existing-row paste never creates overflow rows automatically. Use Paste rows here on a table where row creation is available.

You can pick any number of rows in your table and either copy them to your clipboard (to paste into a spreadsheet) or download them as a file. A floating toolbar appears as soon as you select at least one row and disappears when you clear the selection.

One row: focus the row in the table grid and press Space. Add rows one at a time: hold Ctrl (Windows / Linux) or Cmd (Mac) and press Space on another focused row. Select a range: select the first row, then hold Shift while moving with the arrow keys. Every row between them is selected. The toolbar shows the count of selected rows and stays visible while you work.

With your rows selected, click Copy TSV in the toolbar. The selected rows are copied in the order they currently appear in the grid. The visible columns are placed on your clipboard with a header row of column labels. Switch to a spreadsheet, press Ctrl/Cmd+V, and the rows paste into cells, ready to use. If you only need one field value, copy the focused cell instead of the whole row. See Copy and paste table values.

Click Download CSV to download the selected rows as a spreadsheet-friendly CSV file. Your browser saves the file to your usual downloads location. Use JSON only when you need the raw structured row payload for a technical workflow.
Click the × at the right end of the toolbar — or, while the toolbar is focused, press Escape. The toolbar disappears and no rows remain selected.

The toolbar also shows Delete, Edit visibility, and Set row color. All three are visible but not yet available — they are waiting on a platform update. Clicking them does nothing. Selecting rows in one view does not carry over to another view or to another table. Switching views or tables clears the selection.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Clicking a row opens the record instead of selecting it. Click opens record details on some workspace routes. Use keyboard selection: focus the row and press Space. The toolbar does not appear after selecting a row. The focus may be inside a cell editor or another control rather than on the row. Press Escape to close the editor, move focus back to the row, then press Space. A "Copy failed" message appears after clicking Copy TSV. Your browser blocked clipboard access for this site. Allow clipboard access in your browser's site settings for this environment, then copy again. Delete, Edit visibility, or Set row color does nothing when clicked. These buttons are labeled "Backend pending" and are not yet active. Nothing is wrong, and no setting turns them on — they stay unavailable until the platform adds batch support. The selection is cleared when I switch to another view. Selections are per-view and per-session — they are not saved. Re-select your rows after switching views.
The toolbar above your table has two filtering tools. They work together and are both only about the table in front of you — they do not search the rest of your workspace.
documents.s: Narrow the current table with filters

documents.t: The Filter visible rows… box in the toolbar narrows the table as you type. It matches against whatever text is already loaded in the visible rows, in whatever script the text is written. Type a term and the table immediately hides rows that do not contain it. Clear the box and all rows come back. The filter box works on rows already loaded in the table. If the record you want lives in a different collection, it will not appear here — use the Search database… control at the top of the workspace instead. This text is not saved with the view. When you navigate away and return, the filter box is empty. For a filter you want to keep, use the filter builder below and save the arrangement as a view.
documents.s: The filter box — quick narrowing as you type

documents.t: Click Filter in the toolbar to open the filter builder. Each filter condition targets one field. Pick the field, then set a value with a control suited to that field's kind: Field kind What you set Text A word or phrase, typed in a text box Number A number, typed in a number box Date A date, picked with a date control Choice (single or multiple) One of the field's option values, picked from a list Any other field kind takes a word or phrase, matched against the value as it is displayed in the table. A row stays visible when the field's displayed value contains what you set. Matching ignores letter case. Comparisons such as greater-than, before and after, or ranges are not available in the filter builder. Date fields are the exception to the "contains" rule: when both the filter value and the row value are readable as dates, the table matches the same calendar date. A stored value with a time and timezone can still match the date you picked. A field that only looks like a date but is configured as Text keeps text matching until its field type is changed or a future conversion workflow is used. The table narrows as soon as you set a value, and the condition appears as a chip in the toolbar, shown after "filtering by". The chip names the field and the value, with a count of the rows that currently match, so you can see at a glance what is active.
documents.s: The filter builder — conditions by column

documents.t: Add more than one condition by picking another field in the filter builder. All active conditions must match a row for it to stay visible — the conditions work together. Each field carries one condition: setting a new value for a field replaces that field's earlier value. The filter box and the filter builder also compose: you can apply column conditions and then type in the filter box to narrow further.
Click the × on any chip to remove that condition. The table widens to include rows that now match. Click Clear — visible when at least one chip is active — to remove every condition at once.

You do not need a search term to use filters. If you want to survey a slice of your corpus — all records with a particular choice value, all rows that mention a particular place — open the filter builder, set your conditions, and browse the matching rows directly. No typing in the search box required.

Filters set while a saved view is active are remembered on that view. Open or create a view, set your conditions, and the next time you open that view your filters are already applied. See What happens to saved views after a re-import for how saved filters behave when a field changes.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The filter box does not find a record you expect. The box narrows rows already loaded in this table; the record may be in a different collection. Use the Search database… control at the top of the workspace to search across all collections you can access. A filter condition I set is gone when I come back to the table. You set the condition using the quick filter box, which is not stored. Conditions from the filter builder chips persist only when a saved view is active. Set the condition in the filter builder, then save the view. The filter box was matching rows, but a record I know matches is missing. The filter box works on text visible in loaded rows; a field that is not displayed as a column is not matched. Open the filter builder instead and target the specific field you want to filter on. I cannot find the Filter button. In a narrow window the toolbar lays its controls out on more than one line. Widen the window, or look for the button on the toolbar's following line. After I clear all chips, rows I expected do not reappear. The quick filter box may also have a term in it. Check the filter box in the toolbar and clear it. The filter builder does not show the field I want to filter on. The filter builder lists the fields configured for your collection. Contact your environment administrator if a field you need is missing from the filter builder.

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — when to use search rather than filtering. What happens to saved views after a re-import — how your saved filters survive source updates. Share a search — copy a URL that includes your filters so a colleague sees the same rows.
Help is available without leaving the workspace, in two places.

The Help page (/app/workspace/help) lists the available guides grouped by topic — working with your data, finding and sharing, and importing. Open a guide to read it in place; each one answers a single task-shaped question in plain language. A direct link to one guide looks like /app/workspace/help/<guide-name>, so you can share a specific guide with a colleague.
Many controls have a small ? affordance beside them. Clicking it opens the matching guide in a drawer, right where you are working — so you can read the relevant help without losing your place.
If a guide does not cover your question, or a control is not behaving as you expect, that is worth reporting to your project's administrator — the help set grows as new behaviour ships.
documents.s: When help does not answer it

documents.t: Adding a row opens a side drawer where you fill in the new record's fields. This entry is about that drawer's interior — the progress pill, the highlighted fields, the Activate row button, and what happens when you close it.
documents.s: Finish a new row in the drawer

documents.t: The drawer opens with one editor per field, in the order your collection shows them. Above the fields, a header line called next save step tells you what the drawer will do next, and a small status pill tells you where the row stands. The pill moves through these states as you work: Pill says What it means Not yet saved You have opened the drawer but nothing is stored on the server yet. Creating draft... The drawer is saving your first field, turning the row into a stored draft. Draft saved The draft is stored and nothing is waiting to be saved. Unsaved edits You have changed a field since the last save. Saving... An edit is being written to the server. Activating... The drawer is turning your draft into an active record. Discarding... The drawer is removing the draft. Needs attention Something failed — look for the message at the top of the form, with a Retry button. The drawer does not save anything the moment it opens. The row becomes a stored draft the first time you fill a field and click out of it (for a collection with required fields, the first required field you fill). Until then the pill reads Not yet saved and closing costs you nothing. When the draft is first stored, a brief Draft row created notice appears with a Review row button.
documents.s: What the drawer shows when it opens

documents.t: Fields that must be filled before the row can become active are marked, and a hint appears beneath a required field if you leave it empty after editing it. The Activate row button stays disabled while any required field is empty. Hover over it to see exactly which fields are still missing — the drawer lists them by name. Each unfilled required field also shows the message Required before activation. You can keep editing and leave a draft with empty required fields for as long as you like; only activation is blocked. To choose which fields are required, see Make a field required.
documents.s: Required fields and the Activate button

documents.t: A few field types are not directly editable in the new-row drawer and show a short reason instead: Linked-record fields wait until the row is a stored draft — you connect records after the draft exists. Lookup fields are derived from linked records and fill in after relations are saved. Composed fields are built from other fields after the row is saved. Media fields are not editable on a draft row yet. This is expected — fill the plain fields here, then add links and media to the record once it exists.
documents.s: Some fields are not editable here yet

documents.t: When every required field has a value, Activate row becomes available. Click it (or press Ctrl + Enter, or Cmd + Enter on a Mac). The drawer saves any pending edits, then activates the row. Activation is not publication. An activated row is a full record your project can see and link to and from — but it is not yet on the public reading site. Publishing is a separate step; see Preview an entry before publishing. After the row activates, the drawer closes and a confirmation notice appears with a Review row button that takes you to the new record.

How closing behaves depends on whether a draft has been stored yet: Nothing saved yet (pill reads Not yet saved) — the close button, Cancel, Esc, or clicking outside closes the drawer. Nothing was stored, so nothing is lost. A draft has been stored — closing opens a Discard this draft row? confirmation. It lists the values currently in the window and offers two choices: Keep editing (also Esc or clicking outside the confirmation) — returns you to the drawer. Discard draft — removes the stored draft from the server. Closing the confirmation with Keep editing does not delete your draft. If you close the whole drawer without discarding, the stored draft stays on the server and the drawer offers to resume it next time you start a new row in that collection.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Activate row is greyed out. A required field is still empty. Hover over the button to see which fields are missing, fill them, and try again. A field shows Required before activation even though I filled it. The value may not have been saved, or a different required field is empty. Click out of the field so it saves, and check every highlighted field. The drawer says Needs attention. A save, activation, or discard call failed. Use the Retry button at the top of the form, or Dismiss and re-enter the value. A field in the drawer is not editable. It is a linked-record, lookup, composed, or media field. Finish the plain fields and activate the row first, then add links and media to the record. Opening the drawer shows You can read this table, but not add rows. Your role has read access but not row-creation access. Use Copy ask-message and send the request to your environment administrator.

Add a new record — the page-level lifecycle of a row, from creating it to activation. Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a row can be activated. Preview an entry before publishing — checking how an activated record will look to public readers.

When your source has two columns whose names are so similar that the platform cannot tell them apart as separate fields, the import stops before writing anything and shows you every problem at once. The report names each set of colliding columns so you know exactly what to fix.
documents.s: Fix colliding column names during import

documents.t: Each column in your source becomes a field with an internal identifier built from its name. Spaces, punctuation, and capitalisation differences are smoothed out so the identifier works consistently across languages and formats. When two differently named columns produce the same identifier after that smoothing — for example, "Author Name" and "Author-Name" both become the same field — the platform cannot accept both without overwriting one with the other. Rather than silently discard data, the import stops and reports every such collision in one message.

For each collision, the report names the identifier the columns would share and lists every source column that produces it — including which table each column comes from when your source has more than one table. If there are several collisions, they all appear together — the import never stops at the first one and leaves the rest hidden.

You have two options. Option 1 — Rename one of the columns in your source. Open your spreadsheet or data source, give the conflicting column a name that is meaningfully different from its counterpart, then run the import again. A small change like adding a word or removing an ambiguous character is enough. Option 2 — Leave one of the colliding columns out during the import review. In the review step, reject the proposed field for one of the colliding columns so only one of them becomes a field. The other column is not deleted from your source — if you need both, rename one there and bring it in with a later import. Your data is never changed or written while a collision is unresolved. The import stops entirely and waits for you to fix the source or adjust your review decisions before it touches anything.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The same column keeps appearing in the collision report after renaming. The new name still smooths out to the same identifier as the other column. Make the names more distinct — change more than capitalisation or a single punctuation mark. The collision report shows columns from different tables in my source. Two differently named columns in different tables feed the same collection and produce the same identifier. Rename the column in one of the tables, or leave one of them out during the import review. The import worked before but now shows a collision after I added a column. A new column you added has a name too similar to an existing one. Rename the new column to something clearly distinct before re-importing.

Rename a field label — giving a field a friendlier name after a successful import without changing your source. Understand what changed after a re-import — what the platform carries forward when the import completes successfully.

Sometimes the import's checks flag a column not because anything is broken, but because its values don't match the type or script the platform expected — and that mismatch is intentional. Approximate dates like "c. 350 BCE", a column that mixes scripts, or free-form notes in a field the platform read as numeric are all normal in scholarly data. When the only objections are advisory like this, you can bring the column in as-is: its values are stored as text, exactly as they appear, with nothing converted or dropped.
documents.s: Keep non-standard values as-is during import

documents.t: If your approved choices would bring in zero rows, the practice run stops and says "Nothing will import yet" rather than completing with nothing. For a column that was flagged only for advisory reasons (a type or script mismatch that may be deliberate), one of the offered actions is Import these as-is (keep non-standard values). This is offered only for advisory flags — a structural problem, such as a duplicate identifier or a missing column, must be corrected and is never offered as keep-as-is.

The flagged column is brought in as a plain text field, and each value is kept exactly as written in your source. The platform does not try to reinterpret the values as numbers or dates, and it does not drop the ones that didn't fit — the point is to preserve what you have rather than force it into a shape it wasn't meant for.

Before anything is written, a DRY RUN card previews the decision: The flagged column moves from skipped to kept, with a note that its values are kept as text. A few example values from your source are shown for context. A Won't touch list bounds what stays exactly as it is — every other approved choice is left alone. A seal states that no source rows are written until you run the import. Nothing is saved from this preview; it is a dry run of the one decision.

Keeping a column as-is is reversible. If you undo the decision, it is fully reversed — a later normal approval will not silently bring the column back in as text. And because the values are stored exactly as written, you can revisit the column in your workspace after the import. A flagged column is a suggestion, not a verdict. The import never forces your data to conform — keeping non-standard values is a supported choice, because what counts as "standard" depends on your material.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The "Import these as-is" action isn't offered for my column The column was flagged for a structural reason (a duplicate identifier or a missing column), not an advisory one Structural problems must be corrected — use the offered fix action or adjust the column in your source, then run the practice run again. I kept a column as-is but want it typed as a date or number instead Keep-as-is stores the column as text by design Go back to the review step and change how that column is mapped, rather than using keep-as-is. The practice run still says "Nothing will import yet" after I kept a column Other approved choices still bring in zero rows Resolve the remaining cause the stop names — fix conflicting columns, return to review, or align the other flagged columns.

Fix colliding column names during import — the other kind of import stop, where two columns would become the same field. Understand what changed after a re-import — what the platform carries forward when you bring the same source in again.

Relation fields connect a record in one collection to one or more records in another. For example, a "Text" record might have an "Author" field that points to a "People" record. Once a link is in place, it appears as a small labelled chip in the field. Linking happens in the Details view or directly in the table cell in the Table view — whichever you find easier to work with.

Open the record you want to edit, or click its cell in the table. Find the relation field (it shows existing links as chips, or says there are no linked records yet). Click into the field. A search box appears. Type part of the name of the record you want to connect to. Matching records appear as you type. Click the record you want. It appears as a chip in the field. The link saves immediately — there is no separate save step. In the table cell, the field also lists records from the target collection for you to browse before you type anything. You can add more than one link to the same field by repeating the search and pick steps. A record that is already linked is not offered again.
Open the record or click its cell. Find the chip for the link you want to remove. Click the × on the chip. The link is removed and the change saves straight away.
The Relations view shows every link for a selected record — both the links it makes and the links other records make to it. Select a link there to see its details, or to remove it.

A newly created row begins as a draft. Links can only point to active records. A row that is still a draft cannot be chosen as a link target until it is activated. While you are filling in a new row, its relation fields become available once the platform has created your draft — enter a value in another field first. From there you can link your draft to active records as you work. In the Table and Details views, link edits on a row that is still a draft are declined. Fill in the row's required fields and activate it; after that, links work normally everywhere. Links you added while drafting are kept.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The search box shows no results when I type. The target collection has no records yet, or your search term does not match any. Add a record to the target collection first, or try a shorter or different search term. The record I want to link to does not appear in the results. It may still be a draft — links can only point to active records. Activate that record first, then search again. The relation field in a new row is not editable yet. The platform creates your draft after you fill in a first value. Enter a value in another field and click out of it, then return to the relation field. The relation field is not visible in the Details view. The field may be hidden in the current view. Open Manage columns from the Table view toolbar and make sure the field is shown. I cannot add a link to my row from the table. The row is still a draft. Fill in the row's required fields and activate it, then add the link. The × to remove a link is not showing. Your role may not include edit access for this collection. Contact your environment administrator.

Build a knowledge environment from scratch without importing — how to create the relation field itself between two collections. Add a new record — the draft stage and how a new row becomes an active record. Make a field required — controlling which fields must be filled before a draft row becomes active.

When a field is required, a draft record cannot be activated while that field is empty. The platform lets you keep drafting, but it will not let the row leave the draft stage until the required fields have values. In the current workspace build, researchers see required fields and the activation gate. Changing which fields are required is handled by your environment administrator or platform operator.

Open the collection whose field should become required. Open the column header menu and note the exact Column label. Tell your environment administrator which collection and field should be required. After they change the configuration, create a draft row and confirm the field shows as required before activation. From now on, any new record in that collection will require a value in this field before it can be activated. Existing records already in the collection are not retroactively blocked.

When you create a new record and blur out of a required field while it is still empty, the form surfaces a validation hint beneath that field. The Activate button stays greyed out until the required field has a value. You can save the draft with the field empty — autosave keeps your progress — but activation is blocked.
documents.s: What "required" means at the record level

documents.t: Required applies to new drafts and activation checks. Existing records are not retroactively blocked in the table just because the setting changed later. Your import does not decide this for you. Requiredness is configuration your team controls. Removing the required flag is also a configuration change for your administrator or operator.

Symptom Likely cause Fix You cannot find a Required toggle. The current workspace column editor does not expose this as a researcher self-serve toggle. Ask your environment administrator to change the field configuration. An existing record shows no required-field hint even though the field is empty. Required applies only to records created after the setting was turned on. Existing records are not retroactively blocked. The Activate button is still grey after filling in the required field. Another required field may also be empty. Check for other red-outlined or hint-bearing fields on the form.
Rename a field label — how to change what a field is called, without losing your data. Build from empty — creating tables and fields without importing a spreadsheet.

Some columns are most useful when one record carries several values at once — a term in each of its languages, a title in each script, a date on each calendar. You set this up once, on the column, and from then on every record can keep a separate value for each. You choose what kind of values the column separates by, and which ones are allowed. The platform never adds or translates a value for you — every value is one you entered.
documents.s: Let a column hold several values

documents.t: Add or edit a column. In the schema window, find the Multiple values section near the bottom. Turn on This column holds more than one value. Two more controls appear. Under A separate value for each, choose what the column separates by: Language, Register, Script, Edition, Calendar, or Custom. In Allowed languages (the label follows your choice — Allowed registers, Allowed scripts, and so on), build the list of values the column accepts. Type a value into Add a language and press Enter. Each entry shows as a chip; the × on a chip removes it. Save the column. From now on, each record can hold one value for every allowed entry. To fill them in, see Add a value in another language.

The list is a set of chips, not free text. When you type a new entry, the platform tidies it into a standard short form before it joins the list — so typing "greek" gives you a GK chip. If you and a colleague add the same value two different ways (one types "GREEK", the other "GK"), they fold into the single chip rather than splitting into two. This keeps every record's values lining up under the same set of headings.

Higher in the same window, This column's language & script sets one language and script for the whole column at once — useful when every value in the column is in the same language. Multiple values is the opposite case: the column keeps a separate value for each entry you allow. The two sections are independent; set whichever fits the column.
documents.s: The column's own language is separate

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The Multiple values controls are greyed out. The column has a fixed text role (such as a URL or email column), which holds a single value by design. Multiple values are not available for those columns; use a plain text column instead. A value you typed turned into a different short form. New entries are tidied into a standard short form so records line up. This is expected — after you add it, the value appears as a chip in its standard short form. Two spellings of the same value collapsed into one chip. The platform folds variant spellings of the same value together. This is intended — it keeps every record under the same headings.
Add a value in another language — filling in the per-record values once the column is set up. Rename a field label — changing what a column is called without losing its data.

The left sidebar lists every table in your knowledge environment. When your environment has many tables, you can pin the ones you use most, gather them into named groups, and collapse or hide everything else — so the tables you need are always at the top, not buried in a long list.
documents.s: Pin and group tables in the sidebar

documents.t: Pinning adds a table to a Favorites group at the top of your sidebar. The table also stays in its regular group. Click the star next to the table's name in the sidebar — or open the table and press Shift+S. The table appears under Favorites at the top of the sidebar. To unpin it, click the star again, or press Shift+S while the table is open. Pinning is yours — it does not change what your colleagues see in their sidebar.

Named groups let you gather related tables under a heading you choose, so the sidebar reflects how you think about your work rather than the order the tables happen to arrive in. Press Ctrl+Shift+G (Cmd+Shift+G on Mac), click Add group at the bottom of the table list, or open the command palette with Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac), type "sidebar", and choose Create sidebar group. The new group appears at the bottom of the table list with its name ready to edit — type a name and press Enter. Drag tables into the group, or drag them between groups to reorganize. Collapse a group by clicking its heading — only that group folds away, and the others stay open. Expand it again the same way.
Recent appears near the top of the sidebar and lists the five tables you opened last. Use it when you remember working in a table but cannot remember where it sits in your groups.

When you want more room for your table, press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on Mac) to collapse the sidebar to a narrow icon rail. Each table is still reachable as an icon. Press Ctrl+B again to expand the sidebar back to full width.
documents.s: Collapse the sidebar to an icon rail

documents.t: If you want to undo all your pinning and grouping and start from scratch: Open the command palette with Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac). Type "reset sidebar" and select Reset sidebar to default groups. This puts the sidebar back to its original layout. Your records and views are not affected — only the sidebar arrangement resets.
documents.s: Reset the sidebar to its defaults

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Shift+S does nothing. Your cursor is in a text box, or no table is open — the shortcut pins the table you currently have open. Click the table in the sidebar to open it, then press Shift+S — or click the star next to its name instead. I cannot find the group I created. New groups are added at the bottom of the table list, and sidebar changes are saved only when you are signed in. Scroll the sidebar down. If the message near the bottom of the sidebar asks you to sign in, sign in and create the group again. Dragging a table into a group does not work. Tables listed under Favorites or Recent cannot be dragged — dragging works from a table's row in its regular groups. Drag the table's row from its own group. Or click the table once, press Space to pick it up, move it with the arrow keys, and press Space again to drop it. The sidebar looks different on another device. Your pins and groups follow your sign-in, but the sidebar's width and its collapsed or expanded state are remembered by the browser you used. Press Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on Mac) or drag the sidebar's edge to set the size you want on each device.
Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — finding records when the sidebar is not the right tool. Find help on a topic — more ways to get answers while you work.
Before an entry is visible to the public, you can see it exactly as a reader will — the same page, the same layout, the same references — so nothing about the published result is a surprise.

In the workspace Publish view. Pick a record from the row list and the public reader rendering appears beside it. The list shows a sample of the table's records for previewing; publishing always covers the whole table. While editing a record. The record drawer shows the reader view next to the editing form. After you save a change, the preview refreshes to the saved version. During an import. The import wizard includes a draft reader preview step, so you can check how approved rows will read on a public page. Previewing publishes nothing — no page goes live until you publish.

The preview is produced by the same renderer as the public entry page, so what you see is what a reader gets: the entry's sections, the field labels in your project's own wording, the references section, and any media. Published pages include only the fields whose visibility is set to Public; fields kept private or workspace-only do not appear on them. The preview reflects your entry as currently saved, not edits still in progress. A change to field visibility reaches the published page when you next publish — after adjusting visibility, labels, or citation rules, publish and preview again to confirm the result.
A record travels through three stages before a public reader can see it. Activation and publication are two separate steps — completing one does not trigger the other.
documents.s: Publish a record — and why activating is not publishing

documents.t: Stage What it means What to do Draft A work in progress. Your project colleagues can see it in the workspace, but it cannot be linked to other records and never reaches the public. Fill in the record; it is saved as you go. Activated A full record in your collection — linkable to other records and ready to publish. Still visible only in the workspace. Activate the record once every required field is filled. Published The record has a public page that anyone with the address can read. Publish from the workspace Publish view (publish access required). A record can sit at the Activated stage for as long as your project needs. Internal review, peer checking, or waiting for a companion record to be ready — all of that happens before you publish. Activation is the internal gate; publication is the public one.

Publishing happens in the workspace Publish view and covers a whole table at a time — every activated record in the table gets its public page built in one pass: Open your collection's table in the workspace. Select the Publish view from the view tabs. (If it is not listed, add it with + Add view.) Select Publish changes. The platform queues the work and shows you progress as it runs. When the job finishes, the receipt tells you how many records were published and whether any were skipped. Records that are already published are refreshed with your latest saved version, and draft records are skipped — so the same action serves a first publication, a single new record, and a table-wide update after a period of internal review. If Publish changes is unavailable to you, your role may not include publish access. See "Who can publish" below.

The public page shows the record as it was last published. When you change a published record — a text correction, a new media item, a citation update — the change reaches the public page the next time you publish. Edit, review, then select Publish changes again.

Publishing requires publish access, which belongs to your environment's administrators. Researchers whose roles include only edit access can add and activate records but cannot publish them. If you are ready to publish but do not have access, contact the administrator of your environment. They can either publish on your behalf or adjust your access.

Activation was designed as an internal milestone — a way to signal that a record is finished: every required field is filled, the record can be linked to other records, and it is ready for internal review. It is a checkpoint for your team, not a release to the public. Publishing is a deliberate, additional act because research is often collaborative and time-sensitive: a project may want to hold records until a companion table is complete, until a review is signed off, or until a specific date. Keeping the two steps separate means your team controls the moment of public release, independently of when individual records are finished internally.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A record is activated but does not appear in the reader. Activation and publication are separate steps; the record has not been published yet. Publish from the workspace Publish view, or ask a colleague with publish access to do so. Publish changes is unavailable, or publishing stops with a permission message. Your role does not include publish access. Contact your environment administrator to publish the records or to adjust your access. You changed a published record but the public page still shows the old version. The public page shows the record as it was last published; edits wait for the next publish. Open the Publish view and select Publish changes again. The publish receipt shows some records skipped. Skipped records are not ready for a public page — most often they are still drafts (not yet activated). Activate the drafts and publish again. If a record you expected to publish keeps being skipped, contact your environment administrator.

Your workspace has two search tools. They are intentionally separate — the right one depends on whether you want to jump straight to a record you already know, or browse, filter, and read across many records in one place.
documents.s: Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read

documents.t: Open quick search from the Search database… control at the top of the workspace, or press Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac). A search panel opens over whatever you are doing. Type a word. Results appear grouped by collection, each one showing the record's label and the fields where your term matched. Select a result and the platform opens that record directly — whichever collection it lives in. The panel also controls the scope: search everything you have access to, search only the current table, or narrow the search to a single collection. Use quick search when: You want to land on one specific record and open it. You know roughly what you are looking for. You are in the middle of editing and need to jump to a related record fast.
documents.s: Quick search — for jumping to a known record

documents.t: Search & Read is a full search page you can dwell in. Open it from the quick search panel — the Open full Search & Read button at the bottom carries your typed term over — or from the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K), where it appears as Search & Read. The result list is built for reading. For any result you can expand its content inline, open a preview panel beside the list, or click through to the record itself. You can page through the results and sort them by relevance, by recently modified, or by label. Filtering goes further than quick search. Switch to Advanced mode to: Scope the search to one collection, or leave it across everything you can access. Each collection carries a type badge, so you can see at a glance what kind of records it holds. Add conditions on field values. Each condition names a field, a match type (contains, equals, or starts with), and a value; a condition can also be negated. Conditions combine with Match all or with any. The page address encodes your query, filters, page, and sort order — paste the address to a colleague and they see the same results. See Share a search. Use Search & Read when: You want to look at several records, not only one. You want to apply filters — by collection, by a field value, by any combination — and see everything that matches. You want to share the search with a colleague. You want to read records without navigating away from the results.
documents.s: Search & Read — for browsing, comparing, and reading in place

documents.t: Quick search Search & Read What it does Jump to one record Browse and read many records in place Filters Scope only — current table or one collection Collection scope, field-value conditions, Match all / any Shareable address No Yes How to open Search control at the top of the workspace, or Ctrl+Shift+F (⌘⇧F on Mac) Open full Search & Read in the quick search panel, or the command palette (Ctrl+K / ⌘K) Best for "Find this record" "Show me everything that matches…"

If quick search finds results but you want to explore the full set, or you want to narrow it with filters: select Open full Search & Read at the bottom of the quick search panel. Your search term carries over. Switch to Advanced mode to add field-level conditions.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Quick search returns no results even though you know the record exists. Search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration; your term may appear only in a field that is not covered. Try a word from a different field of the record. If it still does not appear, contact your environment administrator to review which fields are searchable. You cannot find Search & Read. It opens from the quick search panel or the command palette — there is no permanent menu entry. Your role may also not include access to workspace search. Open quick search and select Open full Search & Read. If the page reports an error or shows no collections, contact your environment administrator. Results show strings of letters and numbers instead of names. The collection has no display field configured, so results fall back to an internal identifier. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection.
Share a search — copy an address that reproduces your exact search and filters. What changed after re-import — using Search & Read to verify changes after an import update.

You can give any field in your collection a name that makes sense in your project's language — regardless of what the original source data called it. Your label is yours. Re-importing your source data never overwrites it.

Open the collection whose field you want to rename. Open the column's header menu with the Column actions button or by right-clicking the column header. Edit the Column label field in the menu and select Rename. If you need to change more than the label, choose Edit column from the same menu. The edit dialog contains the label and the column's other settings. The new label appears immediately in the table columns, in the record detail view, in filters, in the column menu, and in row-copy headers when you copy selected rows.

When you first import a spreadsheet or data source, each field gets a label from your source — the exact column heading as it appears in the original file. For example, if your spreadsheet has a column called "Author full name", the label starts as "Author full name." From that moment on, the label is yours: What the import controls What you control The underlying field identity (which column this is) The label — what it is called in the workspace The raw data values Whether the field is required The field type detection (text, number, date…) Any notes or help text on the field Re-importing the same source updates the data but does not touch your label. Even if the column heading changed in the source, your label is preserved. The import may tell you a column was renamed in the source (it will show as "new" + "removed" in the delta), but it will never silently overwrite what you typed.
documents.s: What the import sets and what you own

documents.t: Your label has no length limit, but short and clear works best in table column headers. Renaming a label does not change any data. Records are not affected. Two fields in the same collection can share a label — the platform does not enforce uniqueness on labels. Unique field identities are managed internally.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The Label field is not editable. Your role may not have permission to change field configuration. Ask a project administrator. After renaming, the old name still appears in a filter chip. Filter chips may cache the name briefly. Refresh the page if the old name persists after a few seconds. Hard-refresh the browser (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R). A re-import brought back the original source name. This should not happen: label is researcher-owned and never overwritten. If it did happen, it is a bug — please report it with the import project ID.

What changed after re-import — what the platform carries forward versus what it updates. Make a field required — other field settings you own that survive re-imports. Build from empty — creating fields from scratch where your label is the only name the field ever has.

A view is a named tab above the table that remembers exactly how you left it — which mode it opens in, which columns are visible, their order and widths, any pinned columns, active filters, sort order, row density, and row color rules. Open the view and everything is waiting for you. Views belong to the table and are visible to everyone working in your environment. When you create a view, your collaborators see it too.
documents.s: Save your table arrangement as a view

documents.t: A saved view stores: Which columns are visible, and in what order. Column widths, pinning (left or right), and sort order. Filter conditions and their values. The view kind it opens in: Table, Details, Relations, Publish, or Media on media tables. Row density (compact, cozy, or comfortable). Row color rules. One thing it does not remember: the quick-filter text in the toolbar. That bar is a temporary per-session search — it is not saved with the view, so you always land on the full filtered result rather than yesterday's text.

Open the table you want to organize. Set up filters, columns, and sort the way you want this view to look. Click + Add view in the view tabs above the table. Type a name — something descriptive like "18th-century records with manuscript citations" — and select Create. The new tab appears. From this point on, any change you make while this view is active — adjusting columns, adding a filter, changing the sort — is stored on the view as you go. Changes are saved to whichever view is active — including the table's default view. If you want to experiment without changing what your collaborators see, duplicate the view first and work in the copy.

The default view is what opens when you first visit the table without following a link to another view. It is shared backend state, and includes the view kind: if the default view is a Details view, the table opens in Details for everyone who starts from the default. Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Set as default. The default is shared: a table has one default view, and it applies to everyone in your environment, not only to you. Your browser may remember a concrete non-default view you opened, but it does not replace the table's default.
documents.s: Set a view as the default

documents.t: Because views are shared, editing one changes it for all your collaborators. Duplicating creates a separate copy you can adjust without touching the original. Like any view, the copy is visible to your collaborators — but your changes no longer affect the view your team relies on. Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Duplicate. The copy appears as a new tab named after the original, with "copy" added. Rename the copy so it is clear which one is the original. Work in the duplicate. When you are happy with the result, you can either keep both views or delete the duplicate once its changes have been folded back into the original.

Open the ⋯ menu on the view tab. Select Delete view and confirm. The view is removed for everyone in your environment. Talk with your collaborators before deleting a shared view — there is no undo. The table's default view cannot be deleted. To remove it, set another view as the default first.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Columns I arranged look different the next time I open the table. Views are shared — a collaborator may have adjusted the same view since your last visit. Or your changes were made on a different view tab. Check which view tab is active. For an arrangement collaborators will not change, duplicate the view and work in the copy. I changed a filter and now my collaborators see the change too. Views are shared — any change to a view reaches everyone immediately. Use Duplicate to make a copy before experimenting. I deleted a view and a colleague lost their work. Deleting removes the view for everyone. Check whether the view can be rebuilt from the column and filter arrangement. Going forward, agree with your team before deleting a shared view. The Set as default option is grayed out. The view may already be the default, or your role is read-only on this table. Look for a Default badge on the tab. If your role is read-only, ask your environment administrator. The Delete view option is grayed out. It is the table's default view — the default cannot be deleted. Set another view as the default first, then delete this one. Creating or changing a view fails. Your role is read-only on this table — creating and changing views needs editing access. Ask your environment administrator.
Saved views and re-imports — what happens to your views when you re-import your source data. Share a search — copy a link that reproduces a view or search for a colleague.

Saved views belong to the table and are shared with everyone in your environment. A re-import does not reset or overwrite a saved view. What your team named it, which columns it includes, which mode it opens in, how it is sorted and filtered — all of that survives. There is one exception: if a field that a view referenced is removed in the re-import (because it no longer exists in your source), the view adapts gracefully.
documents.s: What happens to saved views after a re-import

documents.t: A saved view stores: Which columns are visible and in what order. Column widths, pinning, and sort order. Filter conditions and their values. The view kind: Table, Details, Relations, Publish, or Media on media tables. Row density setting. The view's name. All of this is preserved across re-imports. Data values may update (a field's value in a record changes to match the new source), but the view's layout and filters are not touched.

If your source data no longer includes a field that your saved view referenced — for example, you removed a column from your spreadsheet before re-importing — the platform handles it gracefully: The view keeps working. The removed column is dropped from the display, but the rest of the view (its other columns, filters, sort) is unaffected. The import delta tells you. The re-import summary names the removed field and lists which saved views were affected. You do not have to discover this by accident. If the field comes back, a later re-import that includes the column again will restore it — and the view will include it again automatically.

If a saved view has a column that was removed: The view opens normally. The removed column is absent from the table. A notice at the top of the view (or in the views menu) indicates that one or more columns in this view are no longer available. Filters that reference the removed field are also suspended — the view does not try to filter on a field that no longer exists. You can update the view (remove the reference to the missing column and save again) or leave it as-is and wait for the field to be restored.

Sharing a saved view copies its URL. The recipient opens that saved view, subject to their own permissions. The URL names the view; the live saved-view record supplies the current layout, filters, and view kind. If a collaborator changes the shared view later, the same link opens the updated arrangement.
documents.s: Sharing a saved view with a colleague

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A column I pinned is gone from my view after a re-import. The field was removed in the re-import. Check the import delta summary for "removed" fields. Restore the field in your source and re-import, or update the saved view. Filters in my saved view stopped returning results after a re-import. The field being filtered on was removed, or the value that was filtered on no longer exists in the updated data. Open the filter chips and verify each one; delete and re-create any that reference removed fields. I see no notice about a degraded view but know a column is missing. The notice appears in the views panel; you may have dismissed it. Open the Saved views menu and look for any view marked with a warning indicator.

What changed after re-import — the full delta: new, changed, carried forward, removed, restored. Rename a field label — how your field configuration is preserved across re-imports. Share a search — copying a URL that reproduces a search or view for a colleague.
When you search for a record you know is there and nothing comes back, one of four things is usually happening. Each has a different fix.
documents.s: Find a record when search returns nothing

documents.t: Search matches against the fields your environment includes in its search configuration. If the word you typed appears only in a field that is outside that set, the record will not surface — even though it exists and you can see it by scrolling the table. What to try: type a word from a different field of the record — the label, a short description, or a name you know it carries. If that finds it, the original field is not in the search configuration. If no combination of words finds the record, contact your environment administrator and ask which fields are included in search.
documents.s: 1. The record's field is not included in search
