documents.t: Search is forgiving about some diacritics and strict about others. Ignored (you can leave these off when searching): Breathings in polytonic Greek (smooth and rough) Iota subscripts Circumflex and grave accents Arabic vowel marks (short vowels / harakat) Not ignored (these still count): The acute accent — in Greek and in any Latin-script language The diaeresis (umlaut) This means: typing a word with no accent at all can miss a record whose stored form carries an acute accent. If you are searching a polytonic-Greek collection and your term has an acute accent, include it. If you are not sure of the accent, try a word from another field of the same record instead. Diacritic handling is part of your environment's search configuration, and individual fields can be set to match every mark exactly. If you have confirmed the accent is correct and search still misses the record, contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: 2. Accents and diacritics — what the search ignores and what it does not

documents.t: If your environment stores records with a native-script field, a transliteration, and a translation side by side, a search term in any of those fields can find the record — but only if those fields are searchable and have values. If you search with a transliterated form and nothing comes back: Open the record directly from the table. Check whether the transliteration field has a value. If the field is empty, add the transliteration — or ask your environment administrator whether the transliteration field is included in search. If the transliteration field has a value but search still misses the record, the field may not be in the search configuration. Contact your environment administrator.
documents.s: 3. The transliteration field is empty or not searchable

documents.t: When a collection has no display field configured, search results for that collection cannot show a record name. Each result shows a placeholder instead — "(unlabeled …)", or the collection's name with a "no display field" notice. The records are there and your search did find them; the problem is that you cannot recognize them. If you see this: Look for the type badge beside each result — it names the collection the result belongs to. Contact your environment administrator and ask them to set a display field for that collection. Once set, search results for that collection will show the record's name as the label.
documents.s: 4. Results show a placeholder instead of the record's name

documents.t: Symptom Most likely cause First thing to try No results at all for a term you know is in the record The field is not in the search configuration Try a word from a different field of the record Found nothing with a transliterated term but the record is visible in the table Transliteration field is empty, or not searchable Open the record; check whether the transliteration field has a value Term in native script finds the record but transliterated term does not Transliteration field not in search configuration Contact your environment administrator Search matches most Greek terms but misses a specific word Stored form carries an acute accent your search omitted Retype the term with its acute accent Results appear but show "(unlabeled …)" or a "no display field" notice instead of names No display field set for that collection Contact your environment administrator to set a display field Search panel reports "Search isn't enabled for this workspace yet" Search has not been switched on for this environment Use the table's filter box for the current table; contact your environment administrator for the workspace-wide fix

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool to use and how to escalate from a quick search to a full filtered search. Share a search — copy a link that reproduces your exact search for a colleague.

A 3D model in the workspace has a Mesh→term tab beside its viewer — the first tab in the rail. Each binding links one mesh — one named part of the 3D model — to a term in your vocabulary, so you can see which part of the model carries which term, and review or change that match. Open a 3D model from the Media gallery and select the Mesh→term tab. (For opening media, see Work with media in the workspace.)
documents.s: See which mesh maps to which term

documents.t: The tab opens with three counts — how many parts are mapped, how many are edited, and how many are auto — above a list with one row per binding. Each row shows the model part's raw name as written in the model file, the term it is matched to, and a state chip. The state chip tells you where a binding came from and how settled it is: auto — the platform extracted this binding from the part's name. It is awaiting your review. edited — you (or a colleague) changed an existing binding on this part. linked — you bound a previously-unmapped part to a term by hand. unmapped — the part has no term matched to it yet. The header count of mapped parts covers every part that has a term matched to it — that is, the edited and linked parts together with the auto parts still awaiting review.

The list and the model are linked, so you can move between them either way: Select a row, and that part of the model is highlighted in the viewer and the row stays selected. Click a part in the model, and its row is selected in the list. This lets you check, part by part, that each mesh is matched to the term you expect.

Select a row — or click a part in the model — to open its card above the list. The card shows the part's raw name, the term it is bound to, and where the binding came from, followed by the actions for that part: Approve — confirm an auto binding as correct. Approving settles the binding so a later re-run leaves it alone. (Approve appears only while the part is still auto.) Reassign (or Assign term, when the part has no term yet) — open a picker to bind the part to a different term. Search your vocabulary by typing and choose from the results, each shown by its display label. Searching a word in one language can surface a term that carries that word in another language. You can also paste a term record's id directly to bind it. This writes the link between the part and the term. Strip — remove the term from the part, leaving it unmapped.

Symptom Likely cause Fix There is no Mesh→term tab. The tab appears only on 3D models. Open a media record whose type is a 3D model. The tab shows no bindings. No parts of this model are matched to a term. Open a 3D model whose parts are already matched to terms, or bind a part with Assign term. Clicking a row does not highlight anything in the model. The row's part may not be present in the model that is loaded. Compare the part name in the row with the model, and try a row whose part you can see. There is no Approve button on a part. Approve appears only for auto parts awaiting review; a part you already changed shows as edited or linked. Use Reassign to change the term, or Strip to clear it. The term picker finds nothing when you type. Search may not be activated for your environment, or there is no match for your query. Paste the term record's id into the picker instead — that path works regardless of search.
Work with media in the workspace — open a 3D model from the Media gallery. Tune the 3D camera view — set how a 3D model is framed when it opens.

When you run a search in the Search & Read section, the link in your browser carries the whole search — the words you searched, the filters, the sort, and the page you are on. Copy that link and send it; whoever opens it lands on the same search, with results filtered by their own access.
documents.s: Share a search so a colleague sees the same results

documents.t: Open Search & Read in the workspace and run your search — type your words and press Enter, or build filters in Advanced and select Search. Select Copy link, directly below the search box. The button confirms with Copied. Paste the link into an email, chat message, or document and send it. You can also copy the link from your browser's address bar — once the search has run, the address bar carries the same link. When your colleague opens the link: They see the same search words, the same filter conditions, the same sort, and the same page. They must be signed in to the same knowledge environment. They see only results their own access allows. If a collection is outside their access, its results are absent — sharing a link does not extend anyone's access.

A saved view (a named combination of filters, columns, and sort) has its own link: Open the view in your workspace. Select Copy current view link in the toolbar, or Copy view link in the saved view's menu. Paste and send. Saved views are shared across your knowledge environment, so a colleague with access to that workspace opens the same view — the same columns, filters, and sort. The link points to the view itself: if someone later edits the view, the link opens the edited version.

The search words (if any). Every active filter condition — the field, the match type, the value, and the Match all / any choice. The collection the search is scoped to, if you narrowed it. The sort order and the page you are on. It does not carry the records themselves. The results are live: whoever opens the link runs a fresh search against the knowledge environment as it is at that moment. A link shared today may return different results next month if records were added, edited, or removed. The link reproduces your search faithfully, not a snapshot of your data.
The same link works as a personal bookmark. Add it to your browser bookmarks, and you can return to the same search at any time without rebuilding the filters.

Symptom Likely cause Fix My colleague opens the link but sees fewer results than I did. Their access excludes some collections or records. This is expected — results respect each person's access. If they need access to a collection, contact your environment administrator. The link I copied is missing my newest filter changes. Search words and filters enter the link when the search runs, not while you type. Run the search — press Enter, or select Search in Advanced — and then copy. The link opens but the filters look different from what I sent. The link may have been truncated by a messaging app. Send it as a raw link rather than wrapped display text. A saved-view link shows a different layout than when I sent it. Someone edited the saved view since — views are shared, and the link opens the view as it is now. To keep a layout fixed, duplicate the view under a new name and share the copy's link.
Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — which search tool gives you a shareable link. Saved views and re-imports — what a saved view remembers and how it survives a re-import.

A 3D model can open at a chosen angle and zoom, so everyone who views it starts from the same framing. This framing is a live presentation default — the view a reader lands on. It stays navigable, and it is not frozen into the record's citation; what a citation points to is fixed separately when the record is published. Setting the framing is an environment-admin task: the Viewer tab appears beside a 3D model only for environment admins. Open a 3D model from the Media gallery and select the Viewer tab. (For opening media, see Work with media in the workspace.)

In the viewer, drag to orbit and scroll to zoom until the model is framed the way you want it to open. Select Set as presentation default to read that framing into the tab's controls. Fine-tune if you want: the controls hold the camera target offset and the framing — radius, minimum and maximum distance, and field of view. To start over, select Reset to auto-fit to return to the framing the platform fits to the model automatically. Select Save viewer settings to store the framing on this record. From then on, the model opens with the framing you saved. The Viewer tab is available only to environment admins. If you do not see it on a 3D model, ask your environment administrator to set the framing.

Symptom Likely cause Fix There is no Viewer tab on the 3D model. The Viewer tab is shown only to environment admins. Ask your environment administrator to set the framing, or sign in with an account that has admin access. The model still opens at a different angle after I captured it. The captured framing is not stored until it is saved. After Set as presentation default, select Save viewer settings. I want to undo my framing. The model has an auto-fit framing to fall back to. Select Reset to auto-fit, then Save viewer settings to store it.
Work with media in the workspace — open a 3D model from the Media gallery. See which mesh maps to which term — the Mesh→term tab on a 3D model.
When a reader opens one of your published entries, the References section lists the evidence behind it — one row for each place the entry is attested.
documents.s: Read the references section on a published entry

documents.t: One row per occurrence. If a term is attested in twelve passages, the references section has twelve rows. Each row is independent. Your project's citation style. When you have declared citation rules for a collection, each row is rendered in your own scholarly format — author, work, locator (page, chapter, line), and any abbreviations exactly as your field uses them. The format is yours to control, not a fixed platform style. Paired editions. When an occurrence cites both a modern edition and an earlier one, the row bridges them — the primary citation followed by the paired locator, so a reader sees the equivalence at a glance. A quote, when the occurrence carries one, sits with its row.

Each row's text is chosen in order: your declared citation style first; if a collection has no citation rules, a plainer structural composition of the edition's locator fields; and the occurrence's own label as a last resort. A row always renders something — a missing edition never blanks the row. If the citations read roughly, the citation style for that collection has not been refined yet. Citation styles are tuned per collection (a scholar reviews a proposed style; an administrator applies it); the rows update on the next publish.
Use the draft preview to see the references section exactly as a reader will, before the entry is public — see Preview an entry before publishing.

When you import your source data a second time (a re-import), the platform shows you a delta — only what is new, changed, or different from your last import. It does not ask you to re-review decisions you already made.
documents.s: Understand what changed after a re-import

documents.t: At the top of the import review the platform shows a summary line like: Since your last import: 3 new · 1 changed · 147 carried forward Term What it means New A field or table that did not exist in the previous import. You need to review and approve it. Changed Something that existed before but is now different — a field type changed, a collection was restructured, or the source renamed something. You need to confirm the change. Carried forward A decision you made in a previous import that the platform has automatically recognized and kept. You do not need to act on these.

"Carried forward" means the platform compared your source to the last import and found no difference on a given field or collection — the same data, the same structure, the same decisions you already made. The platform keeps those decisions automatically and does not show them as review cards. You can expand the "Carried forward (K)" disclosure to see the full list if you want to verify what was carried.

A field or collection shows as removed when it existed in your previous import but is no longer present in the new source data. The field is not permanently deleted. Any notes, labels, or settings you made on it are preserved. If you bring the field back in a later import, it is restored — you get your previous settings back. The delta view names every removed field so you know exactly what changed. If a saved view referenced a removed field, the view keeps working but drops that column from its display (see Saved views and re-imports). The platform uses the words "removed" and "restored" — plain language that describes what happened. You will not see the word "inactive" or other system terms. Removed is removed; you can bring it back.
A field shows as restored when it was removed in a previous import and has come back in this one. Your previous settings — any label you gave it, any notes, your required flag — all return with it.

Your configuration edits — labels you renamed, field settings you changed, required flags you turned on — are yours and are not reset by a re-import. Record values depend on the refresh behaviour your administrator or platform operator chose: Edit-preserving refresh matches incoming source rows to existing records, refreshes source-managed values, and keeps researcher-owned values. Full refresh reloads rows from scratch. It is destructive to researcher edits and should be used only for a deliberate start-over. If you are unsure which behaviour a planned re-import will use, ask your environment administrator before it runs. See Rename a field label for the full list of what survives a re-import.

Before the import writes anything, the wizard runs a practice run (sometimes called a dry run). It tells you how many records will be created, updated, or skipped — including how many are blocked by unresolved review items. With carried-forward decisions accounted for, a re-import of mostly unchanged data should show nearly all records ready, not blocked.

Symptom Likely cause Fix The import still shows a full review list as if it were the first time. The platform did not recognize this as a re-import of the same source, or an earlier import was never completed. Check whether the previous import was completed through Stage 6 of the wizard. Only completed imports produce a carried-forward baseline. A field I labelled is showing its original source name in the delta. The delta view shows source-side names for changed items; your label is preserved and will appear in the workspace once you confirm the change. Confirm or carry forward the item in the review. A field I know exists in my source is showing as "removed." The source column may have been renamed in the source system. A renamed column appears as a new column plus a removed column in the delta. Review the "new" items — one of them is likely the renamed version. Approve it, and your label will be carried to the new identity.
Rename a field label — which of your settings survive a re-import. Saved views and re-imports — what happens to your saved views when fields change.

When you run a search in Search & Read, a note may appear above your results saying that a number of collections are hidden. It reads: 2 collections are hidden — they require a review capability you don't hold. This is not an error, and your search worked. It tells you that your environment holds more collections than your current access lets you search, and how many were held back.
documents.s: See why some collections are hidden in Search & Read

documents.t: Your search ran across every collection your access allows, and returned those results. Collections you are not permitted to search are withheld before the results reach you — the platform counts them and shows that count in the note, rather than letting them vanish silently. The number is the difference between all the collections in your environment and the ones your search could reach.

A review capability is one of the access permissions your environment administrator assigns. It governs whether you can search and review a particular kind of record across the whole environment. Some collections are open to anyone on the team; others are restricted to people who hold the review capability for that kind of record. The hidden-collections note appears when at least one collection in your environment falls into the restricted group and you do not hold its capability.

The note never blocks the collections you do have access to. Your results already include every collection your access allows; only the restricted ones are missing. You can keep searching, filtering, and reading those results normally — both in Search & Read and in the quick search panel. You can also still open any individual record you reach by a direct link, even one in a collection you cannot search across. If instead the page tells you that you have no search access at all, your role does not include a review capability on any collection. That is a different message — contact your environment administrator.

Access is assigned by your environment administrator, not changed from the search page. Note which kind of records you are missing — the type of collection you expected to find. Contact your environment administrator and ask for the review capability that covers it. Once they grant it, rerun your search. The hidden-collections note drops by the collections you can now reach, and their records appear in your results.
documents.s: How to get access to a hidden collection

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The note says collections are hidden, but you expected to see them. Your access does not include the review capability for those collections. Contact your environment administrator and ask for the capability that covers the kind of records you need. The note's number does not drop after you were granted access. The new access has not yet taken effect in your session. Reload the page and rerun your search. If it still shows, confirm with your environment administrator that the capability was applied. You see "You don't have search access here" instead of the hidden note. Your role includes no review capability on any collection. This is a separate, full-page message. Contact your environment administrator — you can still open individual records by direct link.

Choose between the quick search bar and Search & Read — the two search tools and how to escalate from one to the other. Find a record when search returns nothing — other reasons a record you expected may not appear. Your environment administrator assigns the access that controls which collections you can search, from the permissions panel in the administrator documentation.

A collection that holds media records — images, 3D models, and other files — has a Media button alongside Table, Details, Relations, and Publish above the table. Other collections do not show it. Select Media to browse those records as a gallery instead of as table rows.
documents.s: Work with media in the workspace

documents.t: The gallery opens with a count of how many media records the collection holds and one card per record. Each card shows a media-type badge (for example, 3D MODEL), the record's title, and its index status. When a record has a thumbnail, the card shows that image; otherwise it shows a generic media icon. Use the Grid / List toggle to switch between a card grid and a compact list. Select a card to open that record on its own.

Selecting a card opens a detail pane with a Back button to return to the gallery, the record's title, and — for a 3D model — the model itself rendered right there, with the model filling the pane and a rail of tabs beside it. Drag to orbit the model and scroll to zoom. Above the model, a Heatmap chip tints its parts by binding state and a Rotate chip auto-rotates it. Beside the viewer is a row of tabs: Mesh→term — for a 3D model, the parts of the model and the terms they are matched to; see See which mesh maps to which term. Files — the files attached to the record, with the count in the tab label. Viewer — for environment admins, the camera framing the model opens at; see Tune the 3D camera view. Info — the record's descriptive text. Version — the record's version and edition history, with the count in the tab label. For environment admins this tab also holds two actions — pinning a citeable edition and re-extracting — described below. Which tabs appear depends on the record's type and your role: the Mesh→term tab is shown for 3D models, and the Viewer tab only for environment admins.
For environment admins, the Version tab adds two actions above the version list. Other roles see the version list read-only.
documents.s: Pin a citeable edition or re-extract (environment admins)

documents.t: Everyday citation already works without pinning — a citation resolves to the current version on its own. Pin a revision as an edition only when you need a fixed, unchanging cut to cite: enter an edition label, then select Pin as citeable edition and confirm. The record's header then shows an EDITION state with a frozen marker, and the version is a permanent, citeable reference — a citation pointing at it stays stable, because the cited content is captured when the record is published, not read live. A frozen edition can no longer be re-extracted (the automatic re-reading of the model file). You can still amend individual Mesh→term bindings by hand: a binding change is a claim about the model — new information, a new term, a reviewer's amendment — not a change to the model file, so it needs no re-extraction and no new version, and it does not disturb a citation already made against the edition.

Re-extract re-reads the model file and refreshes the mesh→term bindings — which part of the model is matched to which term. It never creates a new version or file, and any bindings you set by hand are preserved. Dry run reports what would change without writing anything. Apply writes the refreshed bindings, then the Mesh→term tab and the coverage heatmap update to match. Re-extraction is refused on a frozen edition; to re-extract, re-import the file to start a new working revision.

The Info tab shows the record's title, author, and description, but it does not edit them. These are fields on the media record, edited in the Details view of the collection — not in the viewer. When a record has no descriptive fields yet, the Info tab says so.
documents.s: Where titles and descriptions are edited

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix There is no Media button above my table. The Media button appears only on collections that hold media records. Open a collection whose records are images, 3D models, or other files. The gallery says there is no media yet. The collection holds no media records. Add a media record, or open a collection that already has some. A card shows a generic media icon instead of a thumbnail. That record has no thumbnail set — thumbnails are optional and the icon is the normal fallback. This is expected; open the card to work with the record. An environment admin can add a thumbnail reference for the record if one is wanted. I changed the title in the Info tab but nothing happened. The Info tab shows the title and description; it does not edit them. Open the Details view of the collection and edit the record's fields there. The Version tab won't let me re-extract or pin an edition. Those two actions are shown only to environment admins; other roles see the version list read-only. Ask an environment admin, or sign in with an admin role. Re-extraction says it is refused on a frozen edition. The current version is a pinned, frozen edition, which never changes. Re-import the file to start a new working revision, then re-extract that.
See which mesh maps to which term — the Mesh→term tab on a 3D model. Tune the 3D camera view — set how a 3D model is framed when it opens.

This page walks through one full research loop without a mouse: reach a table, open a record, fill its fields, activate it, preview it, and move on. It collects the keyboard paths that other pages describe in passing and puts them in the order you would actually use them, with the exact keys for each step. Read it when you work by keyboard or screen reader and want a single route through a session, or when you want to know which parts of that route are solid today and which still need a hand from the mouse. Accessibility is the companion reference: it lists every keyboard control and the display settings. This page sequences those controls into a working session and does not repeat the full list. Some steps in this loop are not yet fully reachable by keyboard alone. Those gaps are listed up front, in Where the keyboard path is still incomplete, so you know before you start where you may need to reach for the mouse.

Two things shape what the keyboard does: Mac or Windows / Linux. Shortcuts that use Command (⌘) on a Mac use Control (Ctrl) elsewhere. Where a shortcut appears below, both forms are shown. Where focus is. Shortcuts that act on the whole workspace are ignored while you are typing in a text box, a text area, or a dropdown — so a stray keystroke never fires a command while you write. Step out of the field first (Tab or Escape), then use the shortcut.

When the workspace opens, focus starts in the page. Tab moves forward through the controls — the top bar, then the sidebar of tables, then the table toolbar, then the table itself. Shift+Tab moves back. A clear focus ring marks where you are; the ring is drawn when you navigate by keyboard and stays hidden for mouse clicks. Two faster ways to reach a table: Command palette — press ⌘K (Ctrl+K). A search box opens; type part of a table's name, use the Down and Up arrows to move through the matches, and press Enter to open the one you want. Escape closes the palette without choosing. Sidebar — Tab into the list of tables and press Enter on a table to open it. To give yourself more room, ⌘B (Ctrl+B) hides and shows the sidebar.

Reading before writing saves duplicate records. Two search routes, both keyboard-first: Quick search — press ⌘⇧F (Ctrl+Shift+F). The search panel opens with focus in its box. Type a term; results appear grouped by collection. Use the Down and Up arrows to move through results and Enter to open the highlighted one. Escape closes the panel. Search & Read — for browsing many records, open the command palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K) and choose Search & Read, or escalate to it from the bottom of the quick search panel. Your typed term carries over. Within that page, the typeahead and the results list respond to the Down and Up arrows and Enter. How search treats accents and scripts — and why a search matched or missed — is covered in Searching and reading.
documents.s: 2. Find a record before you create one

documents.t: Open the new-row drawer from the command palette: ⌘K (Ctrl+K), then choose New row. (The drawer is also reachable by tabbing to the toolbar's new-row button and pressing Enter.) The drawer opens as a dialog and focus moves into it. A state pill at the top of the drawer tells you where the record stands — "Not yet saved", "Draft saved", "Unsaved edits", and so on — so you always know what a screen reader would otherwise have to infer.

Inside the drawer: Tab moves from one field to the next; Shift+Tab moves back. Type into a text field, then Tab out — your entry is held as you go. For a dropdown field, the Down and Up arrows move through the options and Enter selects one. For a field that links to another record, type to search, Tab to a result, and press Enter to link it. Required fields are marked, and the drawer will not let the record activate while a required field is empty. A line near the top names the next save step, so the path forward is always stated rather than implied. A field whose editor has not shipped yet shows a short hint in place of an editor. The hint stays in the Tab order and is announced as disabled, so you can tell the field exists and is intentionally not editable — it is not silently skipped.

When the required fields are filled, activate the record with ⌘Enter (Ctrl+Enter) from anywhere in the drawer, or Tab to the Activate row button and press Enter. If a required field is still empty, activation is blocked and the button stays disabled until you fill it. To leave without activating, press Escape. If you have unsaved work, a confirmation appears first so a stray Escape does not discard a draft; confirm or cancel it from the keyboard. A draft you leave behind is kept, and the workspace offers to resume it next time.

Open a record's full view to read it and preview the public page: From the table, Tab to the row and press ⌘Enter (Ctrl+Enter) to open its details. The details view shows every field beside a reader preview rendered with the same engine as the public reader, so you can check how the record will read before anything is published. The path from draft to a published page — who can publish, and the per-field visibility controls — is covered in Public reader.

Several view controls are keyboard-driven: Row density — Tab to the density control and use the Left and Right (or Up and Down) arrows to move between Compact, Cozy, and Comfortable. Your choice is saved with the view. Saved views — the view tabs respond to the Left and Right arrows; Enter or Space opens the focused view. Sidebar groups — ⌘⇧G (Ctrl+Shift+G) creates a group, ⌘⇧E (Ctrl+Shift+E) expands all groups, and ⌘⇧C (Ctrl+Shift+C) collapses them. ⇧S (Shift+S) pins or unpins the current table. Sidebar width — Tab to the resize handle between the sidebar and the table; the Left and Right arrows narrow and widen it, Home and End jump to the minimum and maximum, and Space collapses the sidebar.
documents.s: 7. Adjust the view as you work

documents.t: The platform is being made fully keyboard- and screen-reader-driven, and some of the loop above still has gaps. The honest state today: Some command shortcuts work only from the command palette, not as direct keystrokes. The palette lists hints next to several actions — filtering the current table, creating a new row, undoing and redoing a view change. Those actions are reliable when you select them inside the palette (⌘K / Ctrl+K). The single-key forms shown as hints (such as a lone slash, or a lone letter) are not all wired as global keystrokes yet, so reach these actions through the palette rather than relying on the bare key. Undo and redo by keyboard. The undo and redo buttons show the hints ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z, and the actions are always available from the command palette. Whether the bare key combination fires undo from anywhere in the workspace is still being confirmed; use the palette or the on-screen buttons if a keystroke does not respond. The display-and-reading settings panel is not in the workspace. Font size, line height, font family, and background presets live on your environment's reading and browsing pages, opened with the accessibility button there or with Alt+A. Inside the workspace, use the row density control and your browser's own zoom. See Accessibility. If a control you expect to reach cannot be reached from the keyboard, that is a bug rather than a setting. Tell your environment administrator so it reaches the people who can fix it.
documents.s: Where the keyboard path is still incomplete

documents.t: The workspace exposes named roles and labels to screen readers: the new-row drawer is announced as a dialog with a title, fields that are not yet editable are announced as disabled, the focus ring follows keyboard navigation, and the inline tip panel keeps focus stable when its content updates. Spoken confirmations for every action — for example, a spoken note when an inline edit saves — are still expanding, so a screen reader may not yet announce every state change out loud. The on-screen state pill in the new-row drawer names the current state in text, which a screen reader can read on demand.

Symptom Likely cause Fix A workspace shortcut does nothing. Focus is inside a text box, a text area, or a dropdown, where workspace shortcuts are intentionally ignored. Press Escape or Tab to leave the field, then use the shortcut. A single-key shortcut shown in the command palette does not fire on its own. Not every palette hint is wired as a global keystroke yet. Open the command palette with ⌘K (Ctrl+K) and select the action there. The focus ring disappears. The ring is keyboard-only; a recent mouse click suppressed it. Press Tab once more to bring it back. Escape closes the new-row drawer but a dialog appears first. You had unsaved work, so a discard confirmation is shown before anything is lost. Confirm to discard, or cancel to keep editing. Either choice is reachable by keyboard. Activate row will not respond. A required field is still empty, so activation is blocked. Tab back through the fields, fill the ones marked required, then activate again. You cannot find the display-and-reading settings in the workspace. That panel lives on the reading and browsing pages, not the workspace. Open a reading page and use its accessibility button or Alt+A. In the workspace, use row density and browser zoom.

Accessibility — the full list of keyboard controls, display settings, and the broader accessibility status. Workspace walkthrough — the controls this session moves through. Searching and reading — how search behaves, including across scripts and accents. Adding and editing rows — the draft drawer and what activation means. Public reader — the path from a draft to a published page.

At some point your work leaves the knowledge environment: citations go into a paper, a set of records becomes a bibliography or an appendix, a slice of your corpus turns into a teaching handout, a colleague needs to see exactly what you found. This page sequences that workflow — narrow your records to a working set, get them out as clipboard rows, a file, or a link, and copy citations in your project's citation style. Read it when a deadline is close and your material needs to be somewhere else.

Row selection with a floating toolbar — select any number of rows in a table and a toolbar appears with the actions you can run on the selection. Maturity: Active. Copy selected rows to your clipboard — the visible columns of the selected rows, with a header row of column labels, ready to paste into a spreadsheet or a document table. Maturity: Active. Limit: carries only the columns visible in the current view. Export selected rows as a file — downloads the selected records as a CSV file for spreadsheets, with raw JSON available as an advanced option for tools and scripts. Maturity: Active. Limit: carries only the columns visible in the current view for CSV. Citations in your project's citation style — a published entry, and its draft preview, render citations ready to copy into a bibliography or footnote. Maturity: Active. Limit: how complete a citation reads depends on the fields filled in on the record. Shareable search and view links — a search's address carries the whole search, and a saved view has its own link. Maturity: Active. Limit: whoever opens a link sees only what their own access allows. Stable web addresses for published records — every published record keeps a stable address you can put in a syllabus, a slide, or a footnote. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort.

Three common shapes, three routes: Citations for a paper or a bibliography — you need formatted citation text. Work record by record in the reading view; see Copy citations in your project's style below. A table of records for a handout, appendix, or analysis — you need rows and columns. Filter down to a working set, then copy or export the selection. Something a colleague or a reader opens themselves — you need a link, not a copy; see Share by link instead of by copy. Most projects mix all three: a saved view holds the working set, citations come from the reading view, and the finished records are shared by their public addresses.

Use search and filters to get exactly the records you need in front of you: quick search to find records anywhere you can access, Search & Read for browsing with conditions on field values, and the table's filter builder for column conditions. Searching and reading covers each tool. When the working set is right, save it as a view so you can return to it for the life of the project — see Save your table arrangement as a view. A view remembers your filters, visible columns, order, and sort. Views are shared with everyone working in your environment, so name it descriptively; to refine it without changing what collaborators see, duplicate it first and work in the copy.
documents.s: Narrow to a working set — and save it as a view

documents.t: Click a row to select it. Hold Ctrl (Windows / Linux) or Cmd (Mac) and click to add rows one at a time, or hold Shift and click to select a range. A floating toolbar appears showing the count of selected rows. To paste rows into a spreadsheet or a document table, select Copy TSV. The visible columns of the selected rows go to your clipboard as tab-separated values with a header row of column labels; a message confirms how many rows were copied. Switch to your spreadsheet and paste. To download a spreadsheet file, select Download CSV. The selected records are saved as a CSV file in your usual downloads location. Use JSON only when a technical workflow needs the raw row payload. Two details are worth knowing before a deadline: Copy and CSV follow your view. The clipboard copy and CSV download carry the columns visible in the current view, in their current order — arrange the view first and the paste or file comes out right. JSON is for raw payloads. Use JSON only when a tool or script needs the stored row payload rather than the visible spreadsheet view. A selection lives in the view where you made it: switching to another view or table clears it. The full selection mechanics, including keyboard paths, are in Copy or export selected rows.
documents.s: Select rows, then copy or export

documents.t: Citations come from the reading view, not from the table: Open the published entry — or its draft preview, which shows the entry exactly as a reader will see it, references included, before anything goes live. Find the entry's References area. Rows of evidence carry their citations, and when your project has set up a citation for the record itself, it appears there as its own row. A media item with full citation details carries its own citation too. Select the citation text and copy it into your bibliography, footnote, or document. Each citation is rendered in the citation style your project has adopted — set per collection by your environment administrator and defined in Citation Style Language, the same format reference managers such as Zotero use. Before the citation goes to a venue, check that the active style suits it: compare a rendered citation against the venue's style guide, and if it does not match, collect sample citations and send them to your environment administrator with a request. Citations you can trust explains what the platform guarantees about a citation once it is in print — including why a media item you cite should be a frozen Edition first — and walks through the style-change request. The short copying steps live in Copy a citation for a record or media item.
documents.s: Copy citations in your project's style

documents.t: A link keeps the material live — whoever opens it sees the records as they are at that moment, filtered by their own access. A search, for a colleague in your environment — run the search in Search & Read, then select Copy link below the search box. The link carries your search words, every filter condition, the sort, and the page. See Share a search. A saved view, for your team — a saved view has its own link, from Copy current view link in the toolbar or Copy view link in the view's menu. The link points to the view itself: if the view is edited later, the link opens the edited version. A single record, for a colleague — right-click the row and select Copy row link. The link points to that record in the workspace; the colleague must be signed in to the same knowledge environment. A single record, for anyone — once the record is published, its public page has a stable web address that stays valid even if your project later reorganizes its pages. That address is the one for a syllabus, a slide, or a footnote — readers outside the project need no account. Public reader covers the path from draft to published page.
documents.s: Share by link instead of by copy

documents.t: From a table, the batch outputs are the TSV clipboard copy, the CSV download, and the advanced raw JSON download. There is no Excel workbook export. No workspace control assembles a single bibliography file from many records at once. Citation text is copied per entry from each record's reading view. For reference managers, a published entry's citation is also available in a machine-readable form — see Citations you can trust. The selection toolbar also shows Delete, Edit visibility, and Set row color. All three are labeled "Backend pending" — visible but not active; clicking them does nothing.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Pasted rows are missing columns you expected. The clipboard copy carries only the columns visible in the current view. Unhide the columns — or switch to a view that shows them — then copy again. A "Copy failed" message appears after Copy TSV. Your browser blocked clipboard access for this site. Allow clipboard access in your browser's site settings for this environment, then copy again. The exported file is missing hidden columns. CSV export follows the columns visible in the current table view. Show the columns you need, then download the CSV again. Your selection disappeared after switching views. Selections are per view and per session; switching views or tables clears them. Re-select your rows in the view you are working in. A citation shows placeholders or looks incomplete. The fields the citation draws on are missing or only partly filled in on that record or media item. Open the record and complete those fields; the draft preview shows the corrected citation before publishing. See Copy a citation for a record or media item. A colleague opens your search link and sees fewer results than you did. Results respect each person's access; collections outside their access are absent. This is expected. If they need access to a collection, contact your environment administrator.

Copy or export selected rows — full selection mechanics and the toolbar in detail. Copy a citation for a record or media item — the short task-shaped citation steps. Citations you can trust — what stays fixed once you cite, Editions, and citation styles. Share a search — what a search link carries and how access applies. Save your table arrangement as a view — keeping a working set for the life of a project. Searching and reading — the search tools that build your working set. Public reader — stable addresses and what readers outside your project see.

This page explains what the platform records about you while you work, what it deliberately does not record, and the safety rules that occasionally hold content back. The bias throughout is to keep your project's content inside your project and to minimize what flows anywhere else. Read it when you want to know what the platform sees, when a feature seems to be holding a number back from you, or when a new chat panel appears and you want to understand what it is doing.

Your data stays inside your environment (Active) — your project's records, search queries, and edits live inside your environment's boundary. Researchers in other environments cannot see across it, and the boundary is enforced at the data layer, not by convention. Content-free activity records (Active) — when the platform records that an action happened (a search ran, an import finished, an assistant answered), it stores numbers and short labels — duration, row count, success flag — never the content itself. One-way redaction of sensitive text (Active) — where the platform must keep a record involving text you wrote, the text is replaced with a one-way fingerprint keyed to your environment; the original cannot be reconstructed from it. Text that looks like an email address, a phone number, or an identification number is dropped entirely — not even a fingerprint is kept. Small-sample protection on cross-environment statistics (Active) — a statistic computed across environments is published only when enough separate environments contributed to it that no single environment or small team could be identified from it. Below that threshold, the number is withheld. Tamper-evident activity records (Active) — the platform's activity records cannot be silently edited or deleted; the platform-level log links each entry cryptographically to the one before it, so any alteration becomes visible during routine verification by the platform operator. Chat conversations are not kept (Active) — a chat assistant keeps your conversation only for your current working session, or reads it once to extract the structured details you confirmed and then discards the raw text. No chat surface keeps conversations longer (see below). Data-protection assessment tracking (Active) — when deeper activity recording is switched on for an environment, the platform records that the environment's Data Protection Impact Assessment must be refreshed, and tracks that refresh to completion. Per-environment usage statistics (Active) — whether your environment records usage statistics about features such as in-form tips is a per-environment setting, not a platform-wide constant. Your environment administrator can tell you whether it is on.

If you have only a minute: Your project's data and the queries you type stay inside your project. They are not visible to researchers in other environments, and the platform operator sees only redacted aggregate numbers, never your content. Statistics computed across environments are published only when enough separate environments contributed that no single environment or small team of researchers could be identified from them. Chat panels keep your conversation only for your current session, or read it once to pull out the details you confirmed. No chat surface keeps conversations longer today. The record of who edited what stays inside your environment. It exists to give your editors and your administrator a clear history, not to surveil you.

Your researcher account. Sign-in identity, display name, role, permissions. Stays inside your project. Your edits. Drafts you create, fields you change, rows you activate. Attributable to you within your project, so editors and reviewers can see who did what. Chat conversations, within limits. A chat assistant follows the retention behaviors described below; the default keeps nothing beyond your session.
documents.s: What is recorded about your activity

documents.t: Your search queries do not leave your environment. Searches are matched inside your project. The platform-wide measurement layer never receives the words you typed — by design, it can only hold counts, timings, and one-way fingerprints. No content leaves your workspace. Platform-level activity records hold numbers and short labels, not the content of searches, imports, or conversations. Small-sample statistics are withheld. A cross-environment number with too few contributing environments is not published at all. Sensitive strings are redacted before storage. One-way fingerprint, keyed to your environment; text matching high-risk patterns (email addresses, phone numbers, identification numbers) is dropped entirely. The platform's activity records are tamper-evident. A background guarantee; no action needed from you. Much of this measurement is also switched off unless the platform operator deliberately turns it on — the platform's default posture is not to collect.
documents.s: What is deliberately not recorded or transmitted

documents.t: Two situations: Publication readiness. A draft, a row missing a required field, or a row in a review queue is not eligible for the public reader. The publish view shows what a record still needs before it can go live — see Preview an entry before publishing. Small-sample statistics. Where a precise cross-environment number could identify the behavior of a small group, the platform withholds it. This rule applies to platform-published numbers; it never hides your own data from you inside your workspace.
documents.s: When the workspace holds content back

documents.t: A chat assistant on the platform follows one of these retention behaviors: Session only (the default). The conversation exists for your current working session and disappears when the session ends. Nothing goes into durable storage. Extract only. The conversation is read once by an extractor that pulls out structured details you confirmed (for example, a summary of what you said you were importing); the raw conversation is then discarded immediately. Nothing longer. No chat surface keeps your conversation beyond the two behaviors above. Longer retention is not available today. The chat panel itself tells you what it records: it carries a visible notice stating that questions may be included in usage records and that no workflow changes happen through chat. The assistant can answer questions and explain what it sees, but it cannot change your data at all — it cannot approve, apply, publish, or delete anything. Actions happen only through the regular controls you click. One practical note: records belong to the project, not to you personally. Removing a researcher account does not remove the project's published records. If you are leaving a project and want to know exactly what account removal covers, ask your environment administrator.

Which chat surfaces are enabled, and what each one retains. Whether usage statistics — such as tip acceptance numbers — are being collected in your environment (see Efficiency tips for environment administrators). Whether a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) has been completed for the project. A DPIA names who can see what, for how long, under what conditions. Your administrator can find out its status from the platform operator and tell you what it covers. A worked example: suppose you notice a chat panel today that was not there last week. The right question to your administrator is two-part — "What does this panel retain?" and "Is the DPIA updated to cover it?" If both have clean answers, the surface is operating inside the platform's normal posture. If either is open, the platform's default — nothing kept beyond the session — is what applies until the answers land.
documents.s: What to ask your environment administrator

documents.t: Your project's database records, search index, and change history all live in their own slice of the platform. Operations that touch your project read from your slice. Operations that produce platform-wide numbers read from a separate measurement layer that holds counts and timings, never content. When you type into search, the query is matched inside your slice; the platform-wide layer can learn at most that a search happened, how long it took, and how many results it returned. Multiply by every action on every surface and you get the platform operator's view: a picture of motion without content. Researchers in another environment see less — they cannot see across the boundary at all.
documents.s: What the environment boundary means in practice

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A statistic you expected shows no value, or is missing entirely. Small-sample protection withheld it: too few environments contributed for the number to be published safely. This is intentional. The number appears when more environments contribute. Your environment administrator; Tips and guidance. A new chat panel appeared and you do not know what it retains. The panel was enabled for your environment. Read the panel's own notice about what it records; if it is unclear, ask your administrator what the panel retains and whether the DPIA covers it. Your environment administrator. You cannot find what an administrator can see about your activity. The change history is the answer for "who changed what"; it stays inside your environment and is visible to editors and administrators. Ask your administrator to walk you through the change history for your account's actions. Your environment administrator. You want to verify that the platform's activity records have not been tampered with. The platform-level activity log is tamper-evident by design — verification is run by the platform operator, not the researcher. Ask your environment administrator to request a verification report from the platform operator. Your environment administrator.

Tips and guidance — the tip surface whose usage statistics are covered by small-sample protection. Efficiency tips for environment administrators — the tip surface from the administrator's side, including the per-environment setting for measuring tip activity. Activity measurement for environment administrators — what an administrator can configure about activity recording. Voice and vocabulary — how the wording you see is configured (not a privacy setting, but a related per-environment setting). Standards posture — the compliance framework that backs these privacy guarantees.

When somebody outside your project reads one of your records on the web, they are using the public reader — the reading-facing face of your knowledge environment, with stable URLs, scholarly citations, clean typography, and no editing controls. This page explains what the reader is, how a record reaches it, and how to preview a record before it is public. Read it when you want to know what a reader sees, when you are about to publish, or when you want to share a finished record with someone outside the project. The reader is configurable, so what your readers see depends on your project. The sections below describe how it works; your environment may use all of it or a subset.

Published reading layer — the reader reads from a separate, read-only snapshot of your data, refreshed when your project publishes something new. Readers never touch your working data. Maturity: Active. Stable, citable URLs — every published record has a stable web address that keeps citations valid even if the page is later reorganized. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Side table of contents — a navigation list down the side of the page that highlights where the reader is as they scroll. Maturity: Active. Limit: how fine-grained it is depends on how the record is sectioned. True-to-life preview — an in-workspace preview that renders a record exactly as a reader would see it, with no mockup substitution. Maturity: Active. Limit: the preview lives in your workspace; it is not a public address. Citations for media items — a media item can carry a structured citation in your project's citation style (defined in Citation Style Language, the same format reference managers use), rendered with the record's citations and ready to copy into a bibliography. Maturity: Active. Source-traced citations — citations on the record itself, built by tracing where each piece came from (source manuscript, prior publication, contributor) and rendering that chain. Maturity: Active. Limit: fidelity depends on the source links your project declared at import. References — one row per piece of evidence — every occurrence of the record in the sources gets its own row. Where the project has catalogued a modern and an early edition of the same source, the row bridges them into one scholarly reference (modern citation, then the early edition's locator and abbreviated editor); where the project has full citation styling configured, the row carries a formatted citation; and an occurrence with no published edition at all — a catalogued manuscript or fragment — still appears, shown by its own label. Quotes catalogued on an occurrence display beneath its row, and source citations the rows did not absorb appear once each, deduplicated, below the evidence list. Maturity: Active. Limit: how rich each row reads depends on what the project catalogued — locators, editions, quotes, and abbreviations are project data. Browsable indexes, switchable per project — beside search, readers can browse the whole corpus from an alphabetized index, and a project can publish more than one (for a multilingual corpus, for example by transliteration or by original script), switchable from the reader. Index rows are rich (transliteration, original-script form, and a short gloss together); a character rail jumps to a letter; large letter groups page smoothly. Maturity: Active. Limit: which indexes exist, the default, and what each row shows are configured by your project. Media on the record page — a published record lists its attached media — 2D images, audio, video, 3D models, and molecular visualizations — each item with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source plus its identifier and version. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the media your project attached and published appears. Dark mode and reading-first layout — selectable text, a scholarly typeface, and a darker color scheme readers can switch to, remembered in their browser. Maturity: Active.

The reader is a separate layer from your workspace. The workspace is where you and your colleagues add, edit, review, and approve. The reader is where the world reads what your project has decided to publish. The platform builds the reader from a published snapshot — a separate, read-only copy of your data, refreshed when your project publishes something new. A reader visiting a page does not reach into your workspace; they read from the snapshot. Your editing speed is not affected by outside traffic, and a reader cannot accidentally see a draft.
documents.s: What the reader is, in one paragraph

documents.t: Readers do not have to search to explore. The reader offers a browsable index — an alphabetized list of every published entry — and a project can publish more than one. A multilingual environment commonly offers the same entries by transliteration and by original script; the reader switches between them from the controls at the top of the list. Each index row can show the transliterated form, the original-script form, and a short gloss together, so an entry is recognizable without opening it, and a character rail jumps straight to a letter. Which indexes exist and which is the default are set by your project when it publishes. See Browse entries by index.

Draft. You created it; the workspace knows about it; nobody else sees it (unless you preview it, below). Activated. You selected Activate. The record enters the main table and search results; other researchers can see, link, and cite it. The record is not yet public — activation never publishes by itself. Published. You — or a colleague with publish access — select Publish, for a single record or a whole table at once. The platform builds the record's published snapshot, and the public page goes live. Publication is its own step, separate from activation. Once a record is published, its snapshot refreshes automatically when something publishable changes — an edit to a published field, a media item added to a published record, a typo fix to a published citation. You do not trigger the refresh manually.
documents.s: How a record reaches the reader

documents.t: Use the preview to see exactly what a reader will see, before committing: Open the record in your workspace — a draft, an activated record, or anything you are working on. Open its reader preview. The preview renders the record exactly as a reader would see it — same layout, same fonts, same citations, same media rendering. During an import, the wizard's final step offers the same preview for newly imported records. Read it. Spot anything awkward. Close the preview. The record has not moved; you have only looked at it. The preview is a real rendering, not a mockup. If a citation will look rough in the reader, it looks rough in the preview too — that is the point. See Preview an entry before publishing. The preview reflects the current draft. The published page updates on the next publish, not instantly.

A reader visiting a published page can: Read and select text — lines are individually selectable for quoting and note-taking. Link to a published record through its stable web address; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Copy citations formatted in your project's citation style. Follow media to its source — each attached media item appears with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source. Switch to dark mode (remembered in their browser). A reader cannot edit, comment on, or add anything. The reader is read-only by design.
documents.s: What a reader can do, and what they cannot

documents.t: Draft preview Published Who can see it You and colleagues with workspace access Anyone with the public URL URL Not a public URL — preview-only Stable, citable URL Visible on the public web No Yes Reflects edits On re-opening the preview after a change Only after the published snapshot next refreshes In short: the preview lets you see the reader's view without committing to it. The published view is what the world actually sees.
documents.s: Differences between draft preview and published

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A record was activated but does not appear in the reader. Activation and publication are separate steps; the record has not been published yet. Publish the record, or ask a colleague with publish access to publish it. If you are unsure who publishes in your environment, contact your environment administrator. The preview shows different formatting than the table view. The reader renders from the published layout, not from the editing surface. Some fields render differently. This is intended — the preview is the truthful render. Adjust the record to match the reader layout you want. A citation for a media item shows placeholder or incomplete values. The media record's citation fields are missing or incomplete. Open the media record and complete its citation metadata. If the citation style itself looks wrong, contact your environment administrator. A media item attached in the workspace does not appear on the published page. The published snapshot has not refreshed since the item was attached, or the item is not part of what your project publishes. Wait a short interval and re-check. If the item is still missing, contact your environment administrator. You changed a published record but the change has not surfaced in the reader. The published snapshot refreshes automatically, but small changes are not instant. Wait a short interval and re-check. If the change is overdue, contact your environment administrator. A reader reports a broken section link they previously cited. The record was restructured; the record's own URL stays stable, but links to individual sections are best-effort. Share the record's stable URL and advise the citer of the new section location. If section links break often, contact your environment administrator. The preview is blank or shows a loading state that never finishes. The preview has not yet been built for this record, or it is failing to load. Refresh and retry. If the problem persists, contact your environment administrator.

Searching and reading — how search and the reader work together inside the workspace. Adding and editing rows — how a draft becomes a real record and reaches activation. Preview an entry before publishing — the short task-shaped version of the preview workflow. Browse entries by index — switching indexes and jumping by letter. Read the references section on a published entry — what each evidence row means. Citation integrity (for environment admins) — the companion surface controlling the citation styling the reader presents. Entry surface readiness (for environment admins) — the companion surface controlling what gets published to the reader.

The Publish view is the workspace tab where your table meets its public audience. Here you decide, field by field, which parts of your records appear on published pages, check the result in a reader preview, and then publish the whole table in one pass. Read this when you are preparing a collection for first publication, when you want to keep a working field off the public page, or when edits to published records are waiting to go live. Publishing here is a whole-table action: one run builds or refreshes the public page of every ready record in the table. There is no separate publish button per record — a single new record reaches the public the same way, through a table run that refreshes what is already published and picks up what is new. How a record becomes ready in the first place — draft, activated, published — is covered in Publish a record — and why activating is not publishing.

Per-field visibility — every field in the table is set to Public, Workspace, or Private. The choice saves to the field's configuration the moment you make it and applies to every record in the table. Active. Public fields only on published pages — when a record is published, only its Public fields are included. Fields set to Workspace or Private are left out of the public page. Active. Reader preview with field highlighting — a sample of the table's records, each rendered exactly as a public reader would see it, with two-way highlighting between the field list and the preview. Active. Whole-table publishing with a progress report — one action publishes every ready record, shows progress as it runs, and ends with a receipt: how many records were published, skipped, or failed. Active. Whole-table visibility selector — the Whole table control at the top of the panel is a planning aid only; the control itself says the choice is not saved. Deferred. Preview visitor state — shown in the view but not yet available. Deferred.

Open your collection's table in the workspace and select Publish from the view tabs (alongside Table, Details, and Relations). You can also get here from a column's header menu — Open Publish view... — or by right-clicking a row and choosing Review publish field. The view has two halves: a panel on the left with the field visibility list, the preview row picker, and the publish action; and a reader preview on the right showing the selected record as a public reader would see it.

The Fields list shows every field in the table, in display order, with its label, its internal name, its field type, and a tag for the part of the published page where it appears (or not on reader if it does not render there). Each field has a three-way choice: Public — the field appears on the record's published page. Workspace — the field stays inside your project's workspace. Published pages never include it. Private — the field is marked for its owner only. Like Workspace fields, it never appears on a published page. Fields are Public unless someone restricts them, so a table publishes whole until you decide otherwise. Three things to know about changing a field's visibility: It saves immediately. There is no separate save step — pick a setting and it is stored in the field's configuration. The counts in the panel header (public, workspace, and private fields) update as you go. It is a table-wide decision. Visibility belongs to the field, not to a row. Setting a field to Workspace removes it from the published page of every record in the table. Published pages catch up at the next publish. The setting is saved at once, but a page that is already public keeps showing its last published version. Run Publish changes to apply the current visibility to every published page in the table. If a visibility change is declined — most often because your role does not include field configuration access — the control returns to its previous setting rather than showing a saved state that did not happen. The Whole table selector above the field list is a planning aid for thinking about the table's overall visibility. Its own label tells you the choice is not saved — field-level settings are the ones that count.

The row picker lists a sample of the table's records, in default record order. A note under the list tells you exactly how many of the table's records you are looking at — open the Table view to browse all records. The sample only bounds the preview; publishing always covers the whole table. Pick a record and the preview beside the panel shows it as a public reader would see it. The preview is produced by the same renderer as the public entry page, showing the record as currently saved. Two things connect the preview to the field list: Point at a field in the list and the part of the preview where it renders is highlighted and scrolled into view. Point at a part of the preview and the matching field row lights up — useful for answering "which field is this on the page?" before restricting it. Rest the pointer on the preview's content and a hint names the source column that filled that part of the page. If the preview area reports that no public reader rendering is available for a record yet, the record cannot render a public page in its current state — most often it is still a draft.

Select Publish changes to queue the run. The button needs a workspace table selected, and it works at whole-record granularity: each ready record's public page is built or refreshed in full, applying the current field visibility. While the run is in progress, the view reports how many records have been published so far, and how many were skipped or failed. When it finishes, the receipt gives the final counts: Published — records whose public page was built or refreshed. Skipped — records not ready for a public page, most often drafts. A skip is not an error. Failed — records whose page could not be built. A failure does not stop the run; the platform continues through the rest of the table, counts the failures, and shows the first error message in the receipt. The report belongs to the table you ran it on — switching to another table clears it, so a count never reads as the outcome of the wrong table. Publishing requires publish access. If Publish changes is unavailable to you, or the run is declined with a permission message, contact your environment administrator — the permissions panel page describes how access is assigned.

Both show the same saved reader rendering, so use whichever fits the task: Details panel — best while editing one record: the saved reader preview sits next to the record you are working on. See Preview an entry before publishing. Publish view — best for table-level decisions: checking how field visibility plays out across several records, spot-checking a sample, and then publishing.
documents.s: Publish view preview or Details panel preview?

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix A field you set to Workspace or Private still shows on the public page. Published pages keep their last published version; visibility changes wait for the next publish. Select Publish changes, then check the page again. A visibility setting snaps back to its previous value. The save was declined — most often your role does not include field configuration access. Contact your environment administrator. Publish changes is unavailable. No workspace table is selected, or a publish run is already in progress. Select a table from the sidebar and wait for any running publish to finish. If the button stays unavailable, your role may not include publish access — contact your environment administrator. The receipt shows skipped records. Skipped records are not ready for a public page — most often they are still drafts. Activate the drafts and publish again. See Publish a record. The run ends with a publish failed message. The publish job stopped before it finished, or some records could not be built — the receipt shows the first error. Run Publish changes again. If the same records keep failing, contact your environment administrator with the error message from the receipt. The record you want to preview is not in the row picker. The picker shows a sample of the table's records, not all of them. The sample is only for spot-checking — publishing covers the whole table regardless. To check a specific record, open it from the Table view and use the Details panel's saved reader preview.

Publish a record — and why activating is not publishing — the draft → activated → published stages, and who can publish. Preview an entry before publishing — every place a reader preview appears, including the record drawer and the import wizard. Public reader — what published pages look like from the reader's side. Adding and editing rows — drafts, activation, and editing; what makes a record ready to publish. Workspace walkthrough — the table, the Details panel, and the view tabs this page builds on.

This page is for reading a published knowledge environment from the outside — as someone who received a link, found a record through a search engine, or wants to browse a project's corpus without a workspace account. It walks through arriving at a page, reading a record, copying a citation, and moving between records. Read it if you are an external reader making sense of what you see, or if you are a researcher who wants to know exactly what a reader encounters once your project publishes. What you see depends on how the project configured its published pages. The sections below describe how the reading layer works; a given project may use all of it or a subset. For the publisher's side of this — how a record becomes a published page, and how to preview before publishing — see Public reader.

Stable, citable URLs — every published record has a stable web address, so a link shared today still resolves to the same record later. Maturity: Active. Limit: stability is per record; links to individual sections within a page are best-effort. Browsable indexes — beside searching, you can browse the whole corpus from an alphabetized index, and a project can publish more than one (for a multilingual corpus, often one by transliteration and one by original script). Maturity: Active. Limit: which indexes exist and what each row shows are set by the project. Record pages with a side contents list — a published record reads as titled sections with a navigation list down the side that highlights where you are as you scroll. Maturity: Active. Limit: how fine-grained the contents list is depends on how the record is sectioned. A references section — the evidence behind a record, one row per place the record is attested, rendered in the project's citation style. Maturity: Active. Limit: how rich each row reads depends on what the project catalogued. Copyable citations — citations are rendered in the project's citation style, defined in Citation Style Language — the same format reference managers such as Zotero understand — ready to select and paste into a bibliography. Maturity: Active. Attached media — a record lists its attached media, each item with its label and, where catalogued, a link to its source. Maturity: Active. Limit: only the media the project attached and published appears. Several values shown together — where a record keeps more than one value in a single field (several translations of a term, a transliteration beside its original-script form), the page shows them together on one line. Maturity: Active. Limit: a project can instead choose to show one value per record for such a field; showing them all is the default. Dark mode and reading-first layout — selectable text, a scholarly typeface, and a darker color scheme you can switch to, remembered in your browser. Maturity: Active.
