The workspace keeps several kinds of memory working for you at once: an undo history for changes to how a table is displayed, a browser-side memory of where you left off, and account-level memory of how you organized your sidebar. They behave differently — some are yours alone, some are shared with everyone in your environment. This page explains which is which, so you know what Undo can bring back, why the workspace opens where it does, and why your screen may not match a colleague's.

Undo and redo for view changes (Active) — the table toolbar's Undo and Redo buttons step backward and forward through changes to the active view: filters, sort order, column layout, row color rules, and row density. The history holds up to 20 steps. Confirmation instead of undo for deletion (Active) — deleting a saved view asks you to confirm, right on the view's tab. Deletions never enter the undo history. Shared default view wins for first entry (Active) — each table has one shared default saved view, including its view kind: Table, Details, Relations, Publish, or Media where available. Last concrete view remembered per table (Active) — the browser you are using can remember a specific non-default view tab you last opened in a table. That memory does not replace the table's shared default view kind. Sidebar size remembered per browser (Active) — how wide you made the sidebar, and whether you collapsed it to the icon rail. Sidebar organization saved with your account (Active) — pinned tables, named groups, your table order, which groups you collapsed, and your recently opened tables are stored with your sign-in, not in the browser.

The Undo and Redo buttons sit in the table toolbar, so they are available while the Table tab is active. They cover view changes — changes to how the table is displayed: filters — adding a condition, changing one, or removing it sort order column layout — order, visibility, pinning, and widths row color rules row density Each press of Undo steps back one change, up to 20 steps; Redo re-applies what you undid. Both are also available from the command palette — press Ctrl/Cmd+K and choose Undo view change or Redo view change; the entries appear only when there is something to step through. Undo does more than change your screen. Changes to a view are stored on the view as you go, and the arrangement Undo restores is stored the same way — so a collaborator who opens the view next sees it as you restored it. What Undo does not cover: the records themselves. Editing a value in a cell or in the record panel is a change to your data, not to the view, and the toolbar's Undo will not revert it. To fix a value, edit it again — see Adding and editing rows.
documents.s: What Undo covers — and what it does not

documents.t: Deletions never enter the undo history. Quietly bringing something back with an undo button is the wrong shape for an action that affects everyone in your environment — so the workspace asks before, not after. Deleting a saved view shows a confirmation step on the view's tab itself, and a deleted view is gone for everyone who works in the environment. When you want to experiment with a shared view, Duplicate it first and work on the copy.
documents.s: Why deletions are confirmed, not undone

documents.t: The undo history is short-lived on purpose: it covers what you changed since you arrived at the current view. It starts fresh when you switch to a different view tab or table, and when you reload the page or open the workspace in a new tab. Undo is for the small reversals — the column you hid by mistake, the sort that was not what you wanted. For an arrangement you care about keeping, save it as a view; views remember filters, sort, columns, density, and row colors durably. The workspace walkthrough covers saved views in detail.
documents.s: When the undo history starts over

documents.t: Open a table without naming a view in the address, and the table's shared default view is the starting point. That default includes its view kind — for example, a table can open directly in Table or Details if that is the default view's mode. The browser you are using can also remember a concrete non-default view you opened in that table. That memory is kept per table, in that browser — a different computer, a different browser, or a private window starts fresh. It does not turn the default view into a private personal default. Two things always win over this memory: An explicit link. A view link a colleague sends you opens exactly the view in the link, not your remembered one. The shared default. If no concrete saved-view link or remembered concrete view applies, the workspace uses the table's default view and its view kind. A removed view. If the view you last used no longer exists, the workspace falls back to the table's default view. The sidebar's size is browser-side memory too: its width, and whether you collapsed it to the icon rail, are restored the next time you open the workspace in the same browser. Some things are deliberately not remembered: the toolbar's quick filter text and your row selection clear when you move to another table or view, so you never land on yesterday's narrowing without noticing.
documents.s: What the browser you are using remembers

documents.t: How you organized the sidebar — pinned tables, named groups, the order of your tables, which groups you collapsed, and your recently opened tables — is stored with your sign-in for this environment rather than in the browser. Resizing the sidebar stays with the browser; organizing it stays with you.

Saved views are shared — everyone in your environment sees the same view tabs. Which tab you land on can still differ when one browser follows a concrete view link or remembers a concrete non-default view, while another browser starts from the table's default. You are both looking at the same shared set of views, opened at different tabs. To get back to the shared starting point, select the default view — the first tab in the view tab row. Each table has exactly one default view; Set as default in a view tab's menu changes which view that is, for everyone.
documents.s: Why you and a colleague may not see the same view

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix The Undo button is grayed out. Nothing has changed since you arrived at this view — the history starts over when you switch views or tables, or reload. Re-apply the change by hand. For arrangements you want to keep, save them as a view. Undo did not revert an edit to a record's value. Undo covers view changes only; edits to data are outside it. Edit the value again in the cell or the record panel — see Adding and editing rows. The workspace opened on a different view than your colleague sees. One of you followed a concrete view link or had a remembered concrete view; the other started from the shared default. Select the same view tab, or open the same view link. The workspace did not return you to your last view. You opened a link that names a view, you are in a different browser or a private window, the remembered view was removed, or the shared default view is taking precedence. Open the view's tab again, or ask your team which view should be the default. The sidebar looks different on another computer. Sidebar width and collapse are remembered per browser; only its organization follows your account. Resize or collapse the sidebar once on the new computer — your groups, pins, and table order are already with your account. A deleted view is not in the undo history. Deletions are never undoable, and deleting a view removes it for everyone in the environment. Recreate the view, and next time Duplicate a shared view before experimenting on it.

Workspace walkthrough — every control mentioned here: views, filters, columns, the command palette. Adding and editing rows — how record values are edited and saved. Accessibility — density mode and other display-comfort controls.

The workspace is the table of records of one type — figures, terms, manuscript editions, anything your project tracks — wrapped in a toolbar, a left sidebar, and a set of view tabs. This page walks through what is on the screen, what each control does, and what a typical session looks like. Read it when you first open the workspace, when a control is doing something you did not expect, or when you want to set up a view you can come back to.

Workspace layout (Active) — every table opens in the same shell: a left sidebar listing your tables, a top bar with search and the command palette, a toolbar of table controls, and view tabs that switch between Table, Details, Relations, and Publish. Workspace search (Active) — a quick search panel that finds records across the workspace, grouped by table. Results respect your permissions. When search cannot run, the panel says workspace search is unavailable rather than showing empty results. Search & Read section (Active) — a full search page with a typeahead, an advanced field-condition filter, paged results, and a reading pane that opens a record beside the list. The page address encodes the whole search, so it can be shared or bookmarked. Rows named by your display field (Active) — record labels in the table, the record panel, and search results use the display field your source declared, with a sensible fallback when none is declared. Sidebar organizer and command palette (Active) — pin tables, create named groups, collapse or expand groups, see your recently opened tables, and reset the sidebar to its defaults. The command palette reaches all of these without leaving the keyboard. Current-table quick filter (Active) — a toolbar box that narrows the rows already loaded in the active table. It is not a whole-workspace search. Filters (Active) — composable filter conditions per field. The filter options match the field's type: text fields match typed text, number and year fields take a number, Date fields open a date picker, and choice fields offer their options. Active filters appear as removable chips. Column manager (Active) — reorder, show or hide, search columns, and choose the display column; resize by dragging column edges in the table, and pin columns from the column header menu. Saved views (Active) — named tabs that remember filters, sort, column layout, density, and row colors. Views belong to the table and are shared with everyone who works in your environment. Per-view sharing permissions are not yet available. Density toggle (Active) — compact, cozy, or comfortable row height, remembered per view. Record panel (Active) — open any record to see every field with its editor, related records, and a preview of the saved public page. Fields composed from other fields are labeled read-only — they cannot be edited directly. Batch actions (Active) — select rows from the table grid, then copy them to your clipboard or export them as a file. Buttons labeled "Backend pending" — such as batch delete and batch visibility — are visible but not yet available. Copy view link (Active) — copies a URL that opens the same view for a collaborator, subject to their own permissions.

Your knowledge environment has a sidebar listing the record types you can work with. Click one and you land in its workspace at /app/workspace/<record-type>/. You can bookmark and share the URL. If your project has several record types, each has its own workspace.

Find a record across the workspace. Click Search database… in the top bar, or press Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F. Type at least two characters. Choose Current table when you know the table, or All workspace when you do not — and in workspace scope you can still narrow to one table with the Table selector. Results are grouped by table; move with the arrow keys and press Enter, or click a result to open that record. The panel's Filter current table button hands your search words to the table's quick filter instead. When you want to browse and read many records at once, Open full Search & Read in the panel — or Search & Read in the command palette — opens the full search page, carrying your words over; see Searching and reading. Organize the left sidebar. Pin the tables you use most, gather tables into named groups, and collapse the groups you are not using. Recent lists the tables you opened last. Useful shortcuts: Ctrl/Cmd+K opens the command palette, Ctrl/Cmd+B collapses the sidebar to an icon rail, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+G creates a group, and Shift+S pins or unpins the current table. Reset sidebar to default groups in the command palette puts everything back. Filter the table in front of you. Use the toolbar Filter visible rows box when you only need to narrow rows already loaded in the active table. This quick filter is transient and is not stored with the view. Add filters to narrow. Click Filter and pick a field. The options match the field's type — type a word for text fields, type a number for numeric fields, pick a calendar date for Date fields, or pick options for choice fields. A Date filter matches stored timestamps that fall on the same calendar date; a field that only looks like a timestamp but is still configured as Text keeps text-style matching. The match count updates as you set the condition. Filter chips appear in the toolbar after the "filtering by" lead-in. They compose. Remove a chip by clicking its ×; remove all of them with Clear. Tidy the columns. Click Columns to open the column manager: drag entries to reorder, uncheck columns to hide them, search by label or field key, and choose the display column. Resize a column by dragging its edge in the table itself. Pinning and wrap-text controls live in each column's header menu. Save the arrangement as a view. Views are the tabs above the table. Click + Add view, give it a name like "18th-century figures with manuscript citations", and it starts from your current arrangement. From then on, changes you make while that view is active — filters, sort, columns, density — are stored on the view as you go. The toolbar's Undo and Redo step view changes backward and forward. Open a record. Click the row's Open details button (at the row's actions end) and the record panel opens over the table: every field with its editor, related records, and a preview of the saved public page. Close it with the × in its header, with Escape, or by clicking outside it. Edit in the table. Double-click a cell to edit it. Short values save when you press Enter or move away; larger editors — long text, formatted text — have their own Save and Cancel buttons. Empty cells show empty so blanks are visible without looking like punctuation. Date fields use a date picker and display readable dates; text fields that contain timestamp-shaped strings stay raw text until the field type is changed or converted. If a value cannot be saved, the workspace tells you rather than silently dropping it.
documents.s: The default flow: search, filter, open, edit

documents.t: Switch to the Details tab. It splits the screen: a list of the table's records on one side and the full record on the other. Click through the list and the record pane follows; the list can be narrowed with its own filter box, so you can audit a slice or fact-check a draft against its neighbors without losing your place.

Focus a row and press Space to select it. Use Ctrl/Cmd+Space to add or remove the focused row, and Shift with the arrow keys to extend the selection through a range. A batch toolbar appears showing the count. Copy TSV puts the rows on your clipboard, ready to paste into a spreadsheet. Download CSV downloads the selected records as a spreadsheet file, and JSON exports the raw row payload for technical workflows. Buttons labeled "Backend pending" are not yet available. Clear the selection with the toolbar's × or with Escape.
Click Copy link in the toolbar, or Copy view link in a view tab's menu. Paste the URL into chat or email. Your collaborator opens it and lands on the same view, subject to their own permissions.
documents.s: Sharing a view with a collaborator

documents.t: A saved view remembers filters and their values, sort order, column layout (order, widths, pinning, hidden columns), row density, and row color rules. It does not remember the quick-filter text — that stays per-session so you do not accidentally land on yesterday's search. Views belong to the table, not to you alone: everyone working in your environment sees the same view tabs, and changes to a view reach your collaborators too. Each view's tab menu offers Rename, Duplicate, Pin view, Set as default (the view the table opens with), Copy view link, and Delete view. Deleting a view removes it for everyone, so agree with your collaborators first — Duplicate is the safe way to experiment on a shared view.
documents.s: What saved views remember (and how they are shared)

documents.t: Symptom Likely cause Fix Where to escalate A control mentioned here is missing or grayed out. The control depends on your role, or on a capability not yet available — grayed controls often say "Backend pending". Hover the control; its tooltip states the reason. Contact your environment administrator. Columns you arranged reverted later. The changes were made outside a saved view, so nothing stored them. Click + Add view, name it, and arrange columns while that view is active — changes then stick. n/a Search returns matches in an unexpected language or script form. The field stores several language or script forms, and search matches any of them. This is the intended behavior; see Searching and reading. Contact your environment administrator if matching is wrong for your project. The top search finds a row but the toolbar box does not. They are different tools: the top search looks across the workspace, while the toolbar box only filters rows already loaded in the current table. Open the result from the top search, or switch to the right table before using the toolbar filter. n/a The search panel says workspace search is unavailable. Your role does not include workspace search, or the search request failed. Try the search again; in the meantime, use the toolbar quick filter on the current table. Contact your environment administrator. Editing a cell does nothing. The field is read-only — composed fields, for example, cannot be edited directly — or the value was rejected. Open the record panel and check the field there; rejected values show a message instead of saving silently. Contact your environment administrator about permissions. The record panel will not close. A confirmation dialog is open and is catching the Escape key. Dismiss the dialog first, then press Escape. n/a
